rules.reference: Appellate courts cannot reverse findings on unframed issues of fact
rules.relevance: The court held that an appellate court cannot reverse a trial court's decree based on a factual finding (hardship) when the issue was not framed and no evidence was led to substantiate it.

rules.reference: Hardship as a defense requires pleading and evidence
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that hardship is a substantive defense that must be specifically taken by the defendant and supported by evidence on record to be considered.

rules.reference: Specific performance requires cancellation of subsequent sale deed
rules.relevance: The court held that a suit for specific performance cannot be maintained if a subsequent sale deed exists and the plaintiff has not sought its cancellation.

rules.case_name: Gomathinayagam Pillai & Ors. vs Palaniswami Nadar
rules.reference: Gomathinayagam Pillai & Ors. vs Palaniswami Nadar
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that a purchaser does not need to produce money or a concluded financing scheme to prove readiness and willingness.

rules.case_name: Katta Sujatha Reddy v. Siddamsetty Infra Projects (P) Ltd. & Ors.
rules.reference: Katta Sujatha Reddy v. Siddamsetty Infra Projects (P) Ltd. & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that the 2018 Amendment to the Specific Relief Act is prospective and does not apply to transactions occurring prior to its enforcement.

rules.reference: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal Rules, 2016
rules.relevance: Stipulates that in computing time, the day from which the period is to be reckoned shall be excluded.

rules.reference: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal Rules, 2016
rules.relevance: Mandates that every appeal must be accompanied by a certified copy of the impugned order.

rules.case_name: V Nagarajan v. SKS Ispat and Power Limited & Ors
rules.reference: V Nagarajan v. SKS Ispat and Power Limited & Ors
rules.relevance: Established that limitation commences upon pronouncement and time for obtaining a certified copy is excluded only if an application is made within the limitation period; distinguished on facts as the appellant here had applied for the copy.

rules.case_name: Sagufa Ahmed v. Upper Assam Plywood Products Pvt Ltd
rules.reference: Sagufa Ahmed v. Upper Assam Plywood Products Pvt Ltd
rules.relevance: Held that under the Companies Act, limitation runs from when the copy is made available. The court distinguished this, noting the IBC is a special code with stricter timelines and different statutory language.

rules.reference: Companies Act, 2013
rules.relevance: Section 420(3) mandates free copies, and Section 421(3) starts limitation from when the copy is 'made available'. The court distinguished these from the IBC, holding that the specific language in the Companies Act does not apply to the IBC due to the latter's overriding effect and different legislative intent regarding speed.

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: The court analyzed this rule to determine the procedure for hearing appeals and the timing for formulating questions of law.

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure Amendment Act, 1976
rules.relevance: The court considered this saving clause to determine if the amended Section 100 applied to an appeal admitted before the amendment came into force.

rules.case_name: Kanai Lal Garari And Others v. Murari Ganguly And Others
rules.reference: Kanai Lal Garari And Others v. Murari Ganguly And Others
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to establish that the High Court is obliged to formulate a substantial question of law at the beginning of the hearing.

rules.reference: Constructive Possession in Gift Deeds
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that when a property is tenanted, constructive possession is handed over upon execution of the gift deed, satisfying the requirement of delivery of possession.

rules.case_name: Surat Singh (Dead) vs. Siri Bhagwan & Ors.
rules.reference: Surat Singh (Dead) vs. Siri Bhagwan & Ors.
rules.relevance: Cited to support the principle that the High Court's power to hear an appeal on additional substantial questions of law under the proviso to Section 100(5) is exercisable only after assigning reasons for framing such additional questions.

rules.case_name: Enforcement Directorate vs. Preeti Chandra
rules.citation: Order dated 04.08.2023 in SLP (Crl.) No. 7409 of 2023
rules.reference: Enforcement Directorate vs. Preeti Chandra
rules.relevance: Confirmed that the proviso to Section 45 of the PMLA confers discretion on the court to grant bail to women, rather than creating a mandatory right.

rules.case_name: Nikesh Tarachand Shah v. Union of India
rules.reference: Nikesh Tarachand Shah v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Struck down the twin conditions in Section 45 of PMLA as unconstitutional, leading to amendments in the bail provisions.

rules.case_name: Shri Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and others v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Shri Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and others v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Established that anticipatory bail cannot be sought after arrest, rendering the SLP in the CBI case infructuous.

rules.reference: Duty of advocates as officers of the court
rules.relevance: Advocates must make full and correct disclosure of material facts and assist the court fairly; misrepresentation of facts is strongly deprecated.

rules.case_name: Directorate of Enforcement v. Ashok Kumar Jain
rules.reference: Directorate of Enforcement v. Ashok Kumar Jain
rules.relevance: Held that in economic offences, the accused is not entitled to anticipatory bail.

rules.case_name: Kailash v. Nanhku
rules.reference: Procedure is the handmaid of justice
rules.relevance: Procedural provisions should be construed to advance the cause of justice rather than subvert it, supporting the view that the Registrar's acceptance of the opposition implied an extension of time.

rules.reference: Trade Marks Act, 1999
rules.relevance: Provides that where validity is questioned in an infringement suit, the issue shall be determined only on an application for rectification made to the Appellate Board, notwithstanding Section 57.

rules.reference: Appellate Court's Power to Re-appreciate Evidence
rules.relevance: While appellate courts generally do not re-appreciate evidence when lower courts have concurrent findings, they may intervene if the prosecution story is inherently impossible of belief or contains mutually destructive statements.

rules.reference: Trade Marks Act, 1999
rules.relevance: Establishes that there is one Controller-General who is the Registrar of Trade Marks, with Assistant Registrars acting under his superintendence, validating jurisdiction across locations.

rules.case_name: Collector of Central Excise, Patna & Ors. v. J.T.C. Limited & Anr.
rules.reference: Collector of Central Excise, Patna & Ors. v. J.T.C. Limited & Anr.
rules.relevance: Cited to support the proposition that show-cause notice and personal hearing are necessary before saddling an assessee with additional demand.

rules.case_name: Bhoop Singh Vs. Ram Singh Major and Others
rules.reference: Bhoop Singh Vs. Ram Singh Major and Others
rules.relevance: Established that a compromise decree requires registration only if it creates a new right in praesenti or is collusive; if it declares pre-existing rights, it does not require registration.

rules.case_name: Phool Patti and Another v. Ram Singh (Dead) Through Lrs. and Another
rules.reference: Phool Patti and Another v. Ram Singh (Dead) Through Lrs. and Another
rules.relevance: Confirmed that there is no inconsistency between Bhoop Singh and K. Raghunandan, reinforcing the principle that the presence of pre-existing rights exempts the decree from registration.

rules.case_name: K. Raghunandan and Others v. Ali Hussain Sabir and Others
rules.reference: K. Raghunandan and Others v. Ali Hussain Sabir and Others
rules.relevance: Distinguished on the basis that it involved neighbors without pre-existing rights, whereas the present case involves family members with antecedent titles.

rules.case_name: Gurdwara Sahib Vs. Gram Panchayat Village Sirthala and Another
rules.reference: Gurdwara Sahib Vs. Gram Panchayat Village Sirthala and Another
rules.relevance: The High Court relied on this case to argue that adverse possession cannot be the basis of a declaratory suit, implying no pre-existing title. The Supreme Court noted this view was incorrect.

rules.case_name: Ravinder Kaur Grewal and Others Vs. Manjit Kaur and Others
rules.reference: Ravinder Kaur Grewal and Others Vs. Manjit Kaur and Others
rules.relevance: Expressly overruled Gurdwara Sahib, holding that adverse possession can be used as a 'sword' to claim title, thereby validating the existence of pre-existing rights acquired through adverse possession.

rules.case_name: Mehboob Ali & Another Vs. State of Rajasthan
rules.reference: Mehboob Ali & Another Vs. State of Rajasthan
rules.relevance: Interprets Sections 25, 26, and 27 of the Evidence Act regarding the inadmissibility of confessions made to police.

rules.case_name: Roy Fernandes vs. State of Goa and Others
rules.reference: Roy Fernandes vs. State of Goa and Others
rules.relevance: Explains the two parts of Section 149 IPC: acts committed in prosecution of the common object and acts known to be likely to be committed.

rules.case_name: Rai Sandeep @ Deepu alias Deepu Vs. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: Rai Sandeep @ Deepu alias Deepu Vs. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: Establishes the standard for a 'sterling witness' whose testimony must be consistent, natural, and withstand cross-examination.

rules.case_name: Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Establishes the double test for accomplice evidence: reliability of the witness and sufficient corroboration in material particulars.

rules.reference: Indian Evidence Act, 1872
rules.relevance: Documents must be proved by primary evidence (the original). The uncertified carbon copy of the post-mortem report was inadmissible as it did not fall under exceptions in Section 65.

rules.case_name: UCO Bank & Anr v. Rajinder Lal Capoor
rules.reference: UCO Bank & Anr v. Rajinder Lal Capoor
rules.relevance: Cited alongside Swedish Match to support the proposition that respondents can rely on materials on record to support a judgment.

rules.reference: Distinction between daily wagers and regular employees
rules.relevance: Daily wagers are entitled to minimum wages but not full back wages or substantive reinstatement like regular staff, as they do not hold a permanent post.

rules.reference: Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Establishes that the respondent Corporation is a 'State' entity obligated to follow constitutional requirements of equality and non-arbitrariness in public employment and recruitment rules.

rules.reference: Pleadings are not proof
rules.relevance: Establishes that allegations in a written statement, such as loss of confidence, must be substantiated by evidence to be legally effective.

rules.case_name: Swedish Match AB and Anr. v. Securities and Exchange Board, India & Anr.
rules.reference: Swedish Match AB and Anr. v. Securities and Exchange Board, India & Anr.
rules.relevance: Supports the application of principles akin to Order 41 Rule 33 CPC to allow respondents to support judgments based on record materials.

rules.case_name: Anurag Soni v. State of Chhattisgarh
rules.reference: Anurag Soni v. State of Chhattisgarh
rules.relevance: Distinguishes between a false promise made with no intention to marry (vitiating consent) and a breach of a promise made in good faith.

rules.reference: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
rules.relevance: The court examined whether these provisions, inserted by the 2015 Amendment Act, applied to acts committed in 2015 before the amendment came into force.

rules.case_name: Naim Ahamed v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: Naim Ahamed v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: Established that a mature, married woman who has consensual relations for years cannot claim rape based on a false promise to marry, as her consent is not vitiated by misconception of fact.

rules.reference: Consent and Misconception of Fact
rules.relevance: A mature and intelligent woman who knowingly enters into a relationship, even during the subsistence of her marriage, cannot claim that her consent was obtained under a misconception of fact regarding a promise to marry.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: The specific charge of rape under which the FIR was registered.

rules.reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology by Dr. K.S. Narayan Reddy
rules.relevance: The court referred to this treatise to distinguish medical signs of strangulation/asphyxia from pure burn injuries.

rules.case_name: The State of Uttar Pradesh v. Dr. Ravindra Prakash Mishra
rules.reference: The State of Uttar Pradesh v. Dr. Ravindra Prakash Mishra
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent for the cardinal principles governing conviction based on circumstantial evidence.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code
rules.relevance: The court upheld the conviction for cruelty by the husband and his relatives on account of dowry.

rules.case_name: Balwinder Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Balwinder Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that extra-judicial confession is weak evidence requiring care and caution.

rules.reference: Extra-judicial confession as weak evidence
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that extra-judicial confessions are weak evidence, must be voluntary and truthful, and require independent corroboration to sustain a conviction.

rules.case_name: Natasha Singh vs. CBI (State)
rules.reference: Natasha Singh vs. CBI (State)
rules.relevance: Stated that power must be exercised judiciously to determine truth, not to fill lacunae, change the nature of the case, or cause prejudice to the defense.

rules.case_name: U. T. of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Anr. vs. Fatehsinh Mohansinh Chauhan
rules.reference: U. T. of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Anr. vs. Fatehsinh Mohansinh Chauhan
rules.relevance: Clarified that recalling a witness to find truth is not 'filling a lacuna' unless it causes serious prejudice to the accused resulting in miscarriage of justice.

rules.case_name: Jamatraj Kewalji Govani vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Jamatraj Kewalji Govani vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Established that the power under Section 311 is to be exercised if the court thinks new evidence is needed for a just decision, not merely because the accused brought it suddenly.

rules.case_name: Vipan Kumar Dhir v. State of Punjab and Anr.
rules.reference: Vipan Kumar Dhir v. State of Punjab and Anr.
rules.relevance: The court used this case to explain the impact of supervening circumstances, such as interference in the administration of justice, warranting bail cancellation.

rules.case_name: Natasha Singh v. CBI
rules.reference: Natasha Singh v. CBI
rules.relevance: Clarifies that the power under Section 311 must be exercised judiciously to meet the ends of justice, and the determinative factor is whether the evidence is essential for a just decision.

rules.reference: Equitable principles in contract enforcement
rules.relevance: The court held that there is no basis in principle to hold a housing authority to rates from 1992 after a significant delay and failure by the allottee to pay.

rules.reference: Consumer Protection Act, 1986
rules.relevance: The court determined that the complaint was filed beyond the prescribed period of limitation, rendering it time-barred.

rules.reference: Actus curiae nemini gravabit
rules.relevance: The court relied on this maxim (the act of Court/office shall prejudice no man) to support the principle that a party should not suffer due to office closures or holidays.

rules.case_name: Hossein Ally v. Donzelle
rules.reference: Hossein Ally v. Donzelle
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that law does not compel the performance of an impossibility, supporting the application of the holiday rule.

rules.case_name: Sambasiva Chari v. Ramaswami Reddi
rules.reference: Sambasiva Chari v. Ramaswami Reddi
rules.relevance: Cited for the general principle that a party prevented from doing an act by circumstances beyond their control can do so at the first subsequent opportunity.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: This section permits rent enhancement if the landlord makes improvements. The court analyzed its applicability, noting the improvements were made by the tenant, but used the principle to justify a reasonable rent increase.

rules.reference: Unconditional Tender
rules.relevance: For relief under Section 20(4), the payment or tender must be unconditional; a deposit made while disputing the liability for arrears does not constitute an unconditional tender.

rules.reference: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: Establishes the ground for eviction when a tenant is in arrears of rent for not less than four months and fails to pay within one month of a notice of demand.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: The court considered whether this provision allowed for rent enhancement via oral agreement, concluding it was inapplicable due to the lack of written evidence.

rules.reference: Pleading of Waiver
rules.relevance: A plea of waiver must be specifically raised in the written statement; a court cannot decide on waiver if it is not pleaded by the party.

rules.case_name: MIS Shankar Finance and Investment v. State of A.P & Ors.
rules.reference: MIS Shankar Finance and Investment v. State of A.P & Ors.
rules.relevance: Establishes that a power of attorney holder cannot depose in place of the principal.

rules.case_name: Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao & Anr.
rules.reference: Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao & Anr.
rules.relevance: Establishes that a power of attorney holder cannot depose in place of the principal.

rules.case_name: Man Kaur v. Hartar Singh Sangha
rules.reference: Man Kaur v. Hartar Singh Sangha
rules.relevance: Establishes that a power of attorney holder cannot depose in place of the principal.

rules.provision: Order 6 Rule 3 and Form No. 47, Clause 3
rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure
rules.relevance: Requires strict conformity in pleadings regarding readiness and willingness; the plaint must explicitly state the plaintiff 'has been and still is' ready and willing.

rules.case_name: Janki Vashdeo Bhojwani & Anr. vs. Indusind Bank Ltd. & Ors.
rules.reference: Janki Vashdeo Bhojwani & Anr. vs. Indusind Bank Ltd. & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that a Power of Attorney holder cannot depose for the principal regarding matters of personal knowledge and that non-appearance of the principal raises a presumption against their case.

rules.case_name: Parkash Chand v. State of Himachal Pradesh
rules.reference: Parkash Chand v. State of Himachal Pradesh
rules.relevance: Clarified the essential ingredients of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, including the requirement of no undue advantage or cruel manner.

rules.case_name: Rakesh Kumar alias Babli v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Rakesh Kumar alias Babli v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Supported the view that replies to suggestions in cross-examination can establish the presence of the accused at the scene of the crime.

rules.case_name: Tarun Bora alias Alok Hazarika v. State of Assam
rules.reference: Tarun Bora alias Alok Hazarika v. State of Assam
rules.relevance: Held that suggestions made by defence counsel in cross-examination, if answered in a way that admits facts, can bind the accused and establish presence.

rules.case_name: V. Sreedharan vs. State of Kerala
rules.reference: V. Sreedharan vs. State of Kerala
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to support the view that an incident arising from provocation and resulting in fatal injuries should be prosecuted under Section 304 Part I rather than Section 302 IPC.

rules.reference: Burden of explaining injuries on defense witnesses
rules.relevance: The court held that the prosecution is not called upon to explain injuries on a defense witness if there is no evidence connecting those injuries to the incident.

rules.case_name: Bhikoba Shankar Dhuma (dead) by Lrs. and Others v. Mohan Lal Punchand Tathed and Others
rules.reference: Bhikoba Shankar Dhuma v. Mohan Lal Punchand Tathed
rules.relevance: Holds that surplus land must be determined as on the appointed day even if the holder dies before determination, and liability attaches to the holding.

rules.case_name: Raghunath Luman Wani v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Raghunath Luman Wani v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that ceiling area is determined with reference to the appointed day and does not fluctuate with subsequent changes in family composition or death.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960
rules.relevance: Establishes that no tenure-holder is entitled to hold land in excess of the ceiling area from the commencement date, fixing the liability based on holdings on that specific date.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Rules, 1961
rules.relevance: Provides that if a tenure-holder dies before notice, the authority proceeds against legal representatives as if they were the tenure-holder, determining the ceiling area applicable to the deceased.

rules.reference: U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960
rules.relevance: This provision generally ignores transfers made after January 24, 1971, unless they are proved to be in good faith and for adequate consideration. The court analyzed this in conjunction with Section 5(8) to determine if the exception applied.

rules.case_name: State of Gujarat v. C.G. Desai
rules.reference: State of Gujarat v. C.G. Desai
rules.relevance: Established that service as a Supervisor cannot be counted towards experience required for promotion as a Junior Engineer.

rules.reference: Andhra Pradesh State and Subordinate Service Rules
rules.relevance: Permits temporary appointments to fill emergent vacancies when regular recruitment is delayed.

rules.reference: Andhra Pradesh State and Subordinate Service Rules
rules.relevance: States that seniority is determined by the date of first appointment to the service, class, or category.

rules.reference: G.O. Ms. No. 647
rules.relevance: Dictates that regularization takes effect from the date following the 'last regular appointment' or the date of temporary appointment, whichever is later.

rules.reference: Andhra Pradesh State and Subordinate Service Rules
rules.relevance: Provides for limited recruitment for SC/ST candidates if qualified candidates are not available in general recruitment.

rules.reference: Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985
rules.relevance: The majority interpreted this note, read with HSN explanatory notes, to require labels or indications of use as hair oil, which were absent. The dissenting judge interpreted it to mean suitability for use and retail packing.

rules.reference: Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985
rules.relevance: The dissenting judge relied on this note to argue that goods classifiable under Heading 3305 cannot be classified under any other heading.

rules.reference: Harmonised System of Nomenclature (HSN) as a safe guide
rules.relevance: The majority relied on HSN explanatory notes to interpret Chapter Note 3, while the dissenting judge held that CETA notes prevail over HSN when they differ.

rules.reference: Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985
rules.relevance: The Revenue and the dissenting judge argued for classification under this heading for 'preparations for use on the hair'.

rules.provision: Rule 3 of General Rules for Interpretation
rules.reference: Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985
rules.relevance: The majority held it inapplicable as the product was not classifiable under two headings; the dissenting judge applied Rule 3(c) to prefer the later numerical order.

rules.provision: Clause 10: Candidates must vacate their present course seat by 5:00 PM the previous day to participate in subsequent counsellings.
rules.reference: Christian Medical College Prospectus
rules.relevance: The court examined this rule to confirm the Petitioner had complied with procedural requirements to be eligible for the third counselling.

rules.reference: Strict adherence to admission time schedule
rules.relevance: The court relied on this principle to deny the specific relief of mid-stream admission, as the admission schedule fixed by the Medical Council of India and the Court had concluded.

rules.provision: Refund Rules: Full fee refund if seat is filled; otherwise, the candidate pays for the entire duration.
rules.reference: Christian Medical College Prospectus
rules.relevance: The court considered this rule to identify a potential financial motive for the CMC's conduct, as filling the seat with a sponsored candidate would trigger a refund of the high N.R.I. fees.

rules.provision: Filling up of vacant seats: 'Vacant Seats arising in the N.R.I. Category will be filled from the Sponsored Category.'
rules.reference: Christian Medical College Prospectus
rules.relevance: The court used this provision to establish that the CMC was obligated to offer the vacant N.R.I. seat to the sponsored category candidate and could not arbitrarily withhold it.

rules.reference: Compensation for institutional misconduct
rules.relevance: The court awarded compensation to remedy the grave injustice caused by the CMC's arbitrary and irresponsible conduct in depriving the Petitioner of her lawful right.

rules.case_name: Prakash Singh Badal and Another Vs. State of Punjab and Others
rules.reference: Prakash Singh Badal and Another Vs. State of Punjab and Others
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to hold that offences like cheating (Section 420) are not committed in the discharge of official duty, thus sanction under Section 197 Cr.P.C. is not required.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.)
rules.relevance: The court examined whether sanction under this section was mandatory for prosecuting a public servant for offences under Sections 420, 406, and 161 IPC.

rules.case_name: Rakesh Kumar Mishra Vs. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Rakesh Kumar Mishra Vs. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case, noting it was considered and effectively overruled in Prakash Singh Badal regarding the requirement of sanction for certain offences.

rules.case_name: Rajendra Kumar Sitaram Pande and Others Vs. Uttam and Another
rules.reference: Rajendra Kumar Sitaram Pande and Others Vs. Uttam and Another
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to hold that an order directing issuance of process is quasi-final and subject to revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 Cr.P.C.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code (IPC)
rules.relevance: These were the offences for which the respondent was summoned, forming the basis for the dispute regarding the necessity of sanction.

rules.reference: Proximity and Mens Rea in Abetment

rules.case_name: Geo Varghese Vs. State of Rajasthan and Another
rules.reference: Geo Varghese Vs. State of Rajasthan and Another
rules.relevance: Established that 'instigation' means to goad, urge forward, provoke, incite, or encourage to do an act.

rules.case_name: Hans Raj v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Hans Raj v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Explained that Section 113-A gives discretion to the court to presume abetment based on the nature of cruelty and other circumstances.

rules.case_name: State of Himachal Pradesh v. Gian Chand
rules.reference: State of Himachal Pradesh v. Gian Chand
rules.relevance: Established that delay in lodging FIR is not fatal if a plausible explanation is offered and accepted.

rules.case_name: Ravinder Kumar and Anr. v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Ravinder Kumar and Anr. v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Highlighted genuine causes for delay in FIR, such as grief, ignorance, or lack of transport, particularly in rural settings.

rules.case_name: C.M. Arumugam v. S. Rajgopal and others
rules.reference: C.M. Arumugam v. S. Rajgopal and others

rules.case_name: S. Ambalagan v. B. Devarajan & Ors.
rules.reference: S. Ambalagan v. B. Devarajan & Ors.

rules.relevance: Establishes that a child born to Christian parents is not bound by their religion upon reaching discretion and can revive caste status through genuine reconversion and community acceptance.

rules.case_name: Dr. Anand Teltumbde v. National Investigation Agency
rules.reference: Dr. Anand Teltumbde v. National Investigation Agency
rules.relevance: Provided interpretation of Section 20 and highlighted the insufficiency of similar account statement evidence in a comparable case.

rules.case_name: National Investigation Agency vs. Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali
rules.reference: National Investigation Agency vs. Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali

rules.case_name: Jayendra Saraswathi Swamigal v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.reference: Jayendra Saraswathi Swamigal v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.relevance: Outlined factors for granting bail, including the nature of the offence, character of evidence, and delay.

rules.case_name: Angela Harish Sontakke v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Angela Harish Sontakke v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Relied upon for granting bail under UAPA despite Section 43-D(5) due to five years' incarceration and large number of witnesses.

rules.case_name: Sagar Tatyaram Gorkhe v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Sagar Tatyaram Gorkhe v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Relied upon for granting bail under UAPA due to four years' incarceration and unexamined witnesses.

rules.reference: Competitive Bidding Guidelines

rules.case_name: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited v. Adani Power Maharashtra Limited and Others
rules.reference: MSEDCL v. APML and Others
rules.relevance: Decided common issues in the batch, holding that Change in Law relief should be computed on 'actuals' against 100% of the normative coal requirement assured under NCDP 2007, and that the start date for relief is 1st April 2013.

rules.reference: National Coal Distribution Policy, 2013
rules.relevance: Identified as the 'Change in Law' event that altered the assured coal quantity, triggering the compensation claim.

rules.reference: National Coal Distribution Policy, 2007
rules.relevance: Defined the normative coal requirement assured to the generator, forming the baseline for calculating the shortfall.

rules.case_name: Arun Kumar Agrawal & Anr. vs. National Insurance Company Ltd. & Ors.
rules.reference: Arun Kumar Agrawal & Anr. vs. National Insurance Company Ltd. & Ors.
rules.relevance: Recognizes the monetary value of domestic services rendered by a housewife for calculating loss of dependency.

rules.case_name: Rajesh & Ors. vs. Rajbir Singh & Ors.
rules.reference: Rajesh & Ors. vs. Rajbir Singh & Ors.
rules.relevance: Guides the award of substantial amounts for loss of consortium and loss of love and affection.

rules.case_name: Amresh Kumari vs. Niranjan Lal Jagdish Prasad Jain & Ors.
rules.reference: Amresh Kumari vs. Niranjan Lal Jagdish Prasad Jain & Ors.
rules.relevance: Establishes 9% as the appropriate rate of interest on compensation.

rules.case_name: General Manager, Kerala S.R. TC. vs. Susamma Thomas & Ors.
rules.reference: General Manager, Kerala S.R. TC. vs. Susamma Thomas & Ors.
rules.relevance: Supports the assessment of income by adding future prospects to proven income.

rules.reference: Assessment of Income
rules.relevance: Income assessment must be based on evidence; work on one's own field contributes to income by saving labor costs.

rules.case_name: Chenna Boyanna Krishna Yadav v. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
rules.reference: Chenna Boyanna Krishna Yadav v. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
rules.relevance: Established that 'reasonable grounds' under Section 21(4) of MCOCA means something more than prima facie grounds, requiring substantial probable causes to believe the accused is not guilty.

rules.reference: Criminal Procedure Code, 1973
rules.relevance: Stipulates conditions for bail, which the court imposed on the appellant.

rules.case_name: Chenna Boyanna Krishna Yadav v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Chenna Boyanna Krishna Yadav v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to interpret Section 21(4) of MCOCA, establishing that the conditions for bail are cumulative and 'reasonable grounds' means substantial probable causes, not just prima facie grounds.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure
rules.relevance: The court stipulated that the appellants must remain bound by the conditions specified in this section upon being granted bail.

rules.case_name: Ravitsing Brahmajeetsing Sharma v. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
rules.reference: Ravitsing Brahmajeetsing Sharma v. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
rules.relevance: Established that Section 21(4) of MCOCA must be construed reasonably; the court need not arrive at a positive finding of innocence but must assess broad probabilities and consider the case on its own facts.

rules.case_name: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and Another
rules.reference: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and Another
rules.relevance: Established that simple lack of care, error of judgment, or accident is not proof of negligence; a doctor is liable only if they lack requisite skills or do not exercise reasonable competence.

rules.case_name: M.A Biviji v. Sunita & Ors.
rules.reference: M.A Biviji v. Sunita & Ors.
rules.relevance: Cited for the three essential ingredients of medical negligence: duty of care, breach of duty, and resulting damage.

rules.case_name: Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences v. Prasanth S. Dhananka
rules.reference: Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences v. Prasanth S. Dhananka
rules.relevance: Established that compensation must strike a balance between the victim's demands and the liable party's interests, and that injured persons often suffer more distress than those who die.

rules.reference: Causation in Medical Negligence
rules.relevance: An inference of causation may be drawn if the injury is proximate to the breach of duty, even without positive scientific proof, provided the opposite party does not adduce evidence to the contrary.

rules.case_name: Sarla Verma v. DTC
rules.reference: Sarla Verma v. DTC
rules.relevance: Defined 'just compensation' as that which is adequate, fair, and equitable, aiming for restitutio in integrum.

rules.reference: Procedural Lapse vs. Substantive Proof
rules.relevance: A failure to formally exhibit documents is a procedural lapse that cannot be the basis for rejecting a claim if the factum of the accident and negligence are proved by other evidence.

rules.case_name: United India Insurance Company Ltd. vs Shila Datta & Ors.
rules.reference: United India Insurance Company Ltd. vs Shila Datta & Ors.
rules.relevance: Establishes that a claim petition under the Act is not an adversarial lis but a proceeding regulated by Chapter XII of the Act.

rules.reference: Admission by vehicle owner establishes factum of accident
rules.relevance: The court relied on the owner's admission to prove that the vehicle was involved in the accident, overriding the lack of immediate FIR.

rules.reference: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988
rules.relevance: Notices issued under this section elicited an admission from the vehicle owner regarding the accident, which was crucial for establishing liability.

rules.reference: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988
rules.relevance: These sections provide the statutory basis for filing a claim petition for compensation in motor accident cases.

rules.case_name: Ramlal, Motilal and Chhotelal Vs. Rewa Coalfields Ltd.
rules.reference: Ramlal, Motilal and Chhotelal Vs. Rewa Coalfields Ltd.
rules.relevance: Establishes that the right accrued to a decree-holder by lapse of time should not be lightly disturbed and discretion must be exercised to advance substantial justice only when no negligence is imputable.

rules.case_name: Basawaraj and Anr. Vs. Special Land Acquisition Officer
rules.reference: Basawaraj and Anr. Vs. Special Land Acquisition Officer
rules.relevance: Holds that 'sufficient cause' cannot be liberally interpreted if negligence, inaction, or lack of bona fides is attributed to the party, and condoning delay without sufficient cause violates statutory principles.

rules.case_name: Pundlik Jalam Patil Vs. Executive Engineer, Jalgaon Medium Project
rules.reference: Pundlik Jalam Patil Vs. Executive Engineer, Jalgaon Medium Project
rules.relevance: Reinforces that laws of limitation are based on public policy to ensure an end to litigation and that courts assist the vigilant, not those who slumber over their rights.

rules.case_name: P.K. Ramachandran Vs. State of Kerala and Anr.
rules.reference: P.K. Ramachandran Vs. State of Kerala and Anr.
rules.relevance: Holds that delay cannot be condoned lightly in the absence of a reasonable explanation and that the law of limitation must be applied with rigour.

rules.case_name: Perumon Bhagvathyu Devaswom Perinadu Village vs. Bhargavi Amma (dead) by LRS and Others
rules.reference: Perumon Bhagvathyu Devaswom Perinadu Village vs. Bhargavi Amma (dead) by LRS and Others
rules.relevance: Establishes that a lenient view should be taken regarding delay in appellate matters where litigants rely on counsel for updates, and courts should not fault parties for lack of immediate knowledge if counsel has not informed them.

rules.reference: Article 16(4B) of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The court referred to this provision to clarify that while unfilled reserved vacancies can be treated as a separate class, this does not permit exceeding the 50% ceiling in the year of recruitment.

rules.reference: Kerala Public Service Commission Rules of Procedure
rules.relevance: The court analyzed this rule to determine the procedure for preparing rank lists and supplementary lists, concluding that separate lists for open and reserved categories are necessary to maintain the 50:50 balance.

rules.reference: Kerala Public Service Commission Rules of Procedure
rules.relevance: The court used this definition of 'ranked list' to argue that there is only one ranked list and the supplementary list has no independent statutory backing once the main list is exhausted.

rules.reference: Supplementary list has no independent existence after exhaustion of main list
rules.relevance: The court established that once the main rank list is exhausted, the supplementary list cannot operate independently as it would violate the 50% reservation ceiling.

rules.reference: Kerala State and Subordinate Service Rules, 1958
rules.relevance: The court held that the proviso mandates that reservation, including carry-forward, shall not exceed 50% of the total vacancies in any year, and the High Court violated this by allowing appointments from the supplementary list after the main list was exhausted.

rules.reference: Writ Jurisdiction and Findings of Fact
rules.relevance: The court held that a High Court exercising extraordinary writ jurisdiction should not interfere with concurrent findings of fact recorded by the election dispute resolving authorities (Collector and Commissioner) when supported by evidence such as the minutes.

rules.reference: Bombay Village Panchayats (Sarpanch and Upa-Sarpanch) Election Rules, 1964
rules.relevance: The court used this rule regarding the recording of minutes to support the view that voting by show of hands is the general method, as minutes must record names of voters, whereas secret ballot is an exception.

rules.reference: Bombay Village Panchayats (Sarpanch and Upa-Sarpanch) Election Rules, 1964
rules.relevance: The court interpreted this rule to establish that voting by show of hands is the default method, and voting by secret ballot is only permissible if a member present at the meeting makes a specific demand.

rules.reference: Unlawful prevention from contesting election
rules.relevance: The court held that an election is not valid in law if a prospective candidate is unlawfully prevented from filing nomination papers, regardless of whether specific statutory grounds for election petitions are met.

rules.reference: Punjab Gram Panchayat Election Rules
rules.relevance: The court considered this rule regarding election petitions but held that the specific facts of unlawful prevention did not fall within its enumerated grounds, necessitating a different legal remedy.

rules.case_name: Abdul Rahim & Ors. v. Tufan Gazi and Ors.
rules.reference: Abdul Rahim v. Tufan Gazi
rules.relevance: The court cited this case to establish that Section 12 does not apply where the inability to perform arises from the plaintiff's own conduct.

rules.case_name: William Graham v. Krishna Chandra Dey
rules.reference: William Graham v. Krishna Chandra Dey
rules.relevance: The court relied on this Privy Council decision to hold that it is not open to a court to decree specific performance in part except in exigencies provided in Section 12, and that the court cannot create a new contract.

rules.case_name: Abdul Haq v. Mohammad Yehia Khan
rules.reference: Abdul Haq v. Mohammad Yehia Khan
rules.relevance: The court referred to this case to support the general rule that courts will not compel specific performance unless the whole contract can be executed.

rules.case_name: Surjit Kaur v. Naurara Singh
rules.reference: Surjit Kaur v. Naurara Singh
rules.relevance: The court used this precedent to affirm that specific performance cannot be granted to a party who has not been ready and willing to perform the contract at all stages.

rules.case_name: Pankajakshi (D) through LRs & Ors. v. Chandrika & Ors.
rules.reference: Pankajakshi (D) through LRs & Ors. v. Chandrika & Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this Constitution Bench judgment to hold that while substantial questions of law need not be framed in second appeals under the Punjab Act, the High Court still lacks jurisdiction to reverse findings of fact.

rules.case_name: Rishipal Singh Solanki v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Rishipal Singh Solanki v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: Laid down principles that delay is not a ground for rejection, school records are primary evidence, and in borderline cases, the benefit should go to the accused.

rules.case_name: Pawan Kumar Gupta v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: Pawan Kumar Gupta v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: Distinguished because in that case the plea was previously rejected by lower courts, whereas here it was raised for the first time before the Supreme Court.

rules.reference: Gravity of offence is not a ground to deny juvenile status
rules.relevance: The heinous nature of the crime cannot be used to reject a bona fide claim of juvenility if the age is established.

rules.reference: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015
rules.relevance: Clarifies that the procedure for inquiry by a court under Section 9(2) is not strictly bound by the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, allowing the court to formulate its own procedure.

rules.case_name: Jitendra Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Jitendra Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: Guided the court on the quantum of punishment for juveniles, suggesting that for older juveniles, fine may be the only realistic punishment rather than probation or special home detention.

rules.case_name: Mohd. Shafi v. Mohd. Rafiq & Anr.
rules.reference: Mohd. Shafi v. Mohd. Rafiq & Anr.
rules.relevance: Established that the commission of an offence by a non-accused must appear to the court based on evidence, and discretion must be judicially exercised, not ipse dixit.

rules.case_name: Shashi Kant Singh v. Tarkeshwar Singh & Anr.
rules.reference: Shashi Kant Singh v. Tarkeshwar Singh & Anr.
rules.relevance: The High Court relied on this case, but the Supreme Court distinguished it as it dealt with a different question regarding the conclusion of the trial.

rules.reference: Standard of Satisfaction for Section 319 Cr.P.C.
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that the degree of satisfaction required to summon additional accused is stricter than the prima facie test for framing charges. The power must not be exercised in a casual or cavalier manner.

rules.case_name: Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ram Krishan Rohtagi & Ors.
rules.reference: Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ram Krishan Rohtagi & Ors.
rules.relevance: Held that the power under Section 319 is extraordinary and should be used very sparingly only if compelling reasons exist.

rules.case_name: Ramesh Kumari v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Ors.
rules.reference: Ramesh Kumari v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to establish that the provision of Section 154 Cr.P.C. is mandatory and genuineness of information is not a condition precedent for registration.

rules.case_name: Superintendent and Remembrancer of Legal Affairs, West Bengal v. Mohan Singh
rules.reference: Superintendent and Remembrancer of Legal Affairs, West Bengal v. Mohan Singh
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to support the proposition that a second application under inherent powers may be maintainable if there is a changed set of circumstances.

rules.case_name: Sabitha Ramamurthy v. R.B.S. Channabasavaradhya
rules.reference: Sabitha Ramamurthy v. R.B.S. Channabasavaradhya
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to hold that strict compliance with statutory requirements is necessary to infer vicarious liability under Section 141.

rules.case_name: S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla
rules.reference: S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla
rules.relevance: The court relied on the larger bench decision in the same case which held that specific averments are necessary to satisfy Section 141 and that mere directorship does not create deemed liability.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Empowers a Magistrate to dismiss a complaint or issue process only if there is sufficient ground for proceeding, requiring the complaint to disclose essential ingredients of the offence.

rules.case_name: Gunwala Sales Pvt. Ltd. v. Anu Mehta
rules.reference: Gunwala Sales Pvt. Ltd. v. Anu Mehta
rules.relevance: Held that basic averments are sufficient to send a Director to trial unless incontrovertible evidence is produced to show they were not in charge of the business.

rules.provision: Proviso to Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
rules.reference: Himachal Pradesh Act 17 of 1986
rules.relevance: Allows the Collector to entertain applications for reference beyond six weeks but within six months if sufficient cause is shown.

rules.reference: Acceptance of Award
rules.relevance: An award is not deemed accepted if the interested person objects to the compensation or seeks enhancement, thereby retaining the right to file a reference.

rules.case_name: D. Hanumanth SA & Ors. v. State of Karnataka and Ors.
rules.reference: D. Hanumanth SA & Ors. v. State of Karnataka and Ors.
rules.relevance: Establishes that the Government cannot acquire its own land once it has vested in the State.

rules.case_name: Delhi Airtech Services Pvt. Ltd. and Another Vs. State of U.P. and Another
rules.reference: Delhi Airtech Services Pvt. Ltd. and Another Vs. State of U.P. and Another
rules.relevance: Adopted the approach of determining market value on the date of the belated award while calculating statutory benefits from the date of notification.

rules.case_name: Balwant Narayan Bhagde vs. M.D. Bhagwat & Ors.
rules.reference: Balwant Narayan Bhagde vs. M.D. Bhagwat & Ors.
rules.relevance: The court used this precedent to determine the test for 'actual possession' under Section 16, concluding that the State had validly taken possession of the land.

rules.reference: Non-interference in commercial contracts
rules.relevance: Disputes between rival tenderers are essentially commercial; judicial interference is warranted only if the process is vitiated by mala fides, unreasonableness, or arbitrariness, or if substantial public interest is involved.

rules.case_name: Raunaq International Ltd. Vs. I. V.R. Construction Ltd. & Ors.
rules.reference: Raunaq International Ltd. Vs. I. V.R. Construction Ltd. & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that contract awards are commercial transactions and courts should not intervene under Article 226 unless there is a substantial element of public interest or mala fides.

rules.case_name: Air India Ltd. Vs. Cochin International Airport Ltd. & Ors.
rules.reference: Air India Ltd. Vs. Cochin International Airport Ltd. & Ors.
rules.relevance: Reiterated that while the State must adhere to norms, judicial intervention should be exercised with great caution and only in furtherance of public interest, not merely on legal points.

rules.case_name: Kedarnath Agrawal & Anr. Vs. Dhanraji Devi & Anr.
rules.reference: Kedarnath Agrawal & Anr. Vs. Dhanraji Devi & Anr.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment for the principle that subsequent events can be taken into consideration to do complete justice between the parties.

rules.case_name: Municipal Board of Pratabgarh Vs. Mahendra Singh Chawla
rules.reference: Municipal Board of Pratabgarh Vs. Mahendra Singh Chawla
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment for the principle that the Court under Article 136 is not bound to set aside every order found not in conformity with law if equity demands otherwise.

rules.case_name: Meena (Smt) w/o Balwant Hemke vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Meena (Smt) w/o Balwant Hemke vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to hold that mere recovery of currency notes and a positive phenolphthalein test are insufficient to establish guilt without proof of demand and acceptance.

rules.case_name: Ram Singh vs. Col. Ram Singh
rules.reference: Ram Singh vs. Col. Ram Singh
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to establish the strict standards for admissibility of tape-recorded evidence, including voice identification and exclusion of tampering.

rules.case_name: Ayyasami vs. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.reference: Ayyasami vs. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to support the requirement of corroboration for the testimony of an interested witness in corruption cases.

rules.reference: Standard of proof in corruption cases
rules.relevance: The court held that demand and acceptance must be proved by cogent evidence and beyond reasonable doubt, not merely by preponderance of probabilities.

rules.case_name: Panna Damodar Rathi vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Panna Damodar Rathi vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent for the principle that the sole testimony of an interested complainant cannot be relied upon without independent corroboration.

rules.case_name: Preeti Gupta v. State of Jharkhand
rules.reference: Preeti Gupta v. State of Jharkhand
rules.relevance: The court relied on observations regarding the misuse of Section 498A in matrimonial disputes and the need to scrutinize allegations carefully.

rules.case_name: Arnesh Kumar Vs. State of Bihar and Anr.
rules.reference: Arnesh Kumar Vs. State of Bihar and Anr.
rules.relevance: Observed that Section 498A is often used as a weapon to harass husbands and their relatives, including elderly family members.

rules.reference: Omnibus allegations
rules.relevance: General and omnibus allegations against in-laws without attributing specific roles do not warrant prosecution and amount to an abuse of the process of law.

rules.case_name: Mahmood Ali & Ors. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
rules.reference: Mahmood Ali & Ors. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on the principle that the High Court must look into the FIR with care and read between the lines in frivolous or vexatious proceedings.

rules.case_name: K. Subba Rao v. The State of Telangana
rules.reference: K. Subba Rao v. The State of Telangana
rules.relevance: Established that courts should be careful in proceeding against distant relatives in matrimonial disputes and that relatives should not be roped in based on omnibus allegations without specific instances of involvement.

rules.case_name: Amar Pal Singh vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
rules.reference: Amar Pal Singh vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
rules.relevance: The court cited this case as an identical circumstance where adverse remarks and directions for disciplinary action against a judicial officer were expunged.

rules.reference: Judicial review of administrative assessments
rules.relevance: Courts exercising writ jurisdiction generally do not interfere with administrative assessments of merit and conduct unless they are arbitrary, mala fide, or without any factual basis.

rules.reference: Judicial Observations in Ongoing Investigations
rules.relevance: Observations made by a court during an ongoing investigation are based on allegations, not established facts, and should not prejudice the investigation if clarified.

rules.reference: Appreciation of evidence in writ jurisdiction
rules.relevance: Writ courts do not enter into controversies involving disputed questions of fact and appreciation of evidence, which are matters for departmental inquiries or regular courts.

rules.case_name: State Represented by Inspector of Police v. M. Murugesan & Anr
rules.reference: State Represented by Inspector of Police v. M. Murugesan & Anr
rules.relevance: Clarified that the jurisdiction under Section 439 CrPC is limited to grant or rejection of bail and cannot be used to issue directions for improving the criminal justice system.

rules.reference: Acknowledgement via Balance Sheets and OTS
rules.relevance: Entries in statutory balance sheets and proposals for One Time Settlement (OTS) made within the limitation period constitute valid acknowledgements of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.

rules.case_name: Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited v. Bishal Jaiswal
rules.reference: Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited v. Bishal Jaiswal
rules.relevance: Held that entries in balance sheets can amount to an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act if they are unequivocal, distinguishing cases where liability is denied.

rules.reference: Acknowledgment in Financial Statements
rules.relevance: Financial statements prepared under statutory compulsion can still contain unequivocal admissions of liability that amount to acknowledgments under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, provided they indicate a jural relationship and do not deny the debt.

rules.case_name: Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited. v. Bishal Jaiswal and Ors.
rules.reference: Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited. v. Bishal Jaiswal and Ors.
rules.relevance: Confirmed that entries in balance sheets and financial statements can constitute an acknowledgement of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.

rules.case_name: Babulal Vardharji Gurjar v. Veer Gurjar Aluminium Industries (P) Ltd.
rules.reference: Babulal Vardharji Gurjar v. Veer Gurjar Aluminium Industries (P) Ltd.
rules.relevance: Distinguished on facts; held that it does not establish a general rule that books of account cannot be acknowledgments, but rather addressed a case where no acknowledgment was pleaded.

rules.case_name: C.S. Venkatesh Vs A.S.C. Murthy (Dead) By Lrs. and Ors.
rules.reference: C.S. Venkatesh Vs A.S.C. Murthy (Dead) By Lrs. and Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to determine that readiness and willingness can be inferred from the conduct of the plaintiff and attending circumstances, and that producing ready money is not mandatory if means to generate consideration are proved.

rules.reference: Hardship as a defense requires pleading and evidence
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that hardship is a substantive defense that must be specifically taken by the defendant and supported by evidence on record to be considered.

rules.reference: Appellate courts cannot reverse findings on unframed issues of fact
rules.relevance: The court held that an appellate court cannot reverse a trial court's decree based on a factual finding (hardship) when the issue was not framed and no evidence was led to substantiate it.

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: Prescribes the manner in which averments of readiness and willingness are required to be made in a suit for specific performance.

rules.reference: Specific Relief Act, 1963
rules.relevance: The court referred to the amendment inserting Section 10(a) as a legislative guide indicating that specific performance is no longer purely discretionary, though its retrospective application was kept open.

rules.case_name: Local Government Board v. Arlidge
rules.reference: Local Government Board v. Arlidge
rules.relevance: The court relied on the principle that when a body is entrusted with duties, it should follow its own normal procedure unless expressly prohibited.

rules.reference: Distinction between legislative power and constituent power
rules.relevance: The court established that constitutional amendments are exercises of constituent power, not legislative power, and thus are not 'laws' under Article 13(2).

rules.reference: Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The court relied on this article to establish that the provisional Parliament exercised all powers conferred on Parliament, including the power to amend the Constitution.

rules.reference: Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The court interpreted this article to determine that the power to amend the Constitution is vested in Parliament and that the procedure allows for amendments to bills during passage.

rules.reference: Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The court referred to this article to support the view that parliamentary rules of procedure apply to constitutional amendment bills, allowing for amendments during passage.

rules.case_name: Hans Raj vs. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Hans Raj vs. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Held that proof of suicide within seven years and cruelty does not automatically give rise to a presumption of abetment; the court must consider all other circumstances, including whether the cruelty was likely to drive the woman to suicide.

rules.case_name: Lakhjit Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Lakhjit Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Interpreted Section 113A, holding that the presumption is discretionary and requires proof of cruelty, not just suicide within seven years.

rules.case_name: Hans Raj v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Hans Raj v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Explained that Section 113-A gives discretion to the court to presume abetment based on the nature of cruelty and other circumstances.

rules.reference: Indian Evidence Act
rules.relevance: Creates a presumption of abetment of suicide if cruelty is established within a year of marriage; the court discussed its application and rebuttal.

rules.case_name: Ravinder Kumar and Anr. v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Ravinder Kumar and Anr. v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Highlighted genuine causes for delay in FIR, such as grief, ignorance, or lack of transport, particularly in rural settings.

rules.case_name: State Rep. By The CBI v. Anil Sharma
rules.reference: State Rep. By The CBI v. Anil Sharma
rules.relevance: Held that custodial interrogation is more effective than questioning a suspect protected by anticipatory bail.

rules.case_name: Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy v. CBI
rules.reference: Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy v. CBI
rules.relevance: Held that economic offences constitute a class apart and need a different approach in the matter of bail.

rules.case_name: Nikesh Tarachand Shah v. Union of India
rules.reference: Nikesh Tarachand Shah v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Struck down the twin conditions in Section 45 of PMLA as unconstitutional, leading to amendments in the bail provisions.

rules.case_name: Directorate of Enforcement v. Ashok Kumar Jain
rules.reference: Directorate of Enforcement v. Ashok Kumar Jain
rules.relevance: Held that in economic offences, the accused is not entitled to anticipatory bail.

rules.case_name: State of M.P. and another v. Ram Kishna Balothia and another
rules.reference: State of M.P. v. Ram Kishna Balothia
rules.relevance: Held that anticipatory bail is a statutory right and not an integral part of Article 21 of the Constitution.

rules.reference: Indian Motor Tariff (IMT) 47
rules.relevance: The specific policy clause excluding liability for loss or damage resulting from 'overturning arising out of the operation as a tool' unless an additional premium is paid.

rules.case_name: Lourdes Society Snehanjali Girls Hostel v. H&R Johnson (India) Ltd
rules.reference: Lourdes Society Snehanjali Girls Hostel v. H&R Johnson (India) Ltd
rules.relevance: Established that the NCDRC exceeds its jurisdiction by setting aside concurrent findings of fact recorded by lower forums based on valid and cogent reasons.

rules.case_name: Gurshinder Singh vs. Shriram General Insurance Co. Ltd.
rules.reference: Gurshinder Singh vs. Shriram General Insurance Co. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Established that Condition 1 of insurance policies must be interpreted in two parts: notice to the company for accidents and notice to police for theft. Mere delay in intimating the insurer, when the FIR is lodged immediately, cannot be a ground to deny the claim.

rules.reference: Appellate/Revisional interference with concurrent findings of fact
rules.relevance: Establishes that revisional powers should not be invoked merely to take a different view on facts when there is no jurisdictional error or miscarriage of justice.

rules.case_name: National Insurance Company Limited vs. Nitin Khandelwal
rules.reference: National Insurance Company Limited vs. Nitin Khandelwal
rules.relevance: Established that a breach of policy conditions does not warrant total repudiation if the claim is genuine, allowing for settlement on a non-standard basis with proportionate deductions.

rules.reference: Supreme Court Order in Suo Motu Civil Writ Petition No. 03/2020
rules.relevance: Excluded the period from 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022 for the computation of limitation due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

rules.case_name: Govind Yadav v. New India Assurance Company Limited

rules.relevance: Affirmed that adequate compensation must be awarded for physical injury, loss of earnings, and inability to lead a normal life in cases of permanent disability.

rules.case_name: Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar
rules.reference: Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar
rules.relevance: Established principles for assessing compensation, including heads of damages for permanent disability, loss of future earnings, and loss of amenities.

rules.reference: Objective of compensation

rules.case_name: Mis. Concord of India Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Smt. Nirmala Devi & others
rules.reference: Mis. Concord of India Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Smt. Nirmala Devi & others
rules.relevance: Mandates that the determination of quantum of compensation in motor accident cases must be liberal, not niggardly, valuing life and limb in generous scales.

rules.case_name: Yadav Kumar v. The Divisional Manager, National Insurance Company Ltd.
rules.reference: Yadav Kumar v. The Divisional Manager, National Insurance Company Ltd.
rules.relevance: Defined 'just compensation' as requiring fair, equitable principles and a reasonable approach, not merely a mathematical calculation.

rules.case_name: Ram Pujan and Others v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Ram Pujan and Others v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: The court clarified that while compromise cannot compound non-compoundable offences, the fact of compromise can be taken into account when determining the quantum of sentence.

rules.case_name: Ram Pujan v. State of UP
rules.reference: Ram Pujan v. State of UP
rules.relevance: Clarified that while compromise cannot compound non-compoundable offences, the fact of compromise can be taken into account in determining the quantum of sentence.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Defines the specific offences that can be compounded by persons mentioned in the Table or by the victim with court permission, forming the complete legislative scheme for compounding.

rules.case_name: Surendra Nath Mohanty and Anr. v. State of Orissa
rules.reference: Surendra Nath Mohanty and Anr. v. State of Orissa
rules.relevance: A three-Judge Bench decision reiterating that the course adopted in Ram Pujan and Mahesh Chand regarding compounding non-compoundable offences was not in accordance with law.

rules.case_name: Ishwar Singh v. State of MP
rules.reference: Ishwar Singh v. State of MP
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to support the view that compromise is a relevant circumstance for reducing sentence in non-compoundable offences, particularly when parties are relatives or live in the same village.

rules.case_name: Naramadaben Maganlal Thakker v. Pranjivandas Maganlal Thakker & Ors.
rules.reference: Naramadaben Maganlal Thakker v. Pranjivandas Maganlal Thakker & Ors.
rules.relevance: Distinguished on facts where the gift was found conditional and unaccepted, unlike the present case where title was absolutely transferred and accepted.

rules.case_name: K. Balakrishnan v. K. Kamalam & Ors.
rules.reference: K. Balakrishnan v. K. Kamalam & Ors.
rules.relevance: Affirmed that a donor can transfer title and ownership while reserving possession and enjoyment for life, making the gift valid.

rules.case_name: Lallu Singh v. Gur Narain and Ors.
rules.reference: Lallu Singh v. Gur Narain and Ors.
rules.relevance: Cited for the proposition that Section 123 supersedes the Hindu Law requirement of delivery of possession for a valid gift.

rules.case_name: Thota Sridhar Reddy and Ors. vs. Mandala Ramulamma and Others
rules.reference: Thota Sridhar Reddy and Ors. vs. Mandala Ramulamma and Others
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to confirm that once an ownership certificate is granted under Section 38-E, the title of the protected tenant is complete and subsequent claims by purchasers are divested.

rules.reference: Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950
rules.relevance: The court relied on this provision to determine that the issuance of an occupancy rights certificate vests complete and unambiguous title in the protected tenant, divesting previous owners.

rules.case_name: Munna Lal Jain & Ors. v. Vipin Kumar Sharma & Ors.

rules.relevance: Confirmed that using the deceased's age ensures certainty and avoids disputes regarding dependants' ages.

rules.case_name: National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi & Ors.

rules.case_name: Royal Sundaram Alliance Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Mandala Yadagari Goud & Ors.

rules.case_name: Reshma Kumari & Ors. v. Madan Mohan & Ors.
rules.reference: Reshma Kumari & Ors. v. Madan Mohan & Ors.
rules.relevance: Affirmed that the multiplier is to be applied with reference to the age of the deceased.

rules.case_name: Reshmi Kumari & Ors. Vs. Madan Mohan & Anr.
rules.reference: Reshmi Kumari & Ors. Vs. Madan Mohan & Anr.
rules.relevance: A three-member bench decision that approved the table in Sarla Verma and held that the multiplier should be determined by the age of the deceased.

rules.reference: Guardians and Wards Act, 1890

rules.case_name: Kumar V Jahgirdar v. Chethana Ramatheertha

rules.relevance: This provision mandates that the court shall regard the wishes of the minor as a relevant factor, though not necessarily decisive, when determining custody.

rules.case_name: Anjali Kapoor (Smt.) vs. Rajiv Baijal

rules.case_name: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Guru Charan

rules.relevance: Establishes that the Supreme Court should only interfere with a High Court's acquittal if there are very substantial and compelling reasons, such as perverse findings or manifest injustice.

rules.case_name: State of Rajasthan v. Teja Singh and others

rules.case_name: State of U.P. v. Harihar Bux Singh

rules.case_name: The State of Punjab v. Jagir Singh, Baljit Singh and Karam Singh

rules.relevance: Established that criminal trials must be based on probabilities and intrinsic worth of evidence, not conjectures or surmises.

rules.case_name: Piara Singh and others v. State of Punjab

rules.relevance: Established that evidence of interested witnesses must be scrutinized with care but cannot be rejected merely on that ground if found creditworthy.

rules.reference: Hindu Succession Act, 1956

rules.reference: Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Act, 1920
rules.relevance: The court considered this provision to note that it restricted the right to contest alienations to male-line descendants but did not prevent female heirs from inheriting once succession opened.

rules.reference: Cochin University of Science and Technology Act, 1976

rules.reference: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

rules.reference: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

rules.reference: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

rules.reference: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
rules.relevance: The court relied on these provisions to establish that a written communication is deemed received if delivered to the addressee's place of business, and that receipt occurs on the day of delivery, regardless of refusal to accept.

rules.reference: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
rules.relevance: Defines 'arbitral award' to include an interim award, establishing that interim awards are subject to the same challenge mechanisms as final awards.

rules.reference: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006

rules.reference: Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993

rules.case_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Mastan

rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case as it involved statutory election of remedies under the Motor Vehicles Act, which does not apply to the cumulative remedies under the NPA and DRT Acts.

rules.case_name: Central Bank of India v. Ravindra and Others

rules.relevance: Established that RBI directions have statutory force and are binding on banks; contravention is punishable.

rules.relevance: Established that the power to proceed ex-parte carries the power to inquire into sufficient cause for absence and to set aside the award if notice was not served.

rules.case_name: Lalji Haridas vs. State of Maharashtra and Another

rules.relevance: Established that proceedings before an Income Tax Officer are judicial proceedings and that Section 195 safeguards apply.

rules.case_name: Priti Saraf & Anr. Vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr.
