rules.relevance: Established the principle that courts cannot make out a new case for the prosecution if the case as put forth by the prosecution is disbelieved.

rules.case_name: Hatti Singh v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Hatti Singh v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Reiterated that the 'last seen' theory is only applicable when the time gap is so small that no other person could have committed the crime, and requires corroboration.

rules.reference: NCLT is not a debt collection forum
rules.relevance: The IBC deals with insolvency and bankruptcy, not penalizing solvent companies for non-payment of disputed dues.

rules.case_name: K. Kishan vs. Vijay Nirman Co. (P) Ltd.
rules.reference: K. Kishan vs. Vijay Nirman Co. (P) Ltd.
rules.relevance: Affirms that the IBC cannot be used as a substitute for debt enforcement procedures or to extract money where a real dispute exists.

rules.case_name: Mobilox Innovations Private Limited vs. Kirusa Software Private Limited
rules.reference: Mobilox Innovations Private Limited vs. Kirusa Software Private Limited
rules.relevance: Established that the insolvency process cannot be used as a substitute for debt enforcement and that a plausible, non-spurious dispute requires rejection of the insolvency application.

rules.reference: Existence of a pre-existing dispute
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that if a dispute exists or proceedings are pending before the receipt of the demand notice, the insolvency application must be rejected.

rules.reference: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
rules.relevance: Establishes that a respondent is entitled to raise a counter-claim unless the parties have otherwise agreed, and defines 'arbitration agreement' broadly.

rules.case_name: Raja Jagadish Chandra Deo Dhabal Deb v. Gour Hari Mahato & Ors.
rules.reference: Raja Jagadish Chandra Deo Dhabal Deb v. Gour Hari Mahato & Ors.
rules.relevance: Cited to support the principle that res judicata must be pleaded and issues framed.

rules.reference: Constructive Res Judicata in Administrative Law
rules.relevance: The principle of res judicata plays a restricted role in administrative law and cannot be used to thwart statutory duties or override statutory directions.

rules.reference: Res judicata is a rule of estoppel by judgment based on public policy for finality of litigation
rules.relevance: The court defined the nature of res judicata to determine if it barred the suit.

rules.case_name: Pritam Kaur w/o S. Mukand Singh v. State of Pepsu and Ors.
rules.reference: Pritam Kaur w/o S. Mukand Singh v. State of Pepsu and Ors.
rules.relevance: Referenced regarding the waiver of the plea of res judicata.

rules.reference: Cantonment Land Administration Rules, 1937
rules.relevance: Establishes the maintenance of the General Land Register, entries in which are given due weight as official records of government land.

rules.case_name: Laxmikant v. Satyawan
rules.reference: Laxmikant v. Satyawan
rules.relevance: Establishes that a highest bidder in a public auction does not acquire a vested right until the bid is confirmed by the competent authority, especially when conditions reserve the right to reject.

rules.case_name: Meerut Development Authority v. Assn. of Management Studies
rules.reference: Meerut Development Authority v. Assn. of Management Studies
rules.relevance: Held that disposal of public property must be fair and transparent, and the authority has the right to reject bids if they do not represent market price, provided the action is not arbitrary.

rules.reference: Proper fixation of reserve price based on market potential
rules.relevance: The court found the reserve price was fixed too low and directed it to be fixed after consulting experts to ensure the maximum price for public assets.

rules.reference: Effect of void sale deed on stamp duty refund
rules.relevance: The court held that since the sale deed became void due to the re-auction order, the respondent was entitled to a refund of the stamp duty paid.

rules.reference: Power to do complete justice and balance equities
rules.relevance: The court invoked this principle to order a fresh auction despite the execution of a sale deed, ensuring fairness between the parties and protecting public interest.

rules.case_name: Ramashish Yadav v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Ramashish Yadav v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Distinguished on facts; the court noted that in the present case, the holding of the victim facilitated a fatal attack, unlike the independent acts in Ramashish Yadav.

rules.case_name: Pandurang v. State of Hyderabad
rules.reference: Pandurang v. State of Hyderabad
rules.relevance: Emphasizes that common intention is a question of fact in every case and cannot be determined solely by similarity of facts in other cases.

rules.case_name: Sukhram s/o Ramratan v. State of MP.
rules.reference: Sukhram s/o Ramratan v. State of MP.
rules.relevance: Held that if a co-accused is acquitted, the conviction of the appellant under Section 34 cannot be sustained as they cannot be held to have acted conjointly with an acquitted person.

rules.case_name: Takhaji Hiraji v. Thakore Kubersing Chamansing and Ors.
rules.reference: Adverse Inference for Non-Examination of Witnesses
rules.relevance: If material witnesses who could unfold the genesis of the incident or fill gaps in the prosecution case are not examined despite availability, adverse inference can be drawn against the prosecution.

rules.reference: Motive
rules.relevance: Motive is a double-edged weapon; while it may explain why a crime was committed, it does not prove who committed it and can be used by either party to implicate the other.

rules.case_name: SEBI v. Sahara India Real Estate Corporation Ltd.
rules.reference: SEBI v. Sahara India Real Estate Corporation Ltd.
rules.relevance: The Court relied on this order to establish that the defense of redemption was not open to the companies and the full balance amount remained payable.

rules.reference: Pragmatic approach in hard cases
rules.relevance: The Court adopted a pragmatic approach, balancing personal liberty with public interest and the majesty of law, to ensure the 'law works' and orders are respected.

rules.case_name: Subrata Roy Sahara v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.reference: Subrata Roy Sahara v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.relevance: The Court relied on this judgment to reject the plea that applicants should be exempted from depositing amounts allegedly already redeemed, noting the defense was previously rejected.

rules.reference: Inherent jurisdiction to do complete justice
rules.relevance: The Court exercised its inherent jurisdiction to ensure compliance with its orders and maintain the dignity of the Court, rather than strictly construing the matter under contempt jurisdiction.

rules.reference: Restraint Orders and Compliance
rules.relevance: The Court recognized that restraint orders should not prevent contemnors from taking steps to comply with Court directions, provided adequate safeguards are in place to protect the interests of depositors.

rules.case_name: Action Committee on Issue of Caste Certificate to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the State of Maharashtra and Others v. Union of India and Another
rules.reference: Action Committee on Issue of Caste Certificate to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the State of Maharashtra and Others v. Union of India and Another
rules.relevance: Supports the principle that the determination of reservation benefits is a policy decision left to the State/Government based on specific disadvantages.

rules.case_name: Ashok Kumar and Another Vs. State of Bihar and Others
rules.reference: Ashok Kumar and Another Vs. State of Bihar and Others
rules.relevance: Established that a candidate who participates in a selection process without objection cannot subsequently challenge the process or outcome.

rules.case_name: Shakuntala Ganpatsa Shirbhate v. Industrial Weaving Co-operative Society and Ors.
rules.reference: Shakuntala Ganpatsa Shirbhate v. Industrial Weaving Co-operative Society and Ors.
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court interpreted Rule 9(9)(a) to hold that the provision for temporary year-to-year appointment applies only when the available candidate does not belong to any backward class. If the candidate belongs to a backward class (even if not the specific reserved category), they are entitled to a regular appointment.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Employees of Private Schools Rules, 1981
rules.relevance: This rule governs the filling of reserved posts. It states that if a post reserved for a specific Backward Class category cannot be filled, it may be filled by a candidate from other remaining categories in the specified order. It further states that if no person from any of the backward class categories is available, the post may be filled temporarily on a year-to-year basis by a candidate not belonging to the Backward Classes.

rules.reference: Government Circular dated 11.01.2016
rules.relevance: The court considered this circular, which cancelled the earlier 2011 circular, noting it was issued in light of the Dattatray clarification and was not challenged by the respondent.

rules.case_name: Whitbread, Ex Parte
rules.reference: Whitbread, Ex Parte
rules.relevance: Supports the doctrine of constructive delivery, emphasizing that re-delivery formalities are not required if the intent to secure further advances is clear.

rules.case_name: Keys v. Williams
rules.reference: Keys v. Williams
rules.relevance: Held that deposit of deeds for preparing a mortgage does not preclude the creation of an equitable mortgage if money was already advanced.

rules.reference: Constructive Delivery
rules.relevance: Physical delivery is not strictly necessary if the creditor already holds the deeds and the parties agree to treat them as security; substance prevails over form.

rules.reference: Registration Act, 1908
rules.relevance: Provides that a mortgage by deposit of title deeds takes effect against any subsequently executed and registered mortgage deed.

rules.reference: Mixed Question of Fact and Law
rules.relevance: Determining whether a transaction constitutes a mortgage by deposit of title deeds is a mixed question of fact and law, permitting appellate review of evidence.

rules.reference: Discovery of Facts at Instance of Accused
rules.relevance: Recovery of the body and incriminating articles at the instance of the accused serves as strong corroborative evidence of guilt.

rules.case_name: Malleshappa v. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: Malleshappa v. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: Cited to support the view that a long gap between last seen and death weakens the last seen evidence.

rules.case_name: Anjan Kumar Sarma & Others v. State of Assam
rules.reference: Anjan Kumar Sarma & Others v. State of Assam
rules.relevance: Cited for the proposition that last seen evidence alone cannot form the basis of guilt and for the settled factors regarding circumstantial evidence.

rules.case_name: Ram Chander v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Ram Chander v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that it is the duty of a presiding judge to actively participate in the trial and ask questions to discover the truth under Section 165 of the Evidence Act.

rules.reference: Rarest of the rare cases
rules.relevance: The court applied this principle to determine that the brutal murder of a child after rape warranted the death penalty.

rules.reference: Modi's Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology
rules.relevance: The court cited this text to support the finding that a human body is slightly heavier than fresh water and sinks immediately upon unconsciousness.

rules.reference: Taylor's Principles and Practice of Medical Jurisprudence
rules.relevance: The court relied on this authority to establish that a drowned body typically sinks initially and only floats after putrefaction, contradicting witness testimony.

rules.reference: Theory of last seen together
rules.relevance: The court held that being last seen together is not independently sufficient for conviction if the time gap is large or evidence is contradictory, requiring a complete chain of circumstances.

rules.reference: Benefit of acquittal to non-appealing co-accused
rules.relevance: Establishes that if the prosecution fails to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, the benefit of acquittal should extend to similarly situated non-appealing accused.

rules.case_name: Arjun Marik v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Arjun Marik v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that the 'last seen together' theory alone is not sufficient to complete the chain of circumstances for conviction.

rules.reference: Karnataka Stamp Act, 1957
rules.relevance: Mandates that any person having authority to receive evidence must examine instruments to ascertain if they are duly stamped and impound them if they are not.

rules.case_name: Yellapu Uma Maheswari and another vs. Buddha Jagadheeswararao and others
rules.reference: Yellapu Uma Maheswari and another vs. Buddha Jagadheeswararao and others
rules.relevance: Held that while unregistered documents are inadmissible for primary purposes, they may be used for collateral purposes (like severancy of status) subject to payment of stamp duty and penalty.

rules.reference: Bombay Stamp Act, 1958
rules.relevance: This provision deems an agreement to sell as a conveyance if possession is transferred to the purchaser before, at the time of, or after execution of the agreement without executing a separate conveyance.

rules.reference: Hindu Succession Act, 1955
rules.relevance: Used to establish that the mother and sisters were Class I heirs with antecedent title upon the father's death.

rules.case_name: Kale and others vs. Deputy Director of Consolidation and others
rules.reference: Kale and others vs. Deputy Director of Consolidation and others
rules.relevance: Established the distinction between a mere memorandum recording an existing arrangement (not registrable) and a document that creates or extinguishes rights (registrable).

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: Applies only if the relief sought can be entirely obtained by the personal obedience of the defendant; inapplicable to partition suits.

rules.case_name: Harshad Chiman Lal Modi v. DLF Universal Ltd. & Anr.
rules.reference: Harshad Chiman Lal Modi v. DLF Universal Ltd. & Anr.
rules.relevance: Confirms that Section 20 cannot apply if Section 16 applies, and defines the scope of the proviso to Section 16 regarding personal obedience.

rules.reference: Equity acts in personam
rules.relevance: The court discussed this maxim to explain the proviso to Section 16, concluding it did not apply because the relief sought (possession) could not be obtained solely through personal obedience.

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: Mandates that suits for partition or declaration regarding immovable property must be instituted in the court within whose local limits the property is situated.

rules.case_name: T. Arivandandam v. T. V. Satyapal & Anr.
rules.reference: T. Arivandandam v. T. V. Satyapal & Anr.
rules.relevance: Supports the requirement of a meaningful, not formal, reading of the plaint to avoid illusions created by clever drafting.

rules.case_name: The State of Bihar v. Messrs. Karam Chand Thapar
rules.reference: The State of Bihar v. Messrs. Karam Chand Thapar
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to establish that a binding contract against the Government must be expressed to be made by the Governor/Governor-General, executed in writing, and by authorized persons.

rules.reference: Madhya Pradesh Forest Contract Rules
rules.relevance: The court agreed with the High Court that these rules applied only after a written contract was executed, but remanded the case to see if other rules applied.

rules.reference: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959
rules.relevance: The court held that this section, which allows recovery of money due under a contract as arrears of land revenue, could not be used because no valid contract existed under Article 299(1).

rules.reference: Indian Forest Act, 1927
rules.relevance: The court remanded the matter to determine if this section, read with rules, provided an alternative basis for recovering the deficiency amount.

rules.case_name: Seth Bikhrai Jaipuria v. Union of India
rules.reference: Seth Bikhrai Jaipuria v. Union of India
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to emphasize that the requirements of Section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935 (and by extension Article 299) are mandatory to prevent unauthorized liabilities.

rules.reference: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
rules.relevance: Establishes that a tenant is not entitled to contest eviction proceedings unless they pay or deposit all arrears of rent and continue to do so until the termination of proceedings.

rules.reference: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
rules.relevance: Mandates that if a tenant fails to pay or deposit rent, the Controller shall stop proceedings and order eviction unless the tenant shows sufficient cause to the contrary.

rules.reference: Statutory duty over equitable considerations
rules.relevance: The court held that equitable considerations, such as financial difficulties due to personal events, cannot override the express statutory provision requiring rent payment.

rules.reference: Ignorantia juris non excusat
rules.relevance: The principle that ignorance of law is not excusable was applied to reject the tenant's defense regarding their advocate's lack of awareness.

rules.reference: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: Establishes the ground for eviction when a tenant is in arrears of rent for not less than four months and fails to pay within one month of a notice of demand.

rules.case_name: Chand Rani (dead) by Lrs. v. Kamal Rani (dead) by Lrs.
rules.reference: Chand Rani (dead) by Lrs. v. Kamal Rani (dead) by Lrs.
rules.relevance: Establishes that while time is not presumed to be of the essence in immovable property sales, it can be inferred from express terms, nature of property, and surrounding circumstances.

rules.case_name: Jaswinder Kaur v. Gurmeet Singh
rules.reference: Jaswinder Kaur v. Gurmeet Singh
rules.relevance: Holds that Section 12 does not apply where the inability to perform arises from the plaintiff's own conduct.

rules.case_name: Shyam Sunder and others v. Ram Kumar and Another
rules.reference: Shyam Sunder and others v. Ram Kumar and Another
rules.relevance: Holds that substantive amendments to legislation are prospective in operation unless expressly stated to be retrospective.

rules.reference: Time is not of the essence in agreements for sale of immovable property
rules.relevance: The court applied this principle to reject the vendor's argument that the agreement was cancelled due to delay in payment, unless expressly stated otherwise.

rules.reference: Limitation Act, 1963
rules.relevance: The court cited this to establish the three-year limitation period for filing a suit for specific performance from the date fixed for performance or notice of refusal.

rules.case_name: Ex. Lt. Gen. Avadhesh Prakash v. Union of India and Another
rules.reference: Ex. Lt. Gen. Avadhesh Prakash v. Union of India and Another
rules.relevance: Distinguished on the ground that in the present case, the convening officer had recorded reasons for the unavailability of officers of equivalent rank, unlike in Avadhesh Prakash where no such opinion was recorded.

rules.reference: Limited scope of judicial review in administrative decisions
rules.relevance: The court held that the decision of the convening officer regarding the composition of the Court-Martial is subject to limited judicial review, permissible only if arbitrary, irrational, or unreasonable.

rules.case_name: Brig P.S. Gill v. Union of India and Others
rules.reference: Brig P.S. Gill v. Union of India and Others
rules.relevance: Relied upon to establish that adding tendering stations and granting relaxations with price reductions were within the powers of the competent authority and did not constitute fraud or loss to the exchequer.

rules.reference: Tender Inquiry of the APO
rules.relevance: Cited to demonstrate that the Chief Director of Purchase had the discretion to accept supplies with price reductions for non-conforming specifications, validating the respondent's actions.

rules.reference: APO/MOD Consolidated Order No. 3 of 1987
rules.relevance: Cited to show that the addition of tendering stations was permitted under specific conditions, negating the charge of fraud.

rules.case_name: Rekha Chaturvedi (Smt.) vs. University of Rajasthan and Others
rules.reference: Rekha Chaturvedi (Smt.) vs. University of Rajasthan and Others
rules.relevance: Established that in the absence of a fixed date in rules or advertisement, the last date of application is the benchmark for determining substantive eligibility qualifications.

rules.reference: Rajasthan Judicial Service Rules, 2010
rules.relevance: Provides for reservation to various categories including OBC, MBC, and EWS in recruitment.

rules.case_name: Dolly Chhanda vs. Chairman, Jee & Others
rules.reference: Dolly Chhanda vs. Chairman, Jee & Others
rules.relevance: Held that certificates for reservation are proof of entitlement and rigid principles regarding submission dates need not necessarily result in rejection of candidature.

rules.reference: Rajasthan Judicial Service Rules, 2010
rules.relevance: Requires submission of a character certificate not more than six months prior to the date of application, used by the majority to distinguish eligibility proofs from reservation proofs.

rules.case_name: Ashok Kumar Sonkar vs. Union of India and Others
rules.reference: Ashok Kumar Sonkar vs. Union of India and Others
rules.relevance: The majority distinguished this case, noting it dealt with academic qualifications rather than procedural proof of reservation category.

rules.case_name: Dukhishyam Benupani, Asstt. Director, Enforcement Directorate (FERA) v. Arun Kumar Bajoria
rules.reference: Dukhishyam Benupani v. Arun Kumar Bajoria
rules.relevance: Held that courts should not monitor investigation processes and that blanket protection from arrest hampers interrogation.

rules.case_name: Directorate of Enforcement v. Ashok Kumar Jain
rules.reference: Directorate of Enforcement v. Ashok Kumar Jain
rules.relevance: Held that in economic offences, the accused is not entitled to anticipatory bail.

rules.case_name: Nikesh Tarachand Shah v. Union of India
rules.reference: Nikesh Tarachand Shah v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Struck down the twin conditions in Section 45 of PMLA as unconstitutional, leading to amendments in the bail provisions.

rules.case_name: State Rep. By The CBI v. Anil Sharma
rules.reference: State Rep. By The CBI v. Anil Sharma
rules.relevance: Held that custodial interrogation is more effective than questioning a suspect protected by anticipatory bail.

rules.case_name: Shri Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and others v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Shri Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and others v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Established that anticipatory bail cannot be sought after arrest, rendering the SLP in the CBI case infructuous.

rules.reference: Adverse inference from refusal to join Test Identification Parade
rules.relevance: The majority held that no adverse inference can be drawn from an accused's refusal to join a TIP if the accused raises a suspicion that they were shown to the witnesses prior to the parade. The dissenting judge relied on precedents like Shyam Babu v. State of Haryana to argue that refusal warrants an adverse inference.

rules.reference: Necessity of Test Identification Parade (TIP) for unknown accused
rules.relevance: The court held that when an accused is a stranger to the witness and no TIP was conducted, conviction solely on court identification is unsafe.

rules.case_name: Simon & Ors. v. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: Simon & Ors. v. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: Holds that the purpose of a Test Identification Parade is to corroborate court identification, and its absence or minor defects do not render court identification inadmissible if substantive evidence is reliable.

rules.case_name: Shyam Babu v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Shyam Babu v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Cited by the dissenting judge to support the view that refusal to participate in TIP speaks volumes about participation in the crime.

rules.case_name: Lal Singh & Ors. v. State of U. P.
rules.reference: Lal Singh & Ors. v. State of U. P.
rules.relevance: Held that the possibility of witnesses seeing the accused before the TIP must be ruled out, and delay in TIP is fatal if the witness had only a fleeting glimpse.

rules.case_name: Thrity Hoshie Dolikuka v. Hoshiam J Shavaksha Dolikuka
rules.reference: Thrity Hoshie Dolikuka v. Hoshiam J Shavaksha Dolikuka
rules.relevance: Distinguished to clarify that while interviewing a child is not mandatory in all cases, it is necessary when the child is old enough to form an intelligent preference and it does not cause distress.

rules.reference: Positive test of welfare vs Negative test of fitness
rules.relevance: The court established that custody should be granted based on the positive test that it is in the child's welfare, not merely the negative test that the parent is not unfit.

rules.reference: Guardians and Wards Act
rules.relevance: The court noted that its order regarding custody is subject to the final outcome of proceedings pending under this section.

rules.reference: Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956
rules.relevance: Explicitly states that the welfare of the minor shall be the paramount consideration in appointing or declaring a guardian.

rules.reference: Guardians and Wards Act, 1890
rules.relevance: These sections provide the statutory framework for the court to appoint a guardian and make orders for the custody of a minor, prioritizing the minor's welfare.

rules.case_name: Rohit Tandon vs. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.reference: Rohit Tandon vs. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.relevance: Held that statements recorded under Section 50 PMLA are admissible and can make out a formidable case.

rules.case_name: Enforcement Directorate vs. Preeti Chandra
rules.citation: Order dated 04.08.2023 in SLP (Crl.) No. 7409 of 2023
rules.reference: Enforcement Directorate vs. Preeti Chandra
rules.relevance: Confirmed that the proviso to Section 45 of the PMLA confers discretion on the court to grant bail to women, rather than creating a mandatory right.

rules.case_name: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary and Others vs. Union of India and Others
rules.reference: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary and Others vs. Union of India and Others
rules.relevance: Held that money laundering is an independent offence and the twin conditions of Section 45 PMLA are mandatory.

rules.reference: Duty of advocates as officers of the court
rules.relevance: Advocates must make full and correct disclosure of material facts and assist the court fairly; misrepresentation of facts is strongly deprecated.

rules.reference: Supreme Court Rules 2013
rules.relevance: Mandates that SLPs be confined to pleadings before the lower court; the court used this to highlight the misrepresentation of facts by the appellant's counsel.

rules.case_name: Radhey Shyam & Anr. vs. Chhabi Nath & Ors.
rules.reference: Radhey Shyam & Anr. vs. Chhabi Nath & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that judicial orders of civil courts are not amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 226 and that no Letters Patent Appeal lies against orders passed under Article 227.

rules.case_name: Nusli Neville Wadia vs. New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
rules.reference: Nusli Neville Wadia vs. New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this High Court decision which held the Appellate Officer to be persona designata, finding it untenable in light of Supreme Court precedents.

rules.case_name: Thakur Das (Dead) by LRs Vs. State of M.P. & Anr.
rules.reference: Thakur Das (Dead) by LRs Vs. State of M.P. & Anr.
rules.relevance: Defined 'persona designata' and held that a judicial authority appointed by designation is not persona designata but acts as a court.

rules.case_name: Mukri Gopalan Vs. Cheppilat Puthanpurayil Aboobacker
rules.reference: Mukri Gopalan Vs. Cheppilat Puthanpurayil Aboobacker
rules.relevance: Supported the principle that an authority constituted by designation constitutes a class and functions as a court, not persona designata.

rules.reference: Article 226 and Article 227 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The court noted that the availability of writ jurisdiction under these articles provides a sufficient safeguard against jurisdictional errors by the appellate judicial officer.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: Defines the offences charged. Sections 147, 148, 149, and 364 are non-compoundable offences, affecting the scope for settlement-based quashing.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure
rules.relevance: Governs the taking of cognizance of offences by a Magistrate upon a police report. The court directed the Magistrate to take cognizance under this provision.

rules.case_name: Shambhu Kharwar v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
rules.reference: Shambhu Kharwar v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
rules.relevance: Held that in cases involving long-standing consensual relationships, the crucial ingredients of rape under Section 375 IPC may be absent even if a promise of marriage was made.

rules.case_name: Dharam Pal and Others vs. State of Haryana and Another
rules.reference: Dharam Pal and Others vs. State of Haryana and Another
rules.relevance: A Constitution Bench decision establishing that a Magistrate can summon persons named in column 2 of the charge sheet or others if satisfied of their involvement, affirming the principle that cognizance is of the offence, not the offender.

rules.case_name: Rattiram and Others vs. State of Madhya Pradesh
rules.reference: Rattiram and Others vs. State of Madhya Pradesh
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment for the principle that non-compliance with committal procedures does not vitiate trial unless prejudice or failure of justice is established.

rules.reference: Discretionary nature of back wages
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that reinstatement does not automatically entitle an employee to full back wages; factors such as delay in challenging termination, conduct, aptitude, and prior compensation are relevant to the quantum.

rules.case_name: P.G.I. Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh v. Raj Kumar
rules.reference: P.G.I. Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh v. Raj Kumar
rules.relevance: Reinforced that payment of back wages involves a discretionary element and no straight-jacket formula can be evolved; it must be dealt with based on the facts and circumstances of each case.

rules.case_name: Ranchhodji Chaturji Thakore vs. Superintendent Engineer, Gujarat Electricity Board
rules.reference: Ranchhodji Chaturji Thakore vs. Superintendent Engineer, Gujarat Electricity Board
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case because it involved disciplinary proceedings, whereas the present case involved termination solely due to criminal conviction without separate disciplinary proceedings.

rules.reference: Procedural Law regarding delay
rules.relevance: The court held that the issue of delay in filing the writ petition could not be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court as it was not raised before the High Court.

rules.reference: Circular dated 3rd September 1975 issued by Rajasthan State Electricity Board
rules.relevance: The court held this circular binding on the Corporation. It explicitly mandates that for the period from the date of dismissal to the date of acquittal, an acquitted employee should not be allowed pay and allowances less than what would have been admissible had he remained under suspension.

rules.case_name: Parkash Chand v. State of Himachal Pradesh
rules.reference: Parkash Chand v. State of Himachal Pradesh
rules.relevance: Clarified the essential ingredients of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, including the requirement of no undue advantage or cruel manner.

rules.case_name: Rakesh Kumar alias Babli v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Rakesh Kumar alias Babli v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Supported the view that replies to suggestions in cross-examination can establish the presence of the accused at the scene of the crime.

rules.case_name: Tarun Bora alias Alok Hazarika v. State of Assam
rules.reference: Tarun Bora alias Alok Hazarika v. State of Assam
rules.relevance: Held that suggestions made by defence counsel in cross-examination, if answered in a way that admits facts, can bind the accused and establish presence.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code
rules.relevance: The substantive offences for which the appellant was convicted by the High Court.

rules.case_name: Olga Tellis and Others v. Bombay Municipal Corporation and Others

rules.case_name: Bangalore Medical Trust v. B.S. Muddahalli

rules.case_name: Sahadeo Singh v. Union of India

rules.reference: He who seeks equity must come with clean hands

rules.reference: Motor Vehicles Act, 1939

rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that recruitment rules and eligibility criteria defined in a notification must be strictly followed. Benefits cannot be extended to categories of applicants not explicitly included in the notification.

rules.reference: Scope of Writ Challenge
rules.relevance: A court cannot scrutinize aspects of a selection process or list that were not challenged by the petitioner in the writ petition.

rules.reference: Limitation on judicial interference in recruitment after deadlines
rules.relevance: The court considered that judicial intervention to grant relief in recruitment matters is inappropriate when the statutory or procedural deadlines for application submission have already passed, especially if the applicant does not have a clear right to the claimed benefit.

rules.case_name: Bishnu Biswas v. Union of India
rules.reference: Bishnu Biswas v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Distinguished because the respondent did not challenge the inclusion of the interview/experience component as a new rule, but contested the merit comparison.

rules.reference: Discretion of Selection Committee
rules.relevance: A Selection Committee has the power to evolve criteria for determining suitability among candidates who meet the minimum qualifications, provided the criteria are rational and not arbitrary.

rules.case_name: Sanjay Singh & Anr vs U.P. Public Service Commission
rules.reference: Sanjay Singh & Anr vs U.P. Public Service Commission
rules.relevance: Established guidelines for moderation of marks to ensure uniformity in valuation when multiple examiners are involved, distinguishing it from scaling used for optional subjects.

rules.reference: Punjab Civil Services (Judicial Branch) Rules, 1951
rules.relevance: Governing rules for the examination, including qualification criteria and the absence of provisions for re-evaluation or grace marks.

rules.case_name: H.P. Public Service Commission v. Mukesh Thakur
rules.reference: H.P. Public Service Commission v. Mukesh Thakur
rules.relevance: Held that courts should not generally direct re-evaluation in the absence of a provision in the statute or statutory rules.

rules.case_name: Taniya Malik vs. The Registrar General of Delhi High Court
rules.reference: Taniya Malik vs. The Registrar General of Delhi High Court
rules.relevance: Distinguished on facts; while Taniya Malik held moderation unnecessary where marking was uniform, the present case involved severe prejudice due to strict marking and time constraints.

rules.case_name: Pramod Kumar Srivastava v. Bihar Public Service Commission
rules.reference: Pramod Kumar Srivastava v. Bihar Public Service Commission
rules.relevance: Reiterated that candidates have no right to claim revaluation if not provided for in the relevant rules.

rules.case_name: State of HP. v. Tara Dutt
rules.reference: State of HP. v. Tara Dutt
rules.relevance: Held that the exercise of power under Section 473 to condone delay must be by a speaking order indicating the court's satisfaction; absence of such an order is significant.

rules.case_name: Venka Radhamanohari v. Vanka Venkata Reddy
rules.reference: Venka Radhamanohari v. Vanka Venkata Reddy
rules.relevance: Established that in matrimonial offences involving cruelty, Section 473 should be liberally construed as the offence is often continuing, but the court must still apply its mind to the interest of justice.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajanlal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajanlal
rules.relevance: Laid down parameters for quashing FIRs under Section 482, including when proceedings are manifestly attended with mala fide or result in failure of justice.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code
rules.relevance: Identifies the charges in the FIR filed against the petitioner, which were quashed as part of the settlement.

rules.reference: Dowry Prohibition Act
rules.relevance: Identifies the charge read with IPC sections in the FIR filed against the petitioner, which was quashed as part of the settlement.

rules.case_name: Ashok Rangnath Magar v. Shrikant Govindrao Sangvikar
rules.reference: Ashok Rangnath Magar v. Shrikant Govindrao Sangvikar
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to hold that a High Court can dismiss a second appeal without formulating a substantial question of law if it is satisfied that no such question is involved.

rules.case_name: Md. Mohammad Ali (dead) by LRs v. Jagadish Kalita & Ors.
rules.reference: Md. Mohammad Ali (dead) by LRs v. Jagadish Kalita & Ors.
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case, noting that it involved a situation where the High Court overlooked a proposition of law, unlike the present case where no substantial question arose.

rules.reference: Limited scope of Second Appeal
rules.relevance: The High Court cannot substitute its own findings of fact for those of the first appellate court merely because another view is possible; interference is only permitted if the lower court's findings are based on no material.

rules.case_name: Vidyawati v. Man Mohan
rules.reference: Vidyawati v. Man Mohan
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case, observing that the plea raised by the legal representative there was not in consonance with the original defendant's plea, unlike the present case.

rules.case_name: South Delhi Municipal Corporation & Anr. v. Today Homes and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.
rules.reference: South Delhi Municipal Corporation & Anr. v. Today Homes and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment for the principle that civil court jurisdiction is impliedly barred only where a statute creates a right/liability and provides a complete machinery for enforcement.

rules.case_name: S.S. Chheena v. Vijay Kumar Mahajan & Anr.
rules.reference: S.S. Chheena v. Vijay Kumar Mahajan & Anr.
rules.relevance: Reiterated that abetment involves a mental process of instigation or intentional aid, requiring a clear mens rea and an active act.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. v. Ashok Kumar Srivastava
rules.reference: State of U.P. v. Ashok Kumar Srivastava
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that if circumstantial evidence is capable of two inferences, the one favoring the accused must be accepted, and great care must be taken in evaluation.

rules.case_name: Tulshiram Sahadu Suryawanshi and Ors. vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Tulshiram Sahadu Suryawanshi and Ors. vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to interpret Section 106 of the Evidence Act, stating it applies when facts are especially within the accused's knowledge.

rules.reference: False Explanation as Additional Circumstance
rules.relevance: An inconsistent or false explanation offered by the accused can be used as an additional circumstance to strengthen the chain of evidence against them.

rules.case_name: Amalendu Pal @ Jhantu v. State of West Bengal
rules.reference: Amalendu Pal @ Jhantu v. State of West Bengal
rules.relevance: Clarified that conviction under Section 306 IPC requires proof of direct or indirect acts of incitement proximate to the suicide, not merely harassment.

rules.case_name: Naval Kishore Singh v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Naval Kishore Singh v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Held that Section 313 Cr.P.C. examination is an essential part of a fair trial and must not be a formality; circumstances not put to the accused cannot be used against him.

rules.case_name: Anurag Soni v. State of Chhattisgarh
rules.reference: Anurag Soni v. State of Chhattisgarh
rules.relevance: Distinguishes between a false promise made with no intention to marry (vitiating consent) and a breach of a promise made in good faith.

rules.reference: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
rules.relevance: The court examined whether these provisions, inserted by the 2015 Amendment Act, applied to acts committed in 2015 before the amendment came into force.

rules.reference: Benefit of doubt on age
rules.relevance: In the absence of positive documentary evidence of age, the possibility of the prosecutrix being above 18 cannot be ruled out, entitling the accused to the benefit of doubt.

rules.reference: Consent and Misconception of Fact
rules.relevance: A mature and intelligent woman who knowingly enters into a relationship, even during the subsistence of her marriage, cannot claim that her consent was obtained under a misconception of fact regarding a promise to marry.

rules.case_name: Wellington v. Kirit Mehta
rules.reference: Wellington v. Kirit Mehta
rules.relevance: Established that a clause using permissive language or requiring fresh consent is not an arbitration agreement.

rules.reference: Attributes of Arbitration Agreement
rules.relevance: A valid arbitration agreement requires consensus ad idem to refer disputes to a private tribunal. Clauses requiring further consent or determination by parties are merely enabling provisions, not binding arbitration agreements.

rules.reference: Scope of arbitration clause in partnership deed
rules.relevance: The court held that a dispute regarding the dissolution of a partnership by mutual agreement falls within the scope of an arbitration clause covering disputes 'touching the partnership agreement'.

rules.reference: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
rules.relevance: Provides that an arbitration agreement is not discharged by the death of any party and is enforceable by or against the legal representative of the deceased.

rules.case_name: Khardah Company Ltd. v. Raymon & Company (India) Pvt. Ltd.
rules.reference: Khardah Company Ltd. v. Raymon & Company (India) Pvt. Ltd.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent for the principle that an arbitration clause cannot be enforced if the agreement of which it forms an integral part is held to be illegal or void, and that such declarations are within the jurisdiction of the Civil Court.

rules.reference: Limitation Act, 1963
rules.relevance: The court interpreted this provision to determine the starting point of the limitation period for specific performance suits.

rules.case_name: Almadsaliab Abdul Mulla (2) (Dead) v. Bibijan and Ors.
rules.reference: Almadsaliab Abdul Mulla (2) (Dead) v. Bibijan and Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that 'date fixed for performance' in Article 54 requires a definite, specified date in the calendar.

rules.case_name: Rathnavathi and Another v. Kavita Ganashamdas
rules.reference: Rathnavathi and Another v. Kavita Ganashamdas
rules.relevance: Confirmed that if no specific calendar date is fixed, limitation runs from the date of notice of refusal.

rules.case_name: Vinod Kumar v. Gangadhar
rules.reference: Vinod Kumar v. Gangadhar
rules.relevance: Held that a first appellate court must deal with all issues and evidence, not just preliminary ones.

rules.case_name: Madhukar v. Sangram
rules.reference: Madhukar v. Sangram
rules.relevance: Affirmed the duty of the High Court to decide all issues in a first appeal.

rules.case_name: Atley v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Atley v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Held that failure to prove motive is not fatal to the prosecution case if other circumstances complete the chain of evidence.

rules.reference: Custodial Death
rules.relevance: When death occurs in the custody of the accused, the burden shifts to them to provide a plausible explanation for the cause of death.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samal
rules.reference: Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samal
rules.relevance: Confirmed that a judge has the power to sift and weigh evidence for the limited purpose of finding out if a prima facie case exists, and that grave suspicion justifies framing a charge.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: The initial charge of abetment of suicide against the accused.

rules.case_name: State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh
rules.reference: State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh
rules.relevance: Established that at the stage of framing charges, the court need not meticulously judge the veracity of evidence or weigh probable defenses, but only look for strong suspicion.

rules.case_name: Expeditious Trial of Cases Under Section 138 of NI Act, 1881, In re
rules.reference: Expeditious Trial of Cases Under Section 138 of NI Act, 1881, In re
rules.relevance: Clarified that the observation in Meters and Instruments Ltd. v. Kanchan Mehta regarding closing proceedings without consent was not good law, reinforcing the necessity of consent for compounding.

rules.case_name: JIK Industries Limited & Ors. v. Amarlal V. Jamuni & Anr.
rules.reference: JIK Industries Limited & Ors. v. Amarlal V. Jamuni & Anr.
rules.relevance: Held that consent of the complainant is mandatory for compounding under Section 147 NI Act and distinguished quashing from compounding.

rules.reference: Sub-delegation of Power of Attorney
rules.relevance: A Power of Attorney holder cannot delegate functions to another person unless explicitly permitted in the instrument.

rules.case_name: A. C. Narayanan vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: A. C. Narayanan vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The larger Bench judgment in the same appeal established the legal principles regarding the validity of complaints filed by Power of Attorney holders, requiring explicit assertion of knowledge and authority.

rules.reference: Requirement of Personal Knowledge
rules.relevance: A Power of Attorney holder must have personal knowledge of the transaction to file a complaint and depose as a witness; this must be explicitly asserted in the complaint.

rules.case_name: Balmukand v. Veer Chand
rules.reference: Balmukand v. Veer Chand
rules.relevance: Held that the executing court is competent to deliver possession even if the decree for specific performance was silent on possession, as it is incidental to the sale.

rules.case_name: Hungerford Investment Trust Ltd. v. Haridas Mundhra and Ors.
rules.reference: Hungerford Investment Trust Ltd. v. Haridas Mundhra and Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that a court passing a decree for specific performance retains control over the decree even after it is passed.

rules.reference: Specific Relief Act, 1963
rules.relevance: Section 22(1) allows a plaintiff to ask for possession in an appropriate case. Section 22(2) states no such relief shall be granted unless specifically claimed, but the proviso allows amendment of the plaint 'at any stage of the proceedings'. The court interpreted 'proceedings' to include execution proceedings.

rules.reference: Transfer of Property Act, 1882
rules.relevance: Establishes that the seller is bound to give possession to the buyer upon execution of the sale deed, implying that the liability to deliver possession is inherent in a contract for sale.

rules.case_name: Lala Durga Prasad & Anr. v. Lala Deep Chand & Ors.
rules.reference: Lala Durga Prasad v. Lala Deep Chand
rules.relevance: Held that a sale to a subsequent purchaser with notice is voidable, and the purchaser holds the property subject to the prior contract's specific performance rights.

rules.case_name: Janata Dal vs. H.S. Chowdhary
rules.reference: Janata Dal vs. H.S. Chowdhary
rules.relevance: Distinguished as the third party there was not a victim, unlike the appellants in the present case who suffered loss due to the alleged scam.

rules.case_name: Sanjay Tiwari vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Sanjay Tiwari vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: Distinguished on the ground that the third party in that case had no connection to the proceedings, whereas the present appellants were actual victims of the alleged corrupt practices.

rules.reference: Corruption is an offence against the State
rules.relevance: The court held that corruption by public servants is an offence against the State and society at large, not a private dispute that can be settled by compromise.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: Defines the offences charged. Sections 147, 148, 149, and 364 are non-compoundable offences, affecting the scope for settlement-based quashing.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra vs. Vikram Anantrai Doshi
rules.reference: State of Maharashtra vs. Vikram Anantrai Doshi
rules.relevance: Held that financial frauds affecting societal interest and the economic spine of the nation cannot be regarded as cases with a predominantly civil character.

rules.reference: Distinction between False Promise and Breach of Promise
rules.relevance: A false promise made with fraudulent intention to seduce vitiates consent and may amount to rape, whereas a breach of promise is a civil wrong.

rules.case_name: Pramod Suryabhan Pawar v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Pramod Suryabhan Pawar v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Established the legal test for distinguishing between a 'false promise' to marry (which vitiates consent) and a 'breach of promise' (which does not). A false promise requires an intention to deceive at the time the promise was made.

rules.case_name: Deelip Singh v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Deelip Singh v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Distinguishes between passive submission and conscious decision, and between false promise and breach of promise to marry.

rules.reference: Consent and Misconception of Fact
rules.relevance: A mature and intelligent woman who knowingly enters into a relationship, even during the subsistence of her marriage, cannot claim that her consent was obtained under a misconception of fact regarding a promise to marry.

rules.case_name: Naim Ahamed v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: Naim Ahamed v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: Established that a mature, married woman who has consensual relations for years cannot claim rape based on a false promise to marry, as her consent is not vitiated by misconception of fact.

rules.case_name: State of Delhi v. Gyan Devi
rules.reference: State of Delhi v. Gyan Devi
rules.relevance: Established that at the stage of framing charge, the court examines materials only to see if a prima facie case exists, not to weigh the sufficiency of evidence.

rules.case_name: Chitresh Kumar Chopra v. State (Government of NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: Chitresh Kumar Chopra v. State (Government of NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: Held that at the charge framing stage, the court must determine if facts disclose ingredients of the offence, not whether it will lead to conviction.

rules.reference: Proximity and Mens Rea in Abetment
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that for conviction under Section 306, there must be a positive act proximate to the suicide with clear mens rea to instigate.

rules.case_name: State of M.P. v. Mohanlal Soni
rules.reference: State of M.P. v. Mohanlal Soni
rules.relevance: Confirmed that at the stage of framing charge, the court has to prima facie consider if there is sufficient ground for proceeding, not whether evidence is sufficient for conviction.

rules.case_name: State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy
rules.reference: State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy
rules.relevance: Established that at the stage of framing charge, the court must determine if there is ground for presuming the commission of the offence, without assessing probative value.

rules.reference: Interpretation of 'Possession' and 'Dispossession'
rules.relevance: The court held that 'possession' is a word of open texture; for vacant land, possession implies control and the power to exclude others. Loss of this control due to court delivery constitutes dispossession.

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: The court used this rule to establish that questions of right, title, or interest arising in Rule 97 proceedings must be determined by the executing court and not by a separate suit.

rules.case_name: Shankar Balwant Lokhande (dead) by Lrs. v. Chandrakant Shankar Lokhande and Anr.
rules.reference: Shankar Balwant Lokhande (dead) by Lrs. v. Chandrakant Shankar Lokhande and Anr.
rules.relevance: Distinguished on facts as it involved a preliminary decree under the Limitation Act of 1908 where no final decree had been passed, unlike the present case.

rules.case_name: Bholanath Karmakar and Ors. v. Madanmohan Karmakar
rules.reference: Bholanath Karmakar and Ors. v. Madanmohan Karmakar
rules.relevance: Overruled as it misread the law by holding that limitation for execution of a partition decree does not begin until engrossment on stamp paper.

rules.case_name: W.B. Essential Commodities Supply Corporation v. Swadesh Agro Farming and Storage Pvt. Ltd. and Anr.
rules.reference: W.B. Essential Commodities Supply Corporation v. Swadesh Agro Farming and Storage Pvt. Ltd. and Anr.
rules.relevance: Relied upon for the principle that execution applications must be presented within the prescribed time and that delay in drawing up the decree does not extend limitation.

rules.case_name: Indore Development Authority v. Manoharlal & Ors.
rules.reference: Indore Development Authority v. Manoharlal & Ors.
rules.relevance: Held that 'or' in Section 24(2) means 'and/nor'; lapse requires both non-possession and non-payment. Possession is taken via panchnama.

rules.case_name: Shiv Kumar & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.reference: Shiv Kumar & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.relevance: Overruled Manav Dharam Trust; held that a purchaser cannot claim lapse of acquisition under Section 24(2) to reopen concluded proceedings.

rules.case_name: Nand Kishore Gupta and Ors. v. State of U.P. and Ors.
rules.reference: Nand Kishore Gupta and Ors. v. State of U.P. and Ors.
rules.relevance: Held that development for residential purposes can be a complimentary public purpose to industrial development, weakening the argument that a change in land use created a fresh cause of action.

rules.case_name: Madhya Pradesh Housing Board v. Md. Shafi
rules.reference: Madhya Pradesh Housing Board v. Md. Shafi
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case to reject the argument that the public purpose 'establishment of diamond park' was vague, noting that the appellants were not prejudiced in filing objections.

rules.case_name: Bondu Ramaswamy v. Bangalore Development Authority
rules.reference: Bondu Ramaswamy v. Bangalore Development Authority
rules.relevance: Justified the High Court's discretionary relief of allotting developed plots to balance equities when acquisition proceedings are sustained despite procedural flaws.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Provides that if acts constitute an offence falling within two or more separate definitions of any law in force, the accused may be charged with and tried at one trial for each of such offences.

rules.reference: Corroboration of solitary witness testimony
rules.relevance: Corroboration is a rule of caution, not law; a conviction can be based on the testimony of a single credible witness if their testimony inspires confidence.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code
rules.relevance: Defines the offence of attempt to murder with common intention.

rules.reference: Reliability of Solitary Eye Witness
rules.relevance: The testimony of a solitary eye witness who is an injured person can be relied upon if it is of a sterling quality and corroborated by medical evidence and early disclosure, even if other witnesses turn hostile.

rules.case_name: Sanjay vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Sanjay vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: The appellant relied on this case to argue for a reduced sentence. The court distinguished it because Sanjay involved altering a conviction from Section 302 to 304 Part I, whereas the present case involved sentencing discretion under Section 307 where hurt was caused.

rules.case_name: Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration
rules.reference: Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration
rules.relevance: The Court relied on this decision to reject the 'hands off' doctrine, uphold prisoners' fundamental rights, and affirm the Court's continuing responsibility to ensure constitutional purposes are not defeated by prison administration.

rules.reference: Retention of Authority over Prisoner by Sentencing Judge
rules.relevance: The Court adopted the principle that sentencing courts should retain jurisdiction to ensure the prison system responds to the purposes of the sentence, treating sentences like mandatory injunctions.

rules.reference: Guidelines and Standard Operating Procedure for implementation of the scheme for support to poor prisoners
rules.relevance: The court adopted this SOP to alleviate the situation of undertrial prisoners by establishing empowered committees and funding mechanisms.

rules.reference: Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners
rules.relevance: Referenced to emphasize the habilitative value of imprisonment and the goal of ensuring offenders are able to lead law-abiding lives upon return to society.

rules.provision: Provisions regarding visitors and prisoner safeguards
rules.reference: Jail Manuals
rules.relevance: Mandates the appointment of visitors, including District Judges, to ensure strict compliance with safeguards for prisoners, particularly children.

rules.reference: Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988
rules.relevance: Declared unconstitutional for being manifestly arbitrary and lacking essential safeguards for in rem forfeiture.

rules.reference: Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016
rules.relevance: Held that the in rem forfeiture provision is punitive in nature and can only be applied prospectively.

rules.reference: Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988
rules.relevance: Declared unconstitutional for being manifestly arbitrary due to the absence of mens rea and lack of procedural safeguards.

rules.reference: Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016
rules.relevance: Held unconstitutional as it violated Article 20(1) by attempting to apply penal provisions retrospectively.

rules.case_name: Rayala Corporation (P) Ltd & Ors. v. Director of Enforcement, New Delhi
rules.reference: Rayala Corporation (P) Ltd & Ors. v. Director of Enforcement, New Delhi
rules.relevance: Distinguished because the corresponding provision in the 1947 Act had a proviso requiring adjudication before prosecution, which is absent in the 1973 Act.

rules.reference: The Representation of the People’s Act, 1951
rules.relevance: Requires full particulars of any alleged corrupt practice, including names, dates, and places of commission.

rules.reference: The Representation of the People’s Act, 1951
rules.relevance: Provides that election petitions are tried in accordance with the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, subject to the RP Act.

rules.reference: The Representation of the People’s Act, 1951
rules.relevance: Provides ground for declaring election void if the result was materially affected by improper acceptance of nomination.

rules.reference: The Representation of the People’s Act, 1951
rules.relevance: Defines 'undue influence' as a corrupt practice involving direct or indirect interference with the free exercise of electoral rights.

rules.reference: The Representation of the People’s Act, 1951
rules.relevance: Provides ground for declaring election void if a corrupt practice has been committed by the returned candidate.

rules.reference: National Council for Teacher Education Act, 1993
rules.relevance: Allows the Central Government to issue policy directions to the NCTE, but the Court held that such directions are subject to judicial review if arbitrary or contrary to law.

rules.reference: NCTE Regulations, 2009
rules.relevance: Defines the distinct aims of D.El.Ed. (preparing teachers for Classes I-VIII) and B.Ed. (preparing teachers for Classes VI-XII), establishing that B.Ed. is not designed for primary pedagogy.

rules.reference: Right to Education Act, 2009
rules.relevance: Empowers the academic authority (NCTE) to prescribe minimum qualifications for teachers, emphasizing the need for trained personnel to ensure quality education.

rules.case_name: Dilip Kumar Ghosh v. Chairman
rules.reference: Dilip Kumar Ghosh v. Chairman
rules.relevance: Held that B.Ed. curriculum lacks specific child psychology training required for primary teaching, distinguishing it from primary-specific training.

rules.case_name: Employees’ State Insurance Corporation v. Union of India
rules.reference: Employees’ State Insurance Corporation v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Establishes that administrative instructions cannot amend or supersede statutory rules.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure
rules.relevance: The court relied on this provision to establish that a person cannot take recourse to revision or inherent powers after a revision has been barred or abandoned.

rules.case_name: Krishnan & Anr. v. Krishnaveni & Ors.
rules.reference: Krishnan & Anr. v. Krishnaveni & Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to hold that inherent powers under Section 482 must be exercised sparingly and cannot be used to circumvent the bar on revision under Section 397(3).

rules.case_name: M/s. SWIL Ltd. v. State of Delhi & Anr.
rules.reference: M/s. SWIL Ltd. v. State of Delhi & Anr.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to confirm that there is no bar under Section 190 for issuing process against other persons if material on record indicates their involvement.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: Defines the offences charged. Sections 147, 148, 149, and 364 are non-compoundable offences, affecting the scope for settlement-based quashing.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Determines whether a party can file a revision in the High Court if they have already filed one in the Sessions Court. The court interpreted this to mean that a revision on a distinct issue (merits vs. quantum) is not barred.

rules.case_name: Khatri (II) v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Khatri (II) v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to hold that the State cannot avoid its constitutional obligation to provide services, such as medical aid, on the ground of financial constraints.

rules.case_name: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shuntha
rules.reference: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shuntha
rules.relevance: The court referred to this decision to determine that the question of whether government hospital services fall under the Consumer Protection Act had already been settled, allowing the court to focus on Article 21.

rules.case_name: Pt. Paramanand Katara v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.reference: Pt. Paramanand Katara v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to emphasize the obligation of the State and doctors to render immediate medical aid to injured persons to preserve life.

rules.case_name: Lata Singh vs. State of U.P. and Ors.
rules.reference: Lata Singh vs. State of U.P. and Ors.
rules.relevance: The Court relied on this judgment to affirm that inter-caste marriages are in the national interest and violence against such couples is illegal.

rules.case_name: Rudal Sah v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Rudal Sah v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to establish that adequate compensation can be awarded for the violation of constitutional rights under Part III.

rules.reference: Adverse possession requires hostile possession; possession of a tenant is permissive
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that a tenant's possession is permissive against the landlord and cannot constitute adverse possession during the subsistence of the tenancy.

rules.reference: Limitation period for suit based on title runs from the date of transfer or when dispute arises
rules.relevance: The court determined that the limitation period for the plaintiff's suit commenced from the date of the sale deed (1966) or when the dispute arose, not from 1944.

rules.case_name: Ram Nagina Rai & Anr. v. Deo Kumar Rai (Deceased) by LRs & Anr.
rules.reference: Ram Nagina Rai & Anr. v. Deo Kumar Rai (Deceased) by LRs & Anr.
rules.relevance: Held that when possession is initially permissive, it must be specifically pleaded and proved when it becomes adverse.

rules.case_name: Sunil Kumar & Anr. vs. Ram Parkash & Ors.
rules.reference: Sunil Kumar & Anr. vs. Ram Parkash & Ors.
rules.relevance: Establishes that a Karta can alienate Joint Hindu Family property for legal necessity or benefit of the estate, binding the interests of coparceners.

rules.case_name: Ravinder Kaur Grewal & Ors. v. Manjit Kaur & Ors.
rules.reference: Ravinder Kaur Grewal & Ors. v. Manjit Kaur & Ors.

rules.reference: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Amendment) Act, 1957 (Act XXXVIII of 1957)

rules.case_name: Byram Pestonji Gariwala v. Union Bank of India
