rules.case_name: Pradyat Kumar Bose vs. The Hon’ble the Chief Justice of Calcutta High Court
rules.reference: Pradyat Kumar Bose vs. The Hon’ble the Chief Justice of Calcutta High Court
rules.relevance: Establishes that deputing a competent official to enquire and report does not amount to delegation of essential statutory functions.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: The court examined whether the allegations in the complaint prima facie constituted the offences of criminal breach of trust and cheating, noting the lack of specific evidence to support the claim of prior repayment.

rules.case_name: Thermax Limited and Others Vs. KM. Johny and Others
rules.reference: Thermax Limited and Others Vs. KM. Johny and Others
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that criminal proceedings can be quashed only if there is an absolute absence of requisite averments to make out a case of cheating, distinguishing simple civil disputes.

rules.case_name: Ravindra Kumar Madanlal Goenka and Another vs. Rugmini Ram Raghav Spinners Private Limited
rules.reference: Ravindra Kumar Madanlal Goenka and Another vs. Rugmini Ram Raghav Spinners Private Limited
rules.relevance: Supports the proposition that the availability of a civil remedy does not preclude criminal proceedings if the allegations disclose a criminal offence.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code
rules.relevance: The specific offences of cheating and criminal conspiracy alleged in the FIR.

rules.relevance: Established that the High Court can exercise jurisdiction under Section 482 to quash proceedings even if an application for discharge is pending before the Magistrate.

rules.case_name: Naim Ahamed v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: Naim Ahamed v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: Established that a mature, married woman who has consensual relations for years cannot claim rape based on a false promise to marry, as her consent is not vitiated by misconception of fact.

rules.reference: Consent and Misconception of Fact

rules.relevance: Distinguishes between a false promise made with no intention to marry (vitiating consent) and a breach of a promise made in good faith.

rules.reference: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
rules.relevance: The court examined whether these provisions, inserted by the 2015 Amendment Act, applied to acts committed in 2015 before the amendment came into force.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: The specific charge of rape under which the FIR was registered.

rules.case_name: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Assn. v. Union of India

rules.reference: Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli v. State of Bombay

rules.case_name: Yunis Alias Kariya vs. State of M.P.

rules.relevance: Establishes that the presumption under Section 139 includes the existence of a legally enforceable debt and that the burden is on the accused to rebut this presumption.

rules.case_name: Goa Plast (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Chico Ursula D'Souza
rules.reference: Goa Plast (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Chico Ursula D'Souza
rules.relevance: Established that Section 138 applies when a cheque is dishonoured due to 'stop payment' instructions, not just insufficiency of funds.

rules.case_name: K.N. Beena vs. Muniyappan And Anr
rules.reference: K.N. Beena vs. Muniyappan And Anr
rules.relevance: Held that the burden of proving that a cheque was not issued for discharge of a lawful debt lies on the accused.

rules.case_name: M.S. Narayana Menon v. State of Kerala
rules.reference: M.S. Narayana Menon v. State of Kerala
rules.relevance: Established that presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 are rebuttable by preponderance of probabilities, not proof beyond reasonable doubt.

rules.case_name: Kishan Rao Vs. Shankargouda
rules.reference: Kishan Rao Vs. Shankargouda
rules.relevance: Distinguished on facts as the accused in that case failed to raise any probable defence, whereas the present accused raised a probable defence regarding financial capacity.

rules.reference: Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967
rules.relevance: Empowers courts to take measures to keep the identity and address of witnesses secret if their life is in danger.

rules.reference: National Investigation Agency Act
rules.relevance: In pari materia with Section 44 of the UAPA regarding witness protection.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Allows police to request exclusion of parts of witness statements if disclosure is not essential for justice or is inexpedient in public interest.

rules.reference: Balance between Fair Trial and Witness Protection
rules.relevance: The court must balance the statutory right to disclosure under Section 207 Cr.P.C. with the statutory duty to protect witnesses under Section 44 UAPA.

rules.case_name: Mohd. Hussain v. State (GNCTD)
rules.reference: Mohd. Hussain v. State (GNCTD)
rules.relevance: Establishes the accused's right to receive copies of witnesses' statements to mount an effective defence.

rules.case_name: Karam Kaur v. Jalandhar Improvement Trust and Others
rules.reference: Karam Kaur v. Jalandhar Improvement Trust and Others
rules.relevance: Cited to support the argument that condoning a delay of more than ten years constitutes an abuse of the process of law.

rules.case_name: Md. Alimuddin v. Waizuddin and Anr.
rules.reference: Md. Alimuddin v. Waizuddin and Anr.
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case because in Md. Alimuddin, an application for extension was granted, whereas in the present case, the application was dismissed on merits due to lack of evidence of effort.

rules.case_name: Gomathinayagam Pillai & Ors. vs Palaniswami Nadar
rules.reference: Gomathinayagam Pillai & Ors. vs Palaniswami Nadar
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that a purchaser does not need to produce money or a concluded financing scheme to prove readiness and willingness.

rules.case_name: Johri Singh v. Sukh Pal Singh and Ors.
rules.reference: Johri Singh v. Sukh Pal Singh and Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to establish that the power to extend time is discretionary and can be exercised even after the expiry of the originally fixed period, but depends on the conduct of the party.

rules.case_name: Katta Sujatha Reddy v. Siddamsetty Infra Projects (P) Ltd. & Ors.
rules.reference: Katta Sujatha Reddy v. Siddamsetty Infra Projects (P) Ltd. & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that the 2018 Amendment to the Specific Relief Act is prospective and does not apply to transactions occurring prior to its enforcement.

rules.case_name: Board of Trustees for the Port of Kolkata v. Canoro Resources Ltd.
rules.reference: Board of Trustees for the Port of Kolkata v. Canoro Resources Ltd.
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court held that observations in this case regarding Sections 59 and 61 of the MPT Act were obiter dicta and not binding on the interpretation of the PP Act.

rules.reference: Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971
rules.relevance: Authorizes the removal of goods displayed or spread on public premises without authority, supporting the interpretation that ownership is irrelevant to the power of removal.

rules.reference: Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971
rules.relevance: Empowers the Estate Officer to dispose of property left on public premises by unauthorized occupants, including goods of third parties, to recover arrears.

rules.reference: Major Port Trusts Act, 1963
rules.relevance: The court held these sections, which deal with lien based on privity of contract, are not applicable to proceedings under the PP Act.

rules.case_name: Board of Trustees for the Port of Calcutta v. Indian Rayon Corpn. Ltd.
rules.reference: Board of Trustees for the Port of Calcutta v. Indian Rayon Corpn. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Referenced to establish that it dealt exclusively with lien under the MPT Act and did not conflict with the powers under Section 6 of the PP Act.

rules.reference: Tender Documents
rules.relevance: The court interpreted these clauses to determine if a show cause notice triggered the disclosure requirement for 'initiation of action for blacklisting'.

rules.reference: Bid Document dated 25.11.2016
rules.relevance: The court examined these clauses to determine the scope of FCI's power to blacklist and whether the show cause notice adequately referenced the basis for the proposed action.

rules.case_name: Haryana Financial Corporation v. Kalash Chandra Ahuja
rules.reference: Haryana Financial Corporation v. Kalash Chandra Ahuja
rules.relevance: Addressed the 'prejudice' argument; the court distinguished this case by holding that the extreme nature of blacklisting itself causes prejudice if the specific penalty is not notified.

rules.case_name: Basanti Prasad vs. Bihar School Examination Board and others
rules.reference: Basanti Prasad vs. Bihar School Examination Board and others
rules.relevance: Holds that delay in filing a writ petition can be condoned if satisfactorily explained and no third-party rights are affected, as the Limitation Act does not strictly apply to writ jurisdiction.

rules.case_name: Gorkha Security Services vs. Government (NCT of Delhi) & Ors.
rules.reference: Gorkha Security Services vs. Government (NCT of Delhi) & Ors.
rules.relevance: Establishes that a show cause notice must expressly communicate the intention to blacklist to provide a meaningful opportunity to the affected party to defend against such a severe penalty.

rules.case_name: P. K. Haneefa v. State of Kerala
rules.reference: P. K. Haneefa v. State of Kerala
rules.relevance: Held that Rule 2(b) creates a mandatory quota for direct recruitment and consequently a quota for in-service candidates; appointments in excess of quota do not confer superior seniority.

rules.reference: Kerala State and Subordinate Services Rules 1958
rules.relevance: This rule allows the Commission to consider other qualifications as equivalent to special qualifications in cases where acceptance of equivalent qualifications is provided for in the rules.

rules.reference: Kerala State and Subordinate Services Rules 1958
rules.relevance: This rule provides the legal basis for accepting qualifications not specifically prescribed, if they are recognized by executive order as equivalent, found acceptable by the Commission under Rule 13(b)(i), or presuppose the acquisition of the lower prescribed qualification.

rules.case_name: Jyoti K K v Kerala Public Service Commission
rules.reference: Jyoti K K v Kerala Public Service Commission
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this precedent because, in Jyoti K K, the higher qualification (Degree) clearly presupposed the lower qualification (Diploma) in the same faculty hierarchy, whereas the DHIC did not necessarily presuppose the Sanitary Inspector's Certificate.

rules.reference: Presumption of Lower Qualification
rules.relevance: The principle that for a higher qualification to be accepted under Rule 10(a)(ii), it must clearly indicate or presuppose (subsume) the acquisition of the lower qualification prescribed for the post.

rules.reference: Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
rules.relevance: Provides that in any proceedings for contempt, it may be shown that the alleged contemnor had not intended to insult the dignity of the court or interfere with the due course of justice; the court considered whether the breach substantially interfered with justice.

rules.case_name: P.N. Duda v. P. Shiv Shanker & Ors.
rules.reference: P.N. Duda v. P. Shiv Shanker & Ors.
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that information inviting court action should be placed before the Chief Justice in Chambers if the informant is not named in Section 15 of the Act.

rules.case_name: Rama Narang vs. Ramesh Narang & Another
rules.reference: Rama Narang vs. Ramesh Narang & Another
rules.relevance: Clarified that wilful violation of terms of a consent decree or undertaking can amount to contempt, rejecting the distinction that fraud on a party cannot be contempt.

rules.case_name: Babu Ram Gupta vs. Sudhir Bhasin
rules.reference: Babu Ram Gupta vs. Sudhir Bhasin
rules.relevance: Distinguished between breach of consent orders (fraud on party) and breach of undertakings (fraud on court), though later clarified by Rama Narang.

rules.reference: Subsequent conduct as evidence of intent
rules.relevance: While contempt is determined by the act of disobedience, subsequent conduct can reveal whether the breach was due to inability or a design to hoodwink the court.

rules.case_name: A. C. Narayanan vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: A. C. Narayanan vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The larger Bench judgment in the same appeal established the legal principles regarding the validity of complaints filed by Power of Attorney holders, requiring explicit assertion of knowledge and authority.

rules.reference: Requirement of Personal Knowledge
rules.relevance: A Power of Attorney holder must have personal knowledge of the transaction to file a complaint and depose as a witness; this must be explicitly asserted in the complaint.

rules.reference: Sub-delegation of Power of Attorney
rules.relevance: A Power of Attorney holder cannot delegate functions to another person unless explicitly permitted in the instrument.

rules.case_name: Ashutosh Ashok Parasrampuria v. Gharrkul Industries Pvt. Ltd.
rules.reference: Ashutosh Ashok Parasrampuria v. Gharrkul Industries Pvt. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Held that High Courts should not quash complaints unless unimpeachable evidence shows the director could not have been concerned with the issuance of cheques.

rules.case_name: A.C. Narayanan vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
rules.reference: A.C. Narayanan vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
rules.relevance: Established that a power-of-attorney holder or representative must have personal knowledge of the transaction and that such knowledge must be explicitly asserted in the complaint.

rules.reference: Quashing of proceedings for lack of specific allegations
rules.relevance: Proceedings against accused persons who do not reside with the couple and against whom no specific allegations of harassment are made may be quashed.

rules.reference: Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961
rules.relevance: Prohibits giving and taking of dowry; the court examined if the sister was involved in such acts.

rules.reference: Nullity of investigation in violation of stay order
rules.relevance: An investigation conducted in violation of an express judicial stay order is a nullity in law and cannot be relied upon.

rules.reference: Effect of Divorce Decree on Criminal Liability
rules.relevance: The court observed that a divorce decree does not automatically wipe out criminal offences committed prior to or during the marriage.

rules.case_name: Vinay Tyagi vs. Irshad Ali alias Deepak and others
rules.reference: Vinay Tyagi vs. Irshad Ali alias Deepak and others
rules.relevance: Establishes that a Magistrate must consider all reports (primary and supplementary) cumulatively before taking cognizance, unless a higher court directs otherwise.

rules.case_name: Addanki Narayanappa v. Bhaskara Krishnappa
rules.reference: Addanki Narayanappa v. Bhaskara Krishnappa
rules.relevance: Held that a partner's interest in partnership assets is movable property, even if the assets include immovable property, and thus a deed transferring such interest does not require registration.

rules.case_name: Narhari v. Sankar
rules.reference: Narhari v. Sankar
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that where there is one trial and one decision, the dismissal of one appeal on technical grounds does not bar another appeal on res judicata.

rules.case_name: Sheodan Singh v. Mst. Daryao Kaur
rules.reference: Sheodan Singh v. Mst. Daryao Kaur
rules.relevance: Distinguished on the basis that the subject matter and issues in the present case were different from those in the earlier suit.

rules.reference: Indian Contract Act, 1872
rules.relevance: Applied to hold that when an agreement is discovered to be void, a person who received an advantage under it is bound to restore it or make compensation.

rules.case_name: Bildhu Lal v. Deccan Banking Company Ltd
rules.reference: Bildhu Lal v. Deccan Banking Company Ltd
rules.relevance: Relied upon to support the interpretation that Section 65 allows recovery of money paid under an agreement discovered to be void.

rules.case_name: Subramaniam v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.reference: Subramaniam v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.relevance: Held that the circumstance of husband and wife living together does not conclusively prove guilt in the absence of evidence of violence.

rules.case_name: Devi Lal v. State of Rajasthan
rules.reference: Devi Lal v. State of Rajasthan
rules.relevance: Reiterated that if two views are possible in circumstantial evidence, the benefit of doubt must go to the accused.

rules.case_name: Gargi v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Gargi v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Affirmed that Section 106 of the Evidence Act does not absolve the prosecution of its primary burden of proof.

rules.case_name: Eswarappa alias Doopada Eswarappa v. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: Eswarappa alias Doopada Eswarappa v. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: Relied on regarding medical jurisprudence, specifically that absence of marks of violence or struggle suggests suicide rather than homicidal hanging.

rules.case_name: Tulshiram Sahadu Suryawanshi and Ors. vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Tulshiram Sahadu Suryawanshi and Ors. vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to interpret Section 106 of the Evidence Act, stating it applies when facts are especially within the accused's knowledge.

rules.reference: Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945
rules.relevance: The Appellants held valid Wholesale Drug Licenses under these forms, which would negate liability even if the substance were classified solely as a drug.

rules.reference: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940
rules.relevance: Exempted dual-use substances (capable of use in both food and drug manufacture) from the licensing requirements of Chapter IV.

rules.case_name: R.P. Kapur Vs. State of Punjab
rules.reference: R.P. Kapur Vs. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Established that inherent jurisdiction can be exercised where no legal evidence is adduced or evidence is manifestly inconsistent with the accusation.

rules.reference: Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945
rules.relevance: Reinforced the exemption for dual-use substances from Chapter IV requirements.

rules.reference: Food Safety and Standards Regulations, 2016
rules.relevance: Specifically listed pyridoxal-5-phosphate as a food ingredient.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Value Added Tax Act, 2008
rules.relevance: Creates a deeming fiction that where exempt goods are produced as by-products during the manufacture of taxable goods, the purchased goods are deemed to have been used in the manufacture of taxable goods.

rules.provision: Section 13(1)(a) read with S. No. 2(ii) of the Table

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Value Added Tax Act, 2008
rules.relevance: Restricts ITC to the extent of tax payable on sale value if goods are sold at a price lower than the cost price; the court interpreted the scope of 'goods' here.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Value Added Tax Act, 2008

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Value Added Tax Rules, 2006

rules.case_name: K. Srinivas Rao v. D.A. Deepa
rules.reference: K. Srinivas Rao v. D.A. Deepa
rules.relevance: Establishes that making unfounded defamatory allegations and filing false complaints against a spouse amounts to mental cruelty.

rules.reference: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
rules.relevance: Defines 'domestic relationship' to include live-in relationships, supporting a broader interpretation of 'wife' under Section 125 Cr.P.C.

rules.case_name: Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav v. Anantrao Shivram Adhav

rules.case_name: Tulsa and Ors. v. Durghatiya & Ors.
rules.reference: Tulsa and Ors. v. Durghatiya & Ors.

rules.case_name: Ashok Dulichand v. Madhavlal Dube

rules.case_name: Mis Shah Raichand Amulakh (D) by his heir v. Union of India and Ors.

rules.case_name: Roshanlal Kuthalia and Ors. v. R.B. Mohan Singh Oberai

rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to interpret 'other cause of like nature' in Section 14 of the Limitation Act broadly, covering cases where proceedings fail due to reasons other than strict jurisdictional defects, such as the remedy being inappropriate.

rules.reference: Indian Railways Act, 1890
rules.relevance: This section mandates that claims for refund of overcharges or excess payments must be preferred in writing within six months from the date of delivery of goods. The court held that this specific statutory limitation applies to the petitioner's claim.

rules.reference: Contract Law: Novation and Mutual Agreement

rules.reference: Karnataka Ownership Flats (Regulation of the Promotion of Construction, Sale, Management and Transfer) Act, 1972

rules.relevance: Held that an allottee cannot be made to wait indefinitely for possession and is entitled to a refund with compensation.

rules.case_name: Banda Development Authority, Banda v. Moti Lal Agarwal

rules.reference: Non-compoundable nature of offence

rules.reference: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009

rules.reference: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007
rules.relevance: The court directed the Central Government to exercise powers under this section to issue directions to States for effective implementation.

rules.case_name: Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India and Another
rules.reference: Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India and Another

rules.reference: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009

rules.reference: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009

rules.case_name: Ramashish Yadav v. State of Bihar

rules.reference: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989

rules.relevance: Defines the offence of robbery with hurt, for which the respondent was convicted.

rules.case_name: Baiju alias Bharosa v. State of Madhya Pradesh

rules.relevance: Guides the application of presumptions under Section 114 of the Evidence Act regarding possession of stolen property.

rules.case_name: A Shanker v. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: A Shanker v. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: Cited to support the principle that normal discrepancies due to errors of observation or memory do not render evidence unreliable if they do not affect the core of the case.

rules.case_name: Jadunath Singh v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Jadunath Singh v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Held that absence of a test identification parade is not fatal in all cases.

rules.case_name: Ramanbhai Naranbhai Patel v. State of Gujarat
rules.reference: Ramanbhai Naranbhai Patel v. State of Gujarat
rules.relevance: Clarified that absence of a test identification parade does not make eyewitness evidence inadmissible or useless; value depends on facts and circumstances.

rules.reference: Substantive Evidence vs. Corroboration
rules.relevance: The substantive evidence is the identification in court; a test identification parade is a rule of prudence for corroboration, not a mandatory requirement for admissibility.

rules.case_name: Naval Kishore Singh v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Naval Kishore Singh v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Held that Section 313 Cr.P.C. examination is an essential part of a fair trial and must not be a formality; circumstances not put to the accused cannot be used against him.

rules.reference: Benefit of doubt on age

rules.reference: Standard for exercising power under Section 319 Cr.P.C.
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that summoning an additional accused requires evidence that is more than prima facie but short of satisfaction that unrebutted evidence would lead to conviction, and cannot be based on mere suspicion.

rules.case_name: Hardeep Singh and Ors. Vs. State of Punjab & Ors.
rules.reference: Hardeep Singh and Ors. Vs. State of Punjab & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that the power under Section 319 Cr.P.C. is discretionary and extraordinary, requiring strong and cogent evidence more than a prima facie case but short of satisfaction that unrebutted evidence would lead to conviction.

rules.case_name: Sagar v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
rules.reference: Sagar v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
rules.relevance: Reiterated the caution that the power under Section 319 CrPC must be exercised sparingly and only when circumstances warrant, applying the Hardeep Singh test.

rules.reference: Appellate court's duty to appreciate evidence rather than remand
rules.relevance: The court held that the High Court should have appreciated the material on record to decide on summoning rather than remanding the matter, to avoid prolonging litigation.

rules.case_name: Sagar vs. State of U.P. and Anr.
rules.reference: Sagar vs. State of U.P. and Anr.
rules.relevance: Reinforced the caution that the power under Section 319 should be exercised sparingly and only when circumstances warrant, applying the test laid down in Hardeep Singh.

rules.case_name: B. Madhuri Goud v. B. Damodar Reddy
rules.reference: B. Madhuri Goud v. B. Damodar Reddy
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment for the principle that 'sufficient cause' under the Limitation Act should be given a liberal construction to advance sustainable justice.

rules.case_name: Jotiba Limbaji Kanashenavar v. Ramappa Jotiba Kanashenavar
rules.reference: Jotiba Limbaji Kanashenavar v. Ramappa Jotiba Kanashenavar
rules.relevance: The court distinguished the High Court's reliance on this judgment, holding that the rule against converting simultaneous remedies into consecutive ones cannot be applied as a rigid straitjacket formula.

rules.case_name: Bhanu Kumar Jain v. Archana Kumar and another
rules.reference: Bhanu Kumar Jain v. Archana Kumar and another
rules.relevance: Held that the right to appeal is a statutory right and a defendant can challenge the merits of the suit in a first appeal even if an application under Order IX Rule 13 CPC was dismissed.

rules.case_name: Neerja Realtors (P) Ltd. v. Janglu (Dead) Through Legal Representative
rules.reference: Neerja Realtors (P) Ltd. v. Janglu (Dead) Through Legal Representative
rules.relevance: Confirmed that a defendant has two options (appeal or Order IX Rule 13 application) and that the right of appeal is not taken away by filing an application under Order IX Rule 13.

rules.case_name: Bhivchandra Shankar More v. Balu Gangaram More and others
rules.reference: Bhivchandra Shankar More v. Balu Gangaram More and others
rules.relevance: Affirmed that the scope of Order IX Rule 13 CPC and Section 96(2) CPC are entirely different and that dismissal of the former does not prohibit filing the latter.

rules.reference: Scheduled Castes and The Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
rules.relevance: Defines the offence of intentionally insulting or intimidating a member of a Scheduled Caste or Tribe with intent to humiliate in public view. The court examined whether the complaint disclosed these essential ingredients.

rules.case_name: Swaran Singh & Ors. v. State through Standing Counsel & Ors.
rules.reference: Swaran Singh & Ors. v. State through Standing Counsel & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that 'place within public view' does not include incidents inside a building unless members of the public (other than relatives/friends) are present.

rules.case_name: Hitesh Verma vs. The State of Uttarakhand & Anr.
rules.reference: Hitesh Verma vs. The State of Uttarakhand & Anr.
rules.relevance: Established that the charge-sheet must outline specific utterances to ascertain if they attract Section 3(1)(x) of the SC/ST Act, particularly regarding casteist remarks.

rules.reference: Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
rules.relevance: Defines the offence of intentionally insulting or intimidating with intent to humiliate a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe in any place within public view.

rules.case_name: Fiona Shrikhande and Anr. vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Fiona Shrikhande and Anr. vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Clarified that mere abuse is insufficient for conviction under Section 504 IPC; the insult must be of a degree likely to provoke a breach of public peace.

rules.case_name: Bani Singh and Others v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Bani Singh and Others v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to support the view that cases should not be decided or dismissed for default when counsel is absent.

rules.reference: Order V Rule 2(35) of the Supreme Court Rules, 2013
rules.relevance: The court referred to this rule regarding the powers of the Judge In-Chambers to grant exemption from surrendering and the procedure for non-prosecution if exemption is refused.

rules.reference: Order XXII Rule 5 of the Supreme Court Rules, 2013
rules.relevance: The court cited this rule to establish the requirement for convicts to surrender or seek exemption before filing a Special Leave Petition.

rules.case_name: Sunil Batra (II) vs. Delhi Administration
rules.reference: Sunil Batra (II) vs. Delhi Administration
rules.relevance: The court referred to this case to support the idea that lawyers designated by courts should have facilities to communicate with prisoners to address legal grievances.

rules.case_name: Madan Lal Kapoor v. Rajiv Thapar and Others
rules.reference: Madan Lal Kapoor v. Rajiv Thapar and Others
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent for the principle that a criminal case cannot be dismissed for default in the absence of counsel.

rules.case_name: Krishnanand v. State of M.P.
rules.reference: Krishnanand v. State of M.P.
rules.relevance: Cited by the defense to argue that the burden of proving benami transactions rests strictly on the prosecution; the court acknowledged the principle but applied it in conjunction with evidentiary presumptions.

rules.reference: Distinction between Criminal Conspiracy and Common Intention
rules.relevance: The court relied on the principle that failure to prove criminal conspiracy (Section 120B) does not automatically negate the existence of common intention (Section 34) if the latter is proved by independent evidence.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898

rules.case_name: Shoo Swarup v. The King Emperor
rules.reference: Shoo Swarup v. The King Emperor
rules.relevance: Established that the presumption of innocence is not weakened by an acquittal and that the High Court is entitled to reach its own conclusions on evidence.

rules.reference: Standard for conviction on circumstantial evidence
rules.relevance: Circumstantial evidence must be complete, consistent only with guilt, and wholly inconsistent with innocence to sustain a conviction.

rules.reference: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972
rules.relevance: The court held that forfeiture under this clause requires the misconduct to constitute an offence involving moral turpitude committed in the course of employment, and typically implies conviction.

rules.case_name: Jaswant Singh Gill v. Bharat Coking Coal Limited
rules.reference: Jaswant Singh Gill v. Bharat Coking Coal Limited
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to hold that forfeiture under Section 4(6)(b)(ii) is permissible only if the employee is convicted for an offence involving moral turpitude, and that the Act prevails over employer rules.

rules.case_name: Beed District Central Coop. Bank Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Beed District Central Coop. Bank Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to interpret 'terms' in Section 4(5) as meaning all terms of the contract, preventing the employee from cherry-picking between statute and contract.

rules.reference: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972
rules.relevance: The court interpreted this provision to mean that an employee is entitled to better terms under any award, agreement, or contract, which includes all terms of the contract, not just the quantum of gratuity.

rules.reference: The General Clauses Act, 1897
rules.relevance: The court used this definition to establish that an 'offence' must be an act or omission made punishable by law, placing it in the realm of criminal law.

rules.case_name: Mukut Bihari & Anr. Vs. State of Rajasthan
rules.reference: Mukut Bihari & Anr. Vs. State of Rajasthan

rules.case_name: Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka

rules.relevance: Summarized general principles regarding the powers of appellate courts in appeals against acquittal, including the double presumption of innocence and the requirement of substantial and compelling reasons for interference.

rules.relevance: The court held that demand and acceptance must be proved by cogent evidence and beyond reasonable doubt, not merely by preponderance of probabilities.

rules.case_name: Meena (Smt) w/o Balwant Hemke vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Meena (Smt) w/o Balwant Hemke vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to hold that mere recovery of currency notes and a positive phenolphthalein test are insufficient to establish guilt without proof of demand and acceptance.

rules.case_name: Ayyasami vs. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.reference: Ayyasami vs. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to support the requirement of corroboration for the testimony of an interested witness in corruption cases.

rules.case_name: D. Devaraja v. Obais Sanders Hussain
rules.reference: D. Devaraja v. Obais Sanders Hussain
rules.relevance: Reaffirmed that Section 197 does not extend to every act done by a public servant while in service, but only those in discharge of official duty.

rules.case_name: A. Srinivasulu v. State Rep. by the Inspector of Police
rules.reference: A. Srinivasulu v. State Rep. by the Inspector of Police
rules.relevance: Distinguished on facts; involved criminal conspiracy where co-conspirators were protected, whereas the present case involves direct fabrication of documents which is not a protected official act.

rules.case_name: S.K. Miglani v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: S.K. Miglani v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to affirm that a bank manager cannot claim protection under Section 197 CrPC as they are not removable only with government sanction.

rules.case_name: K. Ch. Prasad v. Smt. J. Vanalatha Devi
rules.reference: K. Ch. Prasad v. Smt. J. Vanalatha Devi
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to hold that a manager in a nationalized bank is not removable save by government sanction, thus Section 197 CrPC is not attracted.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra Vs. Dr. Budhikota Subbarao
rules.reference: State of Maharashtra Vs. Dr. Budhikota Subbarao
rules.relevance: Established the test that protection under Section 197 applies if the alleged act or omission has a 'reasonable connection' with the discharge of official duties.

rules.reference: Modi's Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology
rules.relevance: The court cited this text to support the finding that a human body is slightly heavier than fresh water and sinks immediately upon unconsciousness.

rules.reference: Taylor's Principles and Practice of Medical Jurisprudence
rules.relevance: The court relied on this authority to establish that a drowned body typically sinks initially and only floats after putrefaction, contradicting witness testimony.

rules.case_name: Subramaniam v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.reference: Subramaniam v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.relevance: Held that the circumstance of husband and wife living together does not conclusively prove guilt in the absence of evidence of violence.

rules.case_name: Kundula Bala Subrahmanyam vs. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.reference: Kundula Bala Subrahmanyam vs. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.relevance: Highlighted the special sanctity of a dying declaration made on the verge of death, noting the lack of motive to lie.

rules.case_name: Paniben (Smt.) vs. State of Gujarat
rules.reference: Paniben (Smt.) vs. State of Gujarat
rules.relevance: Reiterated that there is no rule of law requiring corroboration for a dying declaration if the court is satisfied it is true and voluntary.

rules.case_name: Anurag Soni v. State of Chhattisgarh
rules.reference: Anurag Soni v. State of Chhattisgarh
rules.relevance: Distinguishes between a false promise made with no intention to marry (vitiating consent) and a breach of a promise made in good faith.

rules.reference: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
rules.relevance: The court examined whether these provisions, inserted by the 2015 Amendment Act, applied to acts committed in 2015 before the amendment came into force.

rules.reference: Consent and Misconception of Fact

rules.case_name: Naim Ahamed v. State (NCT of Delhi)

rules.relevance: Established that a mature, married woman who has consensual relations for years cannot claim rape based on a false promise to marry, as her consent is not vitiated by misconception of fact.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: The specific charge of rape under which the FIR was registered.

rules.reference: Electricity Act, 2003
rules.relevance: Provides the enabling power for the State Commission to frame regulations consistent with the Act to carry out its functions.

rules.reference: Electricity Act, 2003
rules.relevance: Defines 'area of supply', which the court used to interpret 'area of distribution licensee' as a geographical area including captive consumers.

rules.reference: Electricity Act, 2003

rules.reference: RERC (Renewable Energy Obligation) Regulations, 2007 and RERC (Renewable Energy Certificate and Renewable Purchase Obligation Compliance Framework) Regulations, 2010
rules.relevance: The impugned regulations imposing the renewable purchase obligation and consequences for default.

rules.case_name: Society For Unaided Pvt. Schools of Rajasthan v. U.O.I.

rules.relevance: Established that directive principles can guide the determination of reasonable restrictions under Article 19.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure
rules.relevance: Governs framing of charges if there is ground for presuming the accused has committed an offence.

rules.case_name: State of Gujarat v. Haidarali Kalubhai

rules.relevance: Distinguishes Section 304-A from culpable homicide, noting that Section 304-A excludes intent or knowledge to cause death.

rules.case_name: Niranjan Singh Karam Singh Punjabi v. Jitendra Bhimraj Bijja & Ors.

rules.relevance: Establishes that at the stage of framing charges, the court must evaluate material to see if it discloses the ingredients of the alleged offence.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samal & Ors.
rules.reference: Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samal & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that the Judge must exercise judicial mind to determine if a case for trial has been made out, rather than acting as a mere post office.

rules.reference: Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967
rules.relevance: Section 15 covers acts of individuals or terrorist gangs, and Section 20 does not require an association to be in the schedule for punishing terrorist acts.

rules.case_name: Ram Jag and Ors. v. The State of UP.
rules.reference: Ram Jag and Ors. v. The State of UP.
rules.relevance: Established that delay in lodging an FIR must be viewed with common sense and does not automatically vitiate the prosecution case if reasonably explained.

rules.reference: Modi's Text Book of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology
rules.relevance: Referenced to support the medical possibility that a blunt weapon like a Dhangu could cause an incised wound on hard parts of the body like the scalp.

rules.case_name: Pala Singh and Anr. v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Pala Singh and Anr. v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Held that some delay in the receipt of the special report by the Magistrate does not taint the investigation.

rules.case_name: Sarwan Singh and Ors. v. State of Punjab

rules.relevance: Supported the view that delay in dispatch of the FIR is not a substance that can throw out the prosecution case entirely.

rules.case_name: State of UP. v. Krishna Gopal and Ors.

rules.relevance: Established that cogent and credible ocular evidence is not corroded by contrary medical evidence.

rules.case_name: Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration

rules.case_name: Province of Bombay v. Khusaldas Advani

rules.relevance: The court used this case to distinguish between judicial/quasi-judicial acts and administrative/ministerial acts.

rules.case_name: Union of India and Others v. B. B. Valluvan and Others

rules.relevance: Empowered the Government to issue orders regarding reservation percentages and procedures, giving statutory force to the Government Orders in question.

rules.case_name: Bank of India v. Aarya K. Babu

rules.case_name: Punjab Urban Planning & Development Authority v. Rafiqul Naim Gupta

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: This provision empowers the Court to recall any witness at any stage of the suit to put such questions as the Court thinks fit. The court interpreted the scope of this discretionary power.

rules.case_name: Sunder Theaters Vs. Allahabad Bank, Jhansi
rules.reference: Sunder Theaters Vs. Allahabad Bank, Jhansi
rules.relevance: Established that the power under Order 18 Rule 17 is discretionary, must be exercised with care, and should not be used to fill lacunae in evidence already led.

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: The court identified this as the correct provision dealing with the recall and examination of witnesses, permitting the appellant to file a fresh application under this rule.

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: The court analyzed this provision to determine that it deals exclusively with the tender of expenses to witnesses and does not encompass the prayer to recall a witness for confrontation.

rules.case_name: State of Rajasthan v. Shera Ram alias Vishnu Dutta
rules.reference: Appellate Interference with Acquittal
rules.relevance: Establishes that while appellate courts can re-appreciate evidence, they should not interfere with an acquittal unless the trial court's findings are perverse or based on erroneous appreciation of evidence, not merely because another view is possible.

rules.case_name: Chinnaswamy Reddy v. State of A.P.
rules.reference: Chinnaswamy Reddy v. State of A.P.
rules.relevance: Established that revisional jurisdiction to set aside an acquittal should be exercised only in exceptional cases, distinguishing it from the State's statutory right to appeal.

rules.reference: Standard for granting leave to appeal against acquittal
rules.relevance: The High Court must apply its mind to determine if a prima facie case or arguable points exist, rather than merely checking if the trial court's order was 'perverse'.

rules.case_name: Sita Ram & Ors. v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Sita Ram & Ors. v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that a right of appeal is rooted in the concept of human fallibility and the need for a full-scale re-examination of facts and law.

rules.case_name: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Guru Charan
rules.reference: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Guru Charan
rules.relevance: Establishes that the Supreme Court should only interfere with a High Court's acquittal if there are very substantial and compelling reasons, such as perverse findings or manifest injustice.

rules.case_name: Jumman and Ors. v. The State of Punjab
rules.reference: Jumman and Ors. v. The State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Established that in cases of mutual conflict where it is unclear who was the aggressor, the plea of private defence cannot be assumed for either side, and the case falls under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC.

rules.case_name: Sukhram s/o Ramratan v. State of MP.
rules.reference: Sukhram s/o Ramratan v. State of MP.
rules.relevance: Held that if a co-accused is acquitted, the conviction of the appellant under Section 34 cannot be sustained as they cannot be held to have acted conjointly with an acquitted person.

rules.case_name: Harshadsingh Pahelvansingh Thakore v. State of Gujarat
rules.reference: Harshadsingh Pahelvansingh Thakore v. State of Gujarat
rules.relevance: Distinguished because common intention was proved in that case, whereas here the conviction under Section 304 Part I suggested no intention to murder, making common intention irrelevant.

rules.case_name: Patel Rasiklal Becharbhai Vs. State of Gujarat
rules.reference: Patel Rasiklal Becharbhai Vs. State of Gujarat
rules.relevance: Cited by the majority to support the view that infliction of injury with an agricultural instrument in a sudden quarrel may not constitute intentional murder.

rules.case_name: Shahajan Ali & Ors. v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.
rules.reference: Shahajan Ali & Ors. v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to support the application of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC and conviction under Section 304 Part-II IPC in sudden fights.

rules.reference: Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957
rules.relevance: Empowers the Central Government to issue directions to State Governments for the establishment of DMFs.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Income Tax (Central) - I v. Vatika Township Private Limited
rules.reference: Commissioner of Income Tax (Central) - I v. Vatika Township Private Limited
rules.relevance: Held that the rate of tax is an essential component of a tax regime; uncertainty in the rate renders the levy invalid.

rules.case_name: Thangal Kunju Musaliar v. M. Venkitachalam Potti
rules.reference: Thangal Kunju Musaliar v. M. Venkitachalam Potti
rules.relevance: Held that fixing a commencement date anterior to the notification but subsequent to the passing of the Act is not retrospective operation if it does not affect vested rights.

rules.reference: Essential components of a tax/levy
rules.relevance: The rate of contribution is an essential component; a maximum limit without a specific rate creates fatal uncertainty.

rules.case_name: Mis Govind Saran Ganga Saran v. Commissioner of Sales Tax
rules.reference: Mis Govind Saran Ganga Saran v. Commissioner of Sales Tax
rules.relevance: Established that components of a tax (subject, person, rate, measure) must be clearly ascertainable for the levy to be valid.

rules.reference: Wilfulness in Unauthorized Absence
rules.relevance: The court established that unauthorized absence does not automatically amount to misconduct. The disciplinary authority must prove that the absence was wilful. If the absence is due to compelling circumstances beyond the employee's control, it is not wilful and does not constitute a violation of the Conduct Rules.

rules.reference: Central Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964
rules.relevance: These rules require government servants to maintain devotion to duty and behave in a manner befitting their position. The court interpreted whether unauthorized absence inherently violates these rules or requires proof of wilfulness.

rules.case_name: M.B. Bijlani vs. Union of India and others
rules.reference: M.B. Bijlani vs. Union of India and others
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to affirm that inquiry officers perform a quasi-judicial function and cannot reject relevant testimony on surmises, shift the burden of proof, or base conclusions on irrelevant facts. Conclusions must be based on the preponderance of probability.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. M.M. Sharma
rules.reference: Union of India v. M.M. Sharma
rules.relevance: Held that there is no obligation to communicate reasons for dispensing with inquiry or for imposing dismissal when acting under the security of the State clause.

rules.reference: Principles of Natural Justice in Departmental Proceedings
rules.relevance: The court considered that a limited enquiry into the employee's explanation for not reporting to duty satisfies the requirements of natural justice, as opposed to a full-fledged departmental proceeding.

rules.case_name: Kishor Ghanshyamsa Paralikar (D) through Lrs. V. Balaji Mandir Sansthan Mangrul (Nath) & Another
rules.reference: Kishor Ghanshyamsa Paralikar (D) through Lrs. V. Balaji Mandir Sansthan Mangrul (Nath) & Another
rules.relevance: Distinguished on facts. In that case, the delay was only five days, whereas in the present case, the delay was 853 days with no sufficient explanation.

rules.case_name: V.S. Palanichamy Chettiar Firm v. C. Alagappan and Another
rules.reference: V.S. Palanichamy Chettiar Firm v. C. Alagappan and Another
rules.relevance: Established that provisions for specific performance are stringent. Extension of time is not a matter of course and requires a sufficient explanation for non-compliance. Equity demands discretion not be exercised in favor of a decree holder without adequate explanation.

rules.case_name: K. Kalpana Saraswathi v. P.S.S. Somasundaram Chettiar
rules.reference: K. Kalpana Saraswathi v. P.S.S. Somasundaram Chettiar
rules.relevance: Established that the court has the power under Section 28 to extend time for deposit and that specific performance is an equitable relief requiring the party seeking it to do equity.

rules.reference: Condition Precedent in Specific Performance Decrees
rules.relevance: The court established that payment of the balance consideration is a condition precedent for the execution of the sale deed, whether by the defendants or through the court, and failure to fulfill this condition justifies rescission.

rules.case_name: Kumar Dhirendra Mullick and Others v. Tivoli Park Apartments (P) Ltd.
rules.reference: Kumar Dhirendra Mullick and Others v. Tivoli Park Apartments (P) Ltd.
rules.relevance: Held that a decree for specific performance is preliminary in nature, the contract is not extinguished, and the court retains jurisdiction to extend time or rescind the agreement.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: The initial charge of abetment of suicide against the accused.

rules.case_name: State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh
rules.reference: State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh
rules.relevance: Established that at the stage of framing charges, the court need not meticulously judge the veracity of evidence or weigh probable defenses, but only look for strong suspicion.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samal
rules.reference: Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samal
rules.relevance: Confirmed that a judge has the power to sift and weigh evidence for the limited purpose of finding out if a prima facie case exists, and that grave suspicion justifies framing a charge.

rules.reference: Instigation requires intent to incite the consequence
rules.relevance: Words uttered in a fit of anger without intending the consequence of suicide do not constitute instigation under Section 306 IPC.

rules.reference: Sections 498-A and 306 IPC are independent offences
rules.relevance: A conviction for cruelty under Section 498-A does not automatically lead to a conviction for abetment of suicide under Section 306.

rules.reference: Circumstantial Evidence and Corroboration
rules.relevance: The court relied on the principle that a chain of circumstantial evidence, including extra-judicial confession, recovery of weapons, and 'last seen' testimony, must be complete and corroborated to sustain a conviction.

rules.case_name: Kuldip Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Kuldip Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case, noting that while extra-judicial confession is weak evidence, in the present case it was corroborated by recovery of the body and identification.

rules.case_name: Trimukh Maruti Kirkan v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Trimukh Maruti Kirkan v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case for the principle that failure by a husband to explain his wife's death when they were last seen together is a strong circumstance of guilt.

rules.reference: Admissibility of Confession
rules.relevance: A statement made by the accused under Section 164 of the applicable Code is admissible in evidence, particularly when not retracted.

rules.case_name: Vinayak Shivajirao Pol v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Vinayak Shivajirao Pol v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to hold that a voluntary extra-judicial confession can form the basis of conviction without corroboration if the circumstances inspire confidence.

rules.reference: Substitution of Section 34 for Section 149
rules.relevance: The principle that if facts disclose common intention, conviction under Section 34 can sustain even if charged under Section 149, provided no prejudice is caused.

rules.case_name: Balak Ram v. State of U. P.
rules.reference: Balak Ram v. State of U. P.
rules.relevance: Held that the Supreme Court does not interfere with concurrent findings of fact save in exceptional circumstances.

rules.case_name: The State of Madras v. A. Vaidyanatha Iyer
rules.reference: The State of Madras v. A. Vaidyanatha Iyer
rules.relevance: Established that the Supreme Court can interfere with findings of fact if the High Court has acted perversely or otherwise improperly.

rules.case_name: Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. King Emperor
rules.reference: Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. King Emperor
rules.relevance: Established the distinction and overlap between common intention (Section 34) and common object (Section 149).

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Provides that if acts constitute an offence falling within two or more separate definitions of any law in force, the accused may be charged with and tried at one trial for each of such offences.

rules.reference: Principles governing Section 311 CrPC
rules.relevance: The power under Section 311 must be exercised with caution and circumspection to meet the ends of justice. It should not be exercised if the application is an abuse of the process of law.

rules.case_name: Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court relied on the parameters established in this Constitution Bench judgment to determine whether the evidence on record was strong, trustworthy, and sufficient to justify summoning the appellant under Section 319 Cr.P.C.

rules.case_name: Mohd. Shafi v. Mohd. Rafiq & Anr.
rules.reference: Mohd. Shafi v. Mohd. Rafiq & Anr.
rules.relevance: Held that satisfaction under Section 319 can only be arrived at after cross-examination and that the Court must be satisfied the accused is 'in all likelihood' to be convicted; the present Court found this conflicting with Rakesh.

rules.case_name: Brijendra Singh v. State of Rajasthan
rules.reference: Brijendra Singh v. State of Rajasthan
rules.relevance: Reiterated that the degree of satisfaction required for summoning under Section 319 is higher than that for framing charges and requires strong and cogent evidence.

rules.case_name: P. Sanjeeva Rao v. State of A.P.
rules.reference: P. Sanjeeva Rao v. State of A.P.
rules.relevance: Emphasized that fairness of trial is sacrosanct and courts should err in favor of the accused getting an opportunity to cross-examine witnesses rather than protecting the prosecution against possible prejudice.

rules.case_name: Naim Ahamed v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: Naim Ahamed v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: Established that a mature, married woman who has consensual relations for years cannot claim rape based on a false promise to marry, as her consent is not vitiated by misconception of fact.

rules.case_name: Anurag Soni v. State of Chhattisgarh
rules.reference: Anurag Soni v. State of Chhattisgarh
rules.relevance: Distinguishes between a false promise made with no intention to marry (vitiating consent) and a breach of a promise made in good faith.

rules.reference: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
rules.relevance: The court examined whether these provisions, inserted by the 2015 Amendment Act, applied to acts committed in 2015 before the amendment came into force.

rules.reference: Consent and Misconception of Fact
rules.relevance: A mature and intelligent woman who knowingly enters into a relationship, even during the subsistence of her marriage, cannot claim that her consent was obtained under a misconception of fact regarding a promise to marry.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: The specific charge of rape under which the FIR was registered.

rules.reference: Futility of Relief
rules.relevance: It is not in the interest of justice to direct reconsideration of promotion for an employee who has already retired, as such directions would be futile.

rules.reference: Andhra Pradesh State and Subordinate Service Rules
rules.relevance: Provides for limited recruitment to fill reserved vacancies when candidates are not available in general recruitment; the court analyzed whether this rule overrides the date of appointment for seniority purposes.

rules.reference: Himachal Pradesh State Electricity Board Recruitment and Promotion (Regulations) for Ministerial Employees of the Board, 1972
rules.relevance: Defined the criteria for promotion to non-selection posts as seniority, excluding suitability based on current skill as a ground for rejection.

rules.reference: Andhra Pradesh Civil Service (Executive Branch) Rules, 1992
rules.relevance: Establishes the general principle that seniority is determined by the date of first appointment to the service.

rules.reference: Substantive Right to Consideration
rules.relevance: A substantive employee has a right to be considered for promotion in their own stream; non-consideration infringes Article 16.

rules.reference: General Clauses Act, 1897
rules.relevance: Defines 'month' as a month reckoned according to the British calendar, distinguishing it from a fixed number of days.

rules.case_name: Dodds v. Walker
rules.reference: Dodds v. Walker
rules.relevance: Established that a period of months ends on the corresponding date in the subsequent month, regardless of the varying number of days in each month.

rules.reference: Limitation Act, 1963
rules.relevance: Provides that the day from which the period of limitation is to be reckoned shall be excluded.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tecco Trichy Engineers & Contractors
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tecco Trichy Engineers & Contractors
rules.relevance: Held that for government bodies, delivery of an award on a non-working day does not constitute 'receipt'; the date of receipt is the next working day.

rules.case_name: Bibi Salma Khatoon v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Bibi Salma Khatoon v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Supported the interpretation that 'three months' refers to calendar months and not a fixed period of 90 days.

rules.case_name: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Krishna Master and Others
rules.reference: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Krishna Master and Others
rules.relevance: Established that minor discrepancies in the testimony of rustic witnesses, especially under gruelling cross-examination, should not be blown out of proportion and evidence must be appreciated as a whole.

rules.case_name: Mofil Khan and Another v. The State of Jharkhand
rules.citation: RP(Criminal) No. 641/2015 in Criminal Appeal No.1795/2009 dated 26.11.2021
rules.reference: Mofil Khan and Another v. The State of Jharkhand
rules.relevance: Held that the State has a duty to procure evidence establishing that there is no possibility of reformation and rehabilitation of the accused before imposing the death penalty.

rules.case_name: Krishnan and Another v. State represented by Inspector of Police
rules.reference: Krishnan and Another v. State represented by Inspector of Police
rules.relevance: Held that where ocular evidence is cogent, credible, and trustworthy, minor variances with medical evidence are not of consequence.

rules.case_name: Sushil Sharma v. State (NCT) of Delhi
rules.reference: Sushil Sharma v. State (NCT) of Delhi
rules.relevance: The court relied on the principles laid down in this case to balance aggravating and mitigating circumstances when deciding between death penalty and life imprisonment.

rules.case_name: Rajendra Pralhadrao Wasnik v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Rajendra Pralhadrao Wasnik v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Reiterated that the probability of reformation must be seriously considered and that the prosecution must prove through evidence that the convict cannot be reformed or rehabilitated.

rules.case_name: State of Orissa and Others Vs. Bidyabhushan Mohapatra
rules.reference: State of Orissa and Others Vs. Bidyabhushan Mohapatra
rules.relevance: Established that if an order of dismissal can be supported on any finding of substantial misdemeanour, the court should not interfere even if other charges are unsustainable or vitiated by procedural defects.

rules.case_name: Delhi Transport Corporation vs. D.T.C. Mazdoor Congress and Ors
rules.reference: Delhi Transport Corporation vs. D.T.C. Mazdoor Congress and Ors
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case, noting it dealt with the constitutionality of dispensing with service without enquiry, whereas the present case involved compliance with a binding Tribunal order.

rules.case_name: Basudeo Tiwary vs. Sido Kanhu University and Ors
rules.reference: Basudeo Tiwary vs. Sido Kanhu University and Ors
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case, noting that while natural justice principles apply, the failure to afford an opportunity to show cause was not fatal in this specific context of complying with a binding order after two decades.

rules.reference: Principle of Natural Justice / Hearing of Parties
rules.relevance: The court held that allowing a second appeal without issuing notice to and hearing all respondents violates procedural fairness and cannot be cured by awarding costs.

rules.reference: Pre-conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation & Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994
rules.relevance: These provisions mandate that the Appropriate Authority must issue a notice and afford a reasonable opportunity of hearing before suspending or cancelling registration for breach of the Act or Rules.

rules.reference: Registration Act, 1908
rules.relevance: The court held that the Inspector General's powers under this section are limited to superintendence and rule-making, and do not include the power to cancel registered documents.

rules.reference: Registration Act, 1908
rules.relevance: The court held that this section does not confer quasi-judicial power on the Registering Authority to evaluate title or legality, but only to ascertain execution.

rules.case_name: Thota Ganga Laxmi & Anr. vs. Government of Andhra Pradesh & Ors.
rules.reference: Thota Ganga Laxmi & Anr. vs. Government of Andhra Pradesh & Ors.
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this precedent, holding that its dictum against registering unilateral cancellation deeds was based on specific Andhra Pradesh Rules, which do not exist in Madhya Pradesh.

rules.case_name: Government of U.P. vs. Raja Mohammad Amir Ahmad Khan
rules.reference: Government of U.P. vs. Raja Mohammad Amir Ahmad Khan
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to hold that the Registering Officer becomes functus officio once the document is registered and has no power to impound or cancel it.

rules.reference: Registration Act, 1908
rules.relevance: The court relied on this provision to hold that actions done in good faith by the Registering Officer are not invalid merely due to procedural defects.

rules.case_name: Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The petitioner relied on this judgment, but the High Court and Supreme Court held it was not applicable because the petitioner had already had four earlier applications for anticipatory bail rejected.

rules.reference: Gross misuse of the process of the Court
rules.relevance: The court applied this principle to dismiss the petition and impose a deposit condition, citing the petitioner's absconding and flouting of court directions.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Defines the maximum period of detention pending investigation as 90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for a term of not less than ten years, and 60 days for any other offence. Determines when the right to default bail accrues.

rules.case_name: Rajeev Chaudhary v. State (NCT) of Delhi
rules.reference: Rajeev Chaudhary v. State (NCT) of Delhi
rules.relevance: Held that 'not less than ten years' means a minimum sentence of ten years or more. Offences where the maximum punishment extends to ten years but the minimum is less do not attract the 90-day period.

rules.reference: Indefeasible right to default bail
rules.relevance: Once the statutory period expires without a charge sheet, the accused has an indefeasible right to bail if they offer to furnish bail. This right is availed if claimed before the charge sheet is filed.

rules.case_name: State of M.P. vs. Bhooraji and Others
rules.reference: State of M.P. vs. Bhooraji and Others
rules.relevance: Interprets 'failure of justice' in the context of Section 465 CrPC, supporting the view that proceedings should not be axed down merely for error unless justice fails.

rules.case_name: Nanjappa Vs. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: Nanjappa Vs. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: Clarifies that Section 19(3) bars appellate/revisional interference but does not prevent the Special Judge from discharging an accused if sanction is invalid; emphasizes that objections should be raised at the earliest stage.

rules.reference: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
rules.relevance: Defines the offences and specifies the competent authorities for granting sanction, distinct from the Cr.P.C.

rules.reference: Distinctness of Sanctions
rules.relevance: Sanction under the Prevention of Corruption Act and sanction under Section 197 Cr.P.C. stand on different footings and are granted by different competent authorities.

rules.case_name: Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli v. The State of Bombay
rules.reference: Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli v. The State of Bombay
rules.relevance: Established that the test for sanction is whether the act has a reasonable connection to official duty, not whether the motive was official.

rules.provision: Section 2(ra) read with Schedule V, Item 10
rules.reference: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
rules.relevance: Defines unfair labour practice, prohibiting employers from engaging workmen as badlis, casuals, or temporaries for permanent work to deprive them of permanent status.

rules.reference: Distinction between daily wagers and regular employees
rules.relevance: Daily wagers are entitled to minimum wages but not full back wages or substantive reinstatement like regular staff, as they do not hold a permanent post.

rules.reference: The Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act, 1995
rules.relevance: Protects employees who acquire disability during service, mandating that they not be dispensed with or reduced in rank, and providing for alternative posts if necessary.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab & Others v. Jagjit Singh & Others
rules.reference: State of Punjab & Others v. Jagjit Singh & Others
rules.relevance: The court held this judgment inapplicable as it concerned temporary employees entitled to minimum pay scale, not the reinstatement of retrenched workmen.

rules.reference: U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
rules.relevance: The court relied on this section to establish that the circular dated 07.04.2015 complied with the statutory mandate to give preference to retrenched workmen for re-employment when necessity arises.

rules.case_name: Shahajan Ali & Ors. v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.
rules.reference: Shahajan Ali & Ors. v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to support the application of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC and conviction under Section 304 Part-II IPC in sudden fights.

rules.reference: Sentence Already Undergone
rules.relevance: The court held that since the appellant had already served more than seven years, the sentence already undergone met the ends of justice.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: The court applied this exception to determine if the killing was committed under grave and sudden provocation, thereby reducing the offence from murder to culpable homicide.

rules.reference: Distinction between Murder and Culpable Homicide
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that an act committed in the heat of passion, without premeditation, and under grave and sudden provocation, lacks the intention to cause death required for murder under Section 302.

rules.case_name: State of Gujarat v. Bai Fatima
rules.reference: State of Gujarat v. Bai Fatima
rules.relevance: Establishes that non-explanation of minor and superficial injuries does not affect the prosecution case if the evidence is clear, cogent, and outweighs the omission.

rules.case_name: Ceyaki Shipping Pvt. Ltd. vs. New India Assurance Pvt. Co. Ltd.
rules.reference: Ceyaki Shipping Pvt. Ltd. vs. New India Assurance Pvt. Co. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Distinguished because in that case the insurer was aware of the defects before issuing the policy, whereas here the defects were concealed from the Classification Society.

rules.reference: Marine Insurance Act, 1963
rules.relevance: Establishes that a warranty is a condition that must be exactly complied with; breach discharges the insurer from liability as from the date of breach.

rules.case_name: Sea Lark Fisheries vs. United India Insurance Company and Anr.
rules.reference: Sea Lark Fisheries vs. United India Insurance Company and Anr.
rules.relevance: Affirms the principle of Uberrimae Fidei and the implied warranty of seaworthiness.

rules.case_name: Ranjan Kumar and Brothers v. Oriental Insurance Co.
rules.reference: Ranjan Kumar and Brothers v. Oriental Insurance Co.
rules.relevance: Supports the principle that breach of warranty discharges the insurer's liability and that mere knowledge of breach does not amount to waiver without express representation.

rules.reference: ABS Rules for Building and Classing Steel Vessels-2005 Edition
rules.relevance: Stipulates that failure to report damage to the Classification Society results in automatic suspension of the class and invalidation of the certificate.

rules.case_name: Nandu Singh v. State of M.P.
rules.reference: Nandu Singh v. State of M.P.
rules.relevance: Holds that motive is an important link to complete the chain of circumstances in cases based on circumstantial evidence.

rules.case_name: State of Goa vs. Sanjay Thakran
rules.reference: State of Goa vs. Sanjay Thakran
rules.relevance: Holds that if there is a considerable time gap between the 'last seen together' event and the crime, this circumstance cannot clinchingly fasten guilt.

rules.case_name: Pattu Rajan v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.reference: Pattu Rajan v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.relevance: Establishes that skull superimposition is fallible and cannot be relied upon as the sole incriminating circumstance for identifying a deceased body without supporting medical evidence like DNA.

rules.reference: Reliability of Identification
rules.relevance: The court held that identification is unreliable if the items or persons are distinguishable due to markings (such as paper chits or knots) or if the procedure is flawed (e.g., items washed and sealed before identification).

rules.reference: Theory of last seen together
rules.relevance: The court held that being last seen together is not independently sufficient for conviction if the time gap is large or evidence is contradictory, requiring a complete chain of circumstances.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code (IPC)
rules.relevance: These are the offences under which the First Information Report was registered against the appellants.

rules.reference: Gujarat Control of Terrorism and Organized Crime Act, 2015
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this Act from the Gangsters Act, noting that the former contains specific provisions requiring multiple offences, which are absent in the Gangsters Act.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Control of Organized Crime Act, 1999
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this Act from the Gangsters Act, noting that the former contains specific provisions requiring multiple offences, which are absent in the Gangsters Act.

rules.reference: U.P. Act 16 of 1976
rules.relevance: This provision deleted Section 438 Cr.P.C. (anticipatory bail) in Uttar Pradesh, leading to an increase in petitions under Section 482 Cr.P.C.

rules.case_name: Ram Lal Yadav and others v. State of U.P. and others
rules.reference: Ram Lal Yadav and others v. State of U.P. and others
rules.relevance: The court referred to this Seven-Judge Bench decision to acknowledge the general rule that High Courts cannot interfere with police investigation under Section 482 Cr.P.C., but distinguished the present case based on the specific legal context in U.P.

rules.case_name: Manjuri Bera (Smt) v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr.
rules.reference: Manjuri Bera (Smt) v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to hold that liability to pay compensation does not cease due to the absence of dependency, affirming the right of legal representatives to claim.

rules.reference: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988

rules.case_name: Chhavi Mehrotra vs. Director General, Health Services
rules.reference: Chhavi Mehrotra vs. Director General, Health Services
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case to hold that the High Court was not barred from exercising jurisdiction because the Supreme Court petitions were filed later by different parties and did not specifically bar the High Court.

rules.case_name: State of West Bengal & Ors. vs. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights, West Bengal & Ors.
rules.reference: State of West Bengal & Ors. vs. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights, West Bengal & Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this Constitution Bench decision to hold that a High Court can direct the CBI to investigate a cognizable offence within a State's territory without the State's consent to protect fundamental rights.

rules.case_name: A. Srinivasulu v. State Rep. by the Inspector of Police
rules.reference: A. Srinivasulu v. State Rep. by the Inspector of Police
rules.relevance: Distinguished on facts; involved criminal conspiracy where co-conspirators were protected, whereas the present case involves direct fabrication of documents which is not a protected official act.

rules.reference: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007
rules.relevance: The court directed the Central Government to exercise powers under this section to issue directions to States for effective implementation.

rules.reference: Disaster Management Act, 2005
rules.relevance: The legal basis for lockdown orders; the court interpreted these orders to not prohibit the opening of essential services like Anganwadis.

rules.reference: National Food Security Act, 2013
rules.relevance: Defines the specific nutritional standards (calories and protein) that must be met by the State.

rules.case_name: Chameli Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Chameli Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: Relied upon to define the right to shelter as including adequate living space and infrastructure, deemed a fundamental right subject to economic budgeting.

rules.reference: Guidance Note on operations of Anganwadi Services
rules.relevance: Permitted the resumption of Anganwadi Services outside containment zones, establishing that reopening was feasible and authorized.

rules.case_name: Anand Bihari and Others v. Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation, Jaipur and Another
rules.reference: Anand Bihari and Others v. Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation, Jaipur and Another
rules.relevance: Established that terminating bus drivers for defective eyesight developed during employment is unjustified and discriminatory. Mandated that alternative jobs be provided first, with additional compensation only if alternative jobs are unavailable.
