rules.relevance: Provides for appointment of dependents of officials who become blind or completely unfit ('Nakara'). The court found this inapplicable because the respondents were not certified as blind or completely unfit by a Special Medical Board.

rules.reference: Communication dated 20.8.1992 by Transport Commissioner, Haryana
rules.relevance: Specifically governs drivers medically unfit for heavy vehicles. Requires seeking alternative employment for those incapacitated by occupational hazards before retirement with compensation.

rules.reference: Statutory discretion cannot be fettered by self-created rules or policy
rules.relevance: The court held that the Corporation's circulars denying consideration for alternative jobs unlawfully fettered the statutory discretion required to be exercised in individual cases.

rules.reference: U.P. State Road Transport Corporation Employees (Other than officers) Service Regulations, 1981
rules.relevance: The court interpreted these regulations to determine whether the Corporation had a mandatory obligation or a discretionary power to offer alternative jobs to medically unfit drivers.

rules.case_name: Ujagar Prints & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.reference: Ujagar Prints & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to distinguish between 'incorporation by reference' and 'referential legislation' regarding the application of subsequent amendments.

rules.case_name: Secretary of State v. Hindustan Cooperative Insurance Societies Ltd
rules.reference: Secretary of State v. Hindustan Cooperative Insurance Societies Ltd
rules.relevance: The court relied on this Privy Council decision for the principle that subsequent additions to an incorporated Act are not deemed incorporated unless expressly stated.

rules.case_name: Girnar Traders v. State of Maharashtra and others
rules.reference: Girnar Traders v. State of Maharashtra and others
rules.relevance: Holds that mere inaction or steps that do not result in actual commencement of acquisition cannot defeat the purpose of Section 127, leading to the release of land.

rules.case_name: T. Vijayalakshmi and others v. Town Planning Member and another
rules.reference: T. Vijayalakshmi and others v. Town Planning Member and another
rules.relevance: Establishes that the right to construct is a valuable right that cannot be taken away without clear provision and that the doctrine of legitimate expectation applies to property rights.

rules.case_name: Chhabildas v. State of Maharashtra and others
rules.reference: Chhabildas v. State of Maharashtra and others
rules.relevance: Discussed the interplay of Sections 49, 126, and 127 and the invocation of Article 142 for inordinate delay, providing context for the court's decision not to invoke Article 142 here.

rules.reference: Income Tax Act, 1961
rules.relevance: Provides that property vests in the Central Government 'in terms of the agreement for transfer,' supporting the interpretation that only leasehold rights were conveyed.

rules.case_name: S.N. Ranade Vs. Union of India and Another
rules.reference: S.N. Ranade Vs. Union of India and Another
rules.relevance: Held that government grants should be construed to include all rights of the grantor unless expressly or impliedly excluded.

rules.case_name: Radha Sundar Dutta Vs. Mohd. Jahadur Rahim & Ors.
rules.reference: Radha Sundar Dutta Vs. Mohd. Jahadur Rahim & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that if clauses conflict, the earlier clause prevails, but emphasized harmonious construction where possible.

rules.case_name: Sahebzada Mohammad Kamgarh Shah Vs. Jagdish Chandra Deo Dhabal Deb and Others
rules.reference: Sahebzada Mohammad Kamgarh Shah Vs. Jagdish Chandra Deo Dhabal Deb and Others
rules.relevance: Laid down principles for construing documents, including ascertaining intention from words used and resolving ambiguities.

rules.reference: Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Vikasit Bhoomiyo, Griho, Bhavano Tatha Anya Sanrachanao Ka Vyayan Niyam, 1975 (Rules of 1977)
rules.relevance: The court interpreted these rules to establish that the right of renewal is vested in the lessor (UDA) and is not an absolute or indefeasible right of the lessee, allowing discretion based on public interest.

rules.case_name: Isher Das v. State
rules.reference: Isher Das v. State
rules.relevance: Established that courts should not lightly resort to probation in food adulteration cases due to the menace to public health.

rules.case_name: Trilok Chand v. State of Himachal Pradesh
rules.reference: Trilok Chand v. State of Himachal Pradesh
rules.relevance: Cited as further authority for applying the principle of beneficial construction to reduce sentences to fines.

rules.reference: Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954
rules.relevance: Defines 'adulterated' food; the court interpreted whether the case fell under clause (j) (colouring matter) or clause (l) (quality standards).

rules.reference: Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954
rules.relevance: Defines the offence of selling adulterated food and the corresponding punishment.

rules.case_name: T. Barai v. Henry Ah Hoe
rules.reference: T. Barai v. Henry Ah Hoe
rules.relevance: Established that beneficial amendments reducing punishment can be applied to pending cases under the principle of beneficial construction.

rules.reference: Termination Simpliciter vs. Removal
rules.relevance: The court distinguished between termination simpliciter (no notice/hearing required) and removal for misconduct (requires natural justice), classifying the appellant's discharge as the former.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kohli vs. High Court of J & K & Anr.
rules.reference: Rajesh Kohli vs. High Court of J & K & Anr.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to affirm that the High Court has a duty to consider both judicial performance and probity/conduct before confirming a judicial officer.

rules.case_name: Krishnadevaraya Education Trust v. L.A. Balakrishna
rules.reference: Krishnadevaraya Education Trust v. L.A. Balakrishna
rules.relevance: Held that mentioning unsatisfactory services in a termination order does not ipso facto make it punitive or stigmatic.

rules.case_name: Pavanendra Narayan Verma v. Sanjay Gandhi PG Institute of Medical Sciences
rules.reference: Pavanendra Narayan Verma v. Sanjay Gandhi PG Institute of Medical Sciences
rules.relevance: Provided the test for determining if a termination order is stigmatic; held that stating services were 'not satisfactory' is not stigmatic and does not attract natural justice unless it imputes moral turpitude or misconduct found after a formal enquiry.

rules.case_name: Pavanendra Narayan Verma vs. Sanjay Gandhi PGI of Medical Sciences & Anr.
rules.reference: Pavanendra Narayan Verma vs. Sanjay Gandhi PGI of Medical Sciences & Anr.
rules.relevance: Provided the three-factor test to determine if a termination is punitive: (1) full-scale formal inquiry, (2) allegations of moral turpitude/misconduct, and (3) finding of guilt.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: The court considered the conviction for voluntarily causing hurt, finding it unsupported because the witness who allegedly sustained injuries did not support the prosecution version.

rules.reference: Fair and Impartial Investigation
rules.relevance: The court found the investigation tainted due to interpolation in FIR, doubtful recoveries, and failure to record statements of material witnesses promptly.

rules.case_name: Jarnail Singh and Others v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Jarnail Singh and Others v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Establishes that the testimony of an injured witness has special evidentiary status and cannot be rejected lightly.

rules.case_name: Balak Ram v. State of U. P.
rules.reference: Balak Ram v. State of U. P.
rules.relevance: Held that the Supreme Court does not interfere with concurrent findings of fact save in exceptional circumstances.

rules.case_name: The State of Madras v. A. Vaidyanatha Iyer
rules.reference: The State of Madras v. A. Vaidyanatha Iyer
rules.relevance: Established that the Supreme Court can interfere with findings of fact if the High Court has acted perversely or otherwise improperly.

rules.case_name: Chanmuniya vs. Virendra Kumar Singh Kushwaha & Anr.
rules.reference: Chanmuniya vs. Virendra Kumar Singh Kushwaha & Anr.
rules.relevance: Relied upon for the broad and expansive interpretation of the term 'wife' under Section 125 Cr.P.C. to include those living together as husband and wife.

rules.case_name: Dwarika Prasad Satpathy vs. Bidyut Prava Dixit & Anr.
rules.reference: Dwarika Prasad Satpathy vs. Bidyut Prava Dixit & Anr.
rules.relevance: Relied upon for the principle that Section 125 proceedings are summary in nature and do not require strict proof of marriage rites if cohabitation is established.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.)
rules.relevance: The primary provision under which maintenance was claimed; the court interpreted the term 'wife' broadly to include women deceived by their husbands.

rules.reference: No one can take advantage of their own wrong
rules.relevance: The court held that the petitioner could not deny maintenance by claiming the marriage was void when he had actively concealed his prior marriage to the respondent.

rules.case_name: Savitaben Somabai Bhatiya vs. State of Gujarat & Ors.
rules.reference: Savitaben Somabai Bhatiya vs. State of Gujarat & Ors.
rules.relevance: Distinguished similarly to Yamunabai, as the respondent herein was duped by the petitioner regarding his marital status.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure
rules.relevance: Governs the taking of cognizance of offences by a Magistrate upon a police report. The court directed the Magistrate to take cognizance under this provision.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code
rules.relevance: Defines the offence of insulting the modesty of a woman by words, gestures, or intrusion. The court used this to determine if the alleged conduct constituted an offence.

rules.case_name: Abhinandan Jha v. Dinesh Mishra
rules.reference: Abhinandan Jha v. Dinesh Mishra
rules.relevance: Held that a Magistrate exercises judicial discretion when accepting a police report and must record reasons if accepting a report recommending discharge over the objections of the complainant.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code
rules.relevance: These were the offences for which the accused were summoned and which the High Court quashed without proper reasoning.

rules.case_name: Shiv Shankar Singh v. State of Bihar and Anr.
rules.reference: Shiv Shankar Singh v. State of Bihar and Anr.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to hold that there is no statutory bar against filing a second complaint on the same facts if the earlier complaint was not disposed of on merits.

rules.case_name: Bhagirath vs. Delhi Administration
rules.reference: Bhagirath vs. Delhi Administration
rules.relevance: Constitution Bench decision regarding the power of remission for life convicts, which conflicts with Swamy Shraddananda.

rules.case_name: Swamy Shraddananda vs. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: Swamy Shraddananda vs. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: Held that life imprisonment on commutation of death penalty may mean till end of life, creating a conflict with other precedents regarding remission.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Mandates that the State Government must act after consultation with the Central Government in cases investigated by the CBI or involving Central Government property.

rules.reference: Binding Precedent
rules.relevance: A three-judge bench cannot overrule or examine the correctness of a decision by another three-judge bench or a Constitution Bench.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Defines 'appropriate Government' as the Government of the State within which the offender is sentenced. The court held this determines jurisdiction for remission.

rules.reference: Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972
rules.relevance: Provides that a superannuation pension shall be granted to a government servant who retires on attaining the age of compulsory retirement.

rules.reference: Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972
rules.relevance: Stipulates that pension becomes payable from the date on which a government servant ceases to be borne on the establishment.

rules.reference: Delhi Education Act, 1973
rules.relevance: Defines 'aided school' as a recognized private school receiving aid, establishing that the petitioner's school qualified for the pension scheme.

rules.reference: Delhi School Education Rules, 1973
rules.relevance: Confers power on the Administrator to specify the procedure for payment of pension and gratuity, validating the issuance of the 1975 notification.

rules.case_name: Beed District Central Cooperative Bank Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Beed District Central Cooperative Bank Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that an employee must opt for either the statutory scheme or the employer's scheme in its entirety and cannot combine elements of both to create a hybrid benefit.

rules.reference: Arms Act, 1959
rules.relevance: Previous sanction is required for prosecution under the Arms Act. The failure to produce this sanction invalidated the conviction for illegal possession of arms.

rules.reference: Indian Evidence Act, 1872
rules.relevance: Documents must be proved by primary evidence (the original). The uncertified carbon copy of the post-mortem report was inadmissible as it did not fall under exceptions in Section 65.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: Defines assault or criminal force to deter a public servant from discharge of duty.

rules.reference: Arms Act, 1959
rules.relevance: Pertains to the possession of arms, under which Accused No. 1 was convicted.

rules.case_name: Anuj Jain, Interim Resolution Professional for Jaypee Infratech Limited v. Axis Bank Limited & Ors.
rules.reference: Anuj Jain, Interim Resolution Professional for Jaypee Infratech Limited v. Axis Bank Limited & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that the essential element of financial debt is disbursal against the consideration for the time value of money.

rules.case_name: Mobilox Innovations Pvt. Ltd. v. Kirusa Software Pvt. Ltd.
rules.reference: Mobilox Innovations Pvt. Ltd. v. Kirusa Software Pvt. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Established that the adjudicating authority must check if a plausible contention exists that is not patently feeble or spurious; if a dispute truly exists, the application must be rejected.

rules.case_name: Anuj Jain, Interim Resolution Professional for Jaypee Infratech Limited vs. Axis Bank Limited
rules.reference: Anuj Jain, Interim Resolution Professional for Jaypee Infratech Limited vs. Axis Bank Limited
rules.relevance: Held that a person having only a security interest over the assets of a corporate debtor (such as collateral for a third-party loan) is a secured creditor but not a financial creditor, as they lack the direct engagement in the corporate debtor's functioning required of financial creditors.

rules.case_name: K. Kishan v. Vijay Nirman Company Pvt. Ltd.
rules.reference: K. Kishan v. Vijay Nirman Company Pvt. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Held that a challenge to an arbitral award under Section 34 or 37 of the Arbitration Act constitutes a pre-existing dispute that continues until final adjudication.

rules.reference: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
rules.relevance: Empowers the NCLT to entertain any question of law or fact arising out of insolvency proceedings, supporting the exercise of inherent powers.

rules.case_name: Gurbux Singh v. Bhooralal

rules.relevance: Established that for Order II Rule 2 to apply, the second suit must be based on the same cause of action as the first, and the plaintiff must have been entitled to the omitted relief in the first suit.

rules.case_name: Gomathinayagam Pillai and Ors. Vs. Pallaniswami Nadar
rules.reference: Gomathinayagam Pillai and Ors. Vs. Pallaniswami Nadar

rules.case_name: Lala Durga Prasad and Anr. Vs. Lala Deep Chand and Ors.
rules.reference: Lala Durga Prasad and Anr. Vs. Lala Deep Chand and Ors.
rules.relevance: Supported the direction for a subsequent transferee to join in the conveyance to pass on title to the plaintiff.

rules.case_name: Virgo Industries (Eng.) Private Limited v. Venturetech Solutions Private Limited
rules.reference: Virgo Industries (Eng.) Private Limited v. Venturetech Solutions Private Limited
rules.relevance: Reiterated that Order 2 Rule 2 discourages vexing the defendant with multiple suits and that leave is required to sue for omitted reliefs.

rules.case_name: Mohd. Khalil Khan v. Mahbub Ali Mian
rules.reference: Mohd. Khalil Khan v. Mahbub Ali Mian
rules.relevance: Established the test for determining if a new suit is founded on a cause of action distinct from the former suit.

rules.case_name: Mahendra KC v. State of Karnataka

rules.relevance: Reiterated that the test for quashing is whether allegations prima facie establish the ingredients of the offence, without testing veracity.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Establishes the statutory obligation of the police to register a case upon receiving information disclosing a cognizable offence, without inquiring into the reliability or credibility of the information at that stage.

rules.reference: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
rules.relevance: The court examined whether the allegations prima facie constituted an offence under this special statute or if the invocation was mechanical and unrelated to caste-based atrocities.

rules.case_name: S.W. Palanikar v. State of Bihar

rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to distinguish between civil breach of trust and criminal breach of trust, emphasizing the need for mens rea.

rules.case_name: Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Limited

rules.relevance: Established principles for quashing complaints under Section 482 Cr.P.C., including that proceedings can be quashed if allegations do not prima facie constitute an offence.

rules.reference: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
rules.relevance: The court examined whether these provisions, inserted by the 2015 Amendment Act, applied to acts committed in 2015 before the amendment came into force.

rules.case_name: Anurag Soni v. State of Chhattisgarh

rules.relevance: Distinguishes between a false promise made with no intention to marry (vitiating consent) and a breach of a promise made in good faith.

rules.reference: Pramod Suryabhan Pawar v. State of Maharashtra and Another
rules.relevance: Established that for consent to be vitiated by a promise of marriage, the promise must be false, given in bad faith with no intention to adhere to it at the time, and must have a direct nexus to the sexual act.

rules.relevance: Established that a mature, married woman who has consensual relations for years cannot claim rape based on a false promise to marry, as her consent is not vitiated by misconception of fact.

rules.case_name: M.M.S. Investments, Madura and Others vs. V. Veerappan and Others
rules.reference: M.M.S. Investments, Madura and Others vs. V. Veerappan and Others

rules.case_name: Pushparani S. Sundaram and Ors. v. Pauline Manomani James and Ors.

rules.case_name: Ram Govind Upadhyay v. Sudarshan Singh and Others
rules.reference: Ram Govind Upadhyay v. Sudarshan Singh and Others

rules.reference: Prasanta Kumar Sarkar v. Ashis Chatterjee and another
rules.relevance: Lists factors for bail consideration including prima facie grounds, gravity of accusation, danger of absconding, and character of the accused.

rules.reference: Dr. Narendra K. Amin v. State of Gujarat and another
rules.relevance: Holds that an order granting bail is vulnerable if irrelevant materials are considered or relevant factors are ignored, rendering it perverse.

rules.case_name: Prahlad Singh Bhati v. NCT, Delhi and Another
rules.reference: Prahlad Singh Bhati v. NCT, Delhi and Another
rules.relevance: Cited for factors to consider in bail, including nature of accusations, severity of punishment, and apprehension of witness tampering.

rules.reference: Apportionment of Liability

rules.case_name: Smt. Rumi Dhar v. State of West Bengal & Another

rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to hold that repayment of dues or settlement cannot exonerate an accused from prima facie criminal charges, especially where criminal intention is alleged.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana & Others v. Bhajan Lal & Others

rules.relevance: The prosecution must establish beyond reasonable doubt that the injury inflicted was the sole cause of death, particularly when there is a long time lag and no post-mortem.

rules.case_name: Dablu Kujur v. State of Jharkhand
rules.reference: Dablu Kujur v. State of Jharkhand
rules.relevance: Crystallized the legal position that chargesheets must contain sufficient details and evidence to enable the Magistrate to take cognizance, not just a reproduction of the FIR.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: Defines the offences charged. Sections 147, 148, 149, and 364 are non-compoundable offences, affecting the scope for settlement-based quashing.

rules.case_name: State of Tamil Nadu v. R. Vasanthi Stanley
rules.reference: State of Tamil Nadu v. R. Vasanthi Stanley
rules.relevance: The court referred to this case to support the view that serious economic offences or those affecting financial institutions should not be quashed merely due to settlement or delay.

rules.case_name: Shiji @ Pappu and others vs. Radhika and another
rules.reference: Shiji @ Pappu and others vs. Radhika and another
rules.relevance: Distinguished by the court as applicable to civil disputes or private wrongs, not to serious crimes against society like those in the present appeals.

rules.case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh vs. Manish
rules.reference: State of Madhya Pradesh vs. Manish
rules.relevance: Holds that offences under Sections 307, 294, 34 IPC and the Arms Act are against society and require trial.

rules.reference: Determination of Encroachment
rules.relevance: Encroachment must be determined by actual possession relative to specific survey numbers purchased, not by abstract measurements in a sale deed which may be inaccurate.

rules.reference: Right to Drain Water
rules.relevance: No person has a natural right to have water from their property flow onto a neighbor's land unless specifically granted by deed.

rules.reference: Appellate Jurisdiction
rules.relevance: The High Court is justified in interfering with concurrent findings of fact if the lower courts proceeded on an erroneous legal basis or ignored vital evidence.

rules.reference: Acquisition of Easementary Rights
rules.relevance: Easementary rights by prescription require continuous enjoyment for a statutory period; they cannot be acquired within a short period such as two months between sales.

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: The court analyzed this rule to determine if remand was justified, concluding it was not because the High Court failed to specify why the decree was reversed or why a re-trial was necessary.

rules.case_name: State of Himachal Pradesh v. Asha Ram
rules.reference: State of Himachal Pradesh v. Asha Ram
rules.relevance: Confirmed that conviction can be founded on the testimony of the prosecutrix alone if it inspires confidence, but corroboration is required if there are compelling reasons to doubt the testimony.

rules.case_name: Lalliram & Anr. v. State of Madhya Pradesh
rules.reference: Lalliram & Anr. v. State of Madhya Pradesh
rules.relevance: Held that while injury is not a sine qua non for rape, the absence of injury combined with an incredible version necessitates corroboration.

rules.case_name: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Munshi
rules.reference: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Munshi
rules.relevance: Held that a victim's previous sexual history or loss of virginity is irrelevant to the question of consent and does not license rape.

rules.reference: Sterling Witness Test
rules.relevance: Establishes that while a prosecutrix's testimony can sustain a conviction without corroboration, it must be of 'sterling quality,' meaning unassailable, consistent, and inspiring confidence.

rules.case_name: Narender Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: Narender Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: Held that a woman of 'easy virtue' has the right to refuse sexual intercourse and her evidence should not be discarded based on her character.

rules.reference: Judicial Restraint in Tender Awards
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that constitutional courts should not substitute their view for that of the tendering authority unless the decision is perverse or mala fide.

rules.case_name: Caretel Infotech Ltd. v. Hindustan Petroleum Corpn. Ltd.
rules.reference: Caretel Infotech Ltd. v. Hindustan Petroleum Corpn. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Used to support the proposition that where a specific format is provided for disclosure, bidders are justified in adhering to the literal reading of that format, though this must be read harmoniously with other clauses.

rules.reference: Fraudulent Practice in Bidding
rules.relevance: The court held that suppression of material facts, such as an FIR and charge sheet regarding a collapsed bridge, constitutes a fraudulent practice under the NIT, justifying bid rejection.

rules.reference: Notice Inviting Tender (NIT)
rules.relevance: Defines eligible bidders, including government-owned entities, and stipulates conditions for Joint Ventures, serving as the basis for determining if Respondent No. 2 could bid as a single entity.

rules.case_name: Secy., Deptt. of Home Secy., A.P. v. B. Chinnam Naidu
rules.reference: Secy., Deptt. of Home Secy., A.P. v. B. Chinnam Naidu
rules.relevance: Distinguished on facts; held that unlike 'conviction' which excludes arrest, 'indictment' in the present case included the filing of a charge sheet.

rules.case_name: Vinny Parmvir Parmar v. Parmvir Parmar
rules.reference: Vinny Parmvir Parmar v. Parmvir Parmar
rules.relevance: Guides the determination of permanent alimony based on the wife's status, mode of life, and the husband's financial capacity.

rules.case_name: Ashok Dulichand v. Madhavlal Dube
rules.reference: Ashok Dulichand v. Madhavlal Dube
rules.relevance: Establishes that secondary evidence is admissible only if a proper foundation is laid showing the original is in the possession of the person against whom it is sought to be proved.

rules.reference: Pleading of Grounds for Divorce
rules.relevance: A specific case for desertion must be pleaded in the petition for divorce; a finding cannot be sustained on an unpleaded ground.

rules.case_name: H. Siddiqui (Dead) by Lrs. v. A. Ramalingam
rules.reference: H. Siddiqui (Dead) by Lrs. v. A. Ramalingam
rules.relevance: Holds that secondary evidence is inadmissible if no factual foundation is laid for the non-production of the original document.

rules.case_name: Vishwanath Agrawal v. Sara Vishwanath Agrawal
rules.reference: Vishwanath Agrawal v. Sara Vishwanath Agrawal
rules.relevance: Establishes that a sustained attitude of causing humiliation and calculated torture amounts to mental cruelty.

rules.reference: Benefit of acquittal to non-appealing co-accused
rules.relevance: Establishes that if the prosecution fails to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, the benefit of acquittal should extend to similarly situated non-appealing accused.

rules.reference: Theory of last seen together
rules.relevance: The court held that being last seen together is not independently sufficient for conviction if the time gap is large or evidence is contradictory, requiring a complete chain of circumstances.

rules.reference: Extra-judicial confession as weak evidence
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that extra-judicial confessions are weak evidence, must be voluntary and truthful, and require independent corroboration to sustain a conviction.

rules.case_name: Arjun Marik v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Arjun Marik v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that the 'last seen together' theory alone is not sufficient to complete the chain of circumstances for conviction.

rules.reference: Discovery of Facts at Instance of Accused
rules.relevance: Recovery of the body and incriminating articles at the instance of the accused serves as strong corroborative evidence of guilt.

rules.case_name: Daulat Ram and others v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Daulat Ram and others v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Holds that cancellation of bail requires cogent and overwhelming circumstances or supervening events non-conducive to a fair trial.

rules.case_name: Vipin Kumar Dhir v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Vipin Kumar Dhir v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Holds that bail can be revoked if the court considered irrelevant factors or ignored relevant material, rendering the order legally untenable.

rules.reference: Parameters for grant of bail
rules.relevance: The court considers the likelihood of the accused absconding, tampering with evidence, interfering with witnesses, or influencing the investigation.

rules.case_name: Kalyan Chandra Sarkar v. Rajesh Ranjan @ Pappu Yadav and another
rules.reference: Kalyan Chandra Sarkar v. Rajesh Ranjan @ Pappu Yadav and another
rules.relevance: Establishes parameters for granting bail, including nature of accusation, severity of punishment, and apprehension of witness tampering.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: Establishes the serious nature of the offences, including double murder and unlawful assembly, which weighs against the grant of bail.

rules.reference: Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
rules.relevance: The court examined whether a prima facie case under this section was made out to determine if the statutory bar applied.

rules.case_name: Vilas Pandurang Pawar and Another v. State of Maharashtra and Others
rules.reference: Vilas Pandurang Pawar and Another v. State of Maharashtra and Others
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to establish that Section 18 of the SC/ST Act creates a specific bar to anticipatory bail unless the court prima facie finds that the offence is not made out.

rules.case_name: M.A. Rashid vs. Gopal Chandra
rules.reference: M.A. Rashid vs. Gopal Chandra
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this decision, holding it cannot be taken as a precedent in view of the specific statutory bar under Section 18 of the SC/ST Act.

rules.case_name: R.K. Sangwan & Anr. vs. State
rules.reference: R.K. Sangwan & Anr. vs. State
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this decision, holding it cannot be taken as a precedent in view of the specific statutory bar under Section 18 of the SC/ST Act.

rules.case_name: Vilas Pandurang Pawar and Another vs. State of Maharashtra and Others
rules.reference: Vilas Pandurang Pawar and Another vs. State of Maharashtra and Others
rules.relevance: Held that Section 18 of the SC/ST Act creates a bar for invoking Section 438 of the CrPC unless the court prima facie finds that the offence under the Act is not made out.

rules.case_name: V. Sreedharan vs. State of Kerala
rules.reference: V. Sreedharan vs. State of Kerala
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to support the view that an incident arising from provocation and resulting in fatal injuries should be prosecuted under Section 304 Part I rather than Section 302 IPC.

rules.reference: Government Resolution No.RLP1006/CR621/PRS-3
rules.relevance: Specifies that for crimes against women, a minimum of 20 years of imprisonment (including remission) must be served before consideration for premature release.

rules.reference: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000
rules.relevance: The court directed that the case of Appellant No. 1 be referred to the Juvenile Justice Board to be dealt with under these provisions.

rules.case_name: Hari Ram vs. State of Rajasthan & Anr.
rules.reference: Hari Ram vs. State of Rajasthan & Anr.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to determine that Appellant No. 1 was a juvenile on the date of the incident, necessitating proceedings under the Juvenile Justice Act.

rules.case_name: Harbans Singh & another v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Harbans Singh & another v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Held that corroboration of a dying declaration is not a rule of law or prudence required for conviction.

rules.case_name: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India
rules.reference: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Petitioners relied on this case to argue against mid-process rule changes; the court distinguished it by noting the amendment was published before the actual admission process for 2019-20 commenced.

rules.reference: Graduate Medical Education Regulations, 1997 (as amended by MCI notification dated 04.02.2019)
rules.relevance: Establishes the essential eligibility criteria for PwD admission to MBBS, requiring 40% benchmark disability and specific physical capabilities regarding hands.

rules.reference: Right of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016
rules.relevance: Provides the statutory basis for 5% reservation in government educational institutions for persons with benchmark disability.

rules.reference: Relevant date for eligibility criteria
rules.relevance: The court determined that the relevant date for applying eligibility criteria is when candidates seek admission and appear before the Medical Board, not when the selection brochure is released.

rules.reference: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016
rules.relevance: Defines 'person with disability' broadly, establishing that rights under Chapter III apply to all PwD, not just PwBD.

rules.case_name: Pulukuri Kotayya and others vs. King-Emperor
rules.reference: Pulukuri Kotayya and others vs. King-Emperor
rules.relevance: Established that information supplied by an accused is only one link in the chain of proof and cannot form the sole foundation of a prosecution case.

rules.case_name: Topandas vs. State of Bombay
rules.reference: Topandas vs. State of Bombay
rules.relevance: Affirmed that one person alone cannot be convicted of criminal conspiracy if alleged co-conspirators are acquitted.

rules.case_name: Rabindra Kumar Pal @ Dara Singh v. Republic of India
rules.reference: Rabindra Kumar Pal @ Dara Singh v. Republic of India
rules.relevance: Supported the view that absconding and avoiding arrest is conduct under Section 8 of the Evidence Act pointing to guilt.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: Defines criminal conspiracy as an agreement between two or more persons to commit an illegal act.

rules.case_name: Sanjeet Kumar Singh vs. State of Chhattisgarh
rules.reference: Sanjeet Kumar Singh vs. State of Chhattisgarh
rules.relevance: Held that if independent witnesses turn hostile and create a gaping hole in the prosecution theory regarding search and seizure, the case should collapse.

rules.reference: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997
rules.relevance: Mandates that a tenant must deposit arrears of rent with the Civil Judge to claim protection against eviction on grounds of default.

rules.reference: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997
rules.relevance: Provides procedure for determining disputed rent amounts and allows the court to specify the amount due, which the tenant must pay within one month.

rules.reference: Strict compliance with statutory provisions
rules.relevance: Benefits under Rent Control Acts are subject to strict compliance with statutory provisions, but bona fide mistakes may be considered.

rules.reference: West Bengal Premises Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 2005
rules.relevance: Substituted 'Rent Controller' with 'Civil Judge' effective June 1, 2006, creating the statutory requirement the tenant allegedly failed to meet.

rules.reference: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997
rules.relevance: Mandates that a tenant must pay or deposit arrears of rent within one month of summons or appearance to claim protection against eviction. The proviso allows extension of time only once, not exceeding two months.

rules.reference: Deterrence through heavy fines
rules.relevance: The court established that heavy fines are necessary to make electricity theft a non-profitable venture and curb the tendency.

rules.reference: Indian Electricity Act, 1910
rules.relevance: Defines 'consumer' as any person supplied with energy or whose premises are connected for supply; used to determine liability.

rules.reference: Surprise raids do not require prior notice
rules.relevance: The court held that 48 hours' notice is not envisaged for surprise raids as it would allow destruction of evidence.

rules.reference: Indian Electricity Act, 1910
rules.relevance: Creates a presumption that a consumer knowingly and wilfully prevented a meter from duly registering if artificial means for such prevention exist in their custody. The court distinguished this from Section 39, noting it does not prove theft.

rules.reference: Indian Electricity Rules, 1956
rules.relevance: Imposes absolute liability on a consumer for breaking a meter seal unless they prove they used all reasonable means to prevent it. The court affirmed convictions under this rule.

rules.case_name: L.D. Jaikwal v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: L.D. Jaikwal v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: The Court used this precedent to reject the contemnors' apologies, stating that an apology must be genuine and not a 'slap-say sorry-and forget' tactic offered only when punishment is imminent.

rules.case_name: M v. Home Office
rules.reference: M v. Home Office
rules.relevance: The Court referred to this case to support the principle that findings of contempt can be made against government departments or ministers to vindicate justice and ensure orders are obeyed.

rules.case_name: B.M. Bhattacharjee (Major General) and Anr. v. Russel Estate Corporation and Anr.
rules.reference: B.M. Bhattacharjee (Major General) and Anr. v. Russel Estate Corporation and Anr.
rules.relevance: The Court relied on this precedent to establish that government officers are presumed to know that Court orders must be obeyed implicitly and should not be trifled with.

rules.reference: Bombay Forest Rules, 1942
rules.relevance: The Court noted that Rule 88 became applicable for entire Maharashtra, requiring licenses for operations previously covered by other rules, thereby negating the contemnors' claim that licenses were not required for certain machinery.

rules.case_name: Re: Sri Pravakar Behera
rules.reference: Re: Sri Pravakar Behera
rules.relevance: The Court referred to this case to compare the punishment imposed on a lower-ranking officer, justifying a more stringent custodial sentence for the high-ranking contemnors.

rules.case_name: Rosy Jacob vs. Jacob A Chakramakkal
rules.reference: Rosy Jacob vs. Jacob A Chakramakkal
rules.relevance: Established that custody orders are temporary and interlocutory, and can be modified if the welfare of the child so demands, even if based on consent.

rules.case_name: Mausami Moitra Ganguli vs. Jayant Ganguli
rules.reference: Mausami Moitra Ganguli vs. Jayant Ganguli
rules.relevance: Held that the welfare of the child may have primacy even over statutory provisions.

rules.reference: Welfare of the minor is paramount
rules.relevance: The court applied this principle to determine that custody should remain with the father as the children expressed a clear desire to live with him.

rules.reference: Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956
rules.relevance: Cited as a statute governing custody orders where the welfare of the minor is paramount.

rules.case_name: Mousmi Moitra Ganguli v. Jayant Ganguli
rules.reference: Mousmi Moitra Ganguli v. Jayant Ganguli
rules.relevance: Relied upon for the holding that the welfare and interest of the child, not the rights of the parents, is the determining factor for custody.

rules.reference: Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007
rules.relevance: Defines the scope of the Tribunal's power to interfere with court-martial findings, allowing reappreciation of evidence to determine legal sustainability.

rules.case_name: Union of India and others vs. Sandeep Kumar and others
rules.reference: Union of India and others vs. Sandeep Kumar and others
rules.relevance: Established that the AFT can reappreciate evidence to find if findings are legally unsustainable, not merely because a different view is possible.

rules.case_name: Sahadevan and another vs. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.reference: Sahadevan and another vs. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.relevance: Laid down principles that extra-judicial confessions are weak evidence requiring corroboration and must be voluntary and trustworthy.

rules.case_name: The State of Bombay vs. Kathi Kalu Oghad and others
rules.reference: The State of Bombay vs. Kathi Kalu Oghad and others
rules.relevance: Held that voluntariness of a statement is a question of fact determined by circumstances; custody alone does not imply compulsion.

rules.reference: Army Act, 1950
rules.relevance: The court analyzed this provision regarding intent to defraud to determine the gravity of the first charge.

rules.case_name: Dahya Lal and Ors. v. Rasul Mohammed Abdul Rahim
rules.reference: Dahya Lal and Ors. v. Rasul Mohammed Abdul Rahim
rules.relevance: Established that 'lawful cultivation' under Section 4 does not require authority derived directly from the owner, protecting all persons lawfully cultivating land.

rules.case_name: Gopala Genu Wagale v. Nageshwardeo
rules.reference: Gopala Genu Wagale v. Nageshwardeo
rules.relevance: Distinguished as it dealt with prohibited sub-tenancy, whereas the present Act does not prohibit a person with limited interest from permitting cultivation.

rules.case_name: Latchaiah v. Subramaniam
rules.reference: Latchaiah v. Subramaniam
rules.relevance: Distinguished on facts; the court held that unlike in Latchaiah, the lessor here had a limited interest and was not a trespasser, so the lessee could be a deemed tenant.

rules.reference: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948
rules.relevance: Confers the right on a tenant to purchase the land held by them from the landlord.

rules.reference: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948
rules.relevance: Provides that the certificate of purchase issued by the Tribunal is conclusive proof of purchase.

rules.case_name: P. K. Haneefa v. State of Kerala
rules.reference: P. K. Haneefa v. State of Kerala
rules.relevance: Held that Rule 2(b) creates a mandatory quota for direct recruitment and consequently a quota for in-service candidates; appointments in excess of quota do not confer superior seniority.

rules.reference: Notional Seniority

rules.case_name: Lakshmana Rao Yadavalli & Anr. v. State of Andhra Pradesh & Ors.

rules.relevance: Supported the direction for retrospective appointment and seniority for a candidate wrongfully not appointed.

rules.reference: Kerala State Higher Judicial Services Special Rules, 1961
rules.relevance: Establishes that one-third of permanent posts are reserved for direct recruitment, implying a corresponding two-thirds quota for appointment by transfer/promotion.

rules.reference: Kerala State Higher Judicial Services Special Rules, 1961
rules.relevance: Provides that seniority is determined by the date of first appointment, and for simultaneous appointments, by the serial order in the appointment order.

rules.reference: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
rules.relevance: Defines the offence of penetrative sexual assault and prescribes the punishment, including a minimum sentence of five years, which the court considered in evaluating the adequacy of the trial court's sentence.

rules.case_name: Ram Pyare Mishra v. Prem Shanker and Ors.
rules.reference: Ram Pyare Mishra v. Prem Shanker and Ors.
rules.relevance: The State relied on this case to oppose modification of sentence, noting it resulted in a conviction under Section 304(i) with an eight-year sentence.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: These sections define the offences for which the appellant was convicted and sentenced, forming the basis for the sentencing discretion exercised by the court.

rules.reference: Principles for alteration of sentence
rules.relevance: The court applied principles regarding mitigating factors such as age, lack of criminal antecedents, time elapsed since the incident, and period already undergone in jail to justify reducing the jail sentence and enhancing the fine.

rules.case_name: Sahab Singh and others vs. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Sahab Singh and others vs. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Confirmed that even when exercising suo motu revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 read with Section 401, the High Court must put the convict on notice before enhancing the sentence.

rules.case_name: Arun Vyas v. Anita Vyas
rules.reference: Arun Vyas v. Anita Vyas
rules.relevance: Established that the last act of cruelty starts the limitation period and that Section 473 Cr.P.C. should be construed liberally in favor of a wife subjected to cruelty.

rules.case_name: Y. Abraham Ajith and Ors. v. Inspector of Police, Chennai and Anr.

rules.relevance: Referred regarding the determination of territorial jurisdiction at the pre-trial stage based on the cause of action.

rules.case_name: Venka Radhamanohari v. Vanka Venkata Reddy

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajanlal

rules.relevance: Laid down parameters for quashing FIRs under Section 482, including when proceedings are manifestly attended with mala fide or result in failure of justice.

rules.case_name: Patasibai v. Ratanlal

rules.relevance: Relied on to support the view that the power to reject a plaint under Order VII Rule 11 can be exercised suo motu by the court.

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

rules.case_name: Ratna Commercial Enterprises Ltd. v. Vasutech Ltd.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code (IPC)
rules.relevance: These are the offences under which the First Information Report was registered against the appellants.

rules.case_name: Ram Lal Yadav and others v. State of U.P. and others

rules.relevance: Guiding principles for exercising Section 482 powers, emphasizing that civil disputes should not be converted into criminal cases to apply pressure.

rules.case_name: Ayyasami vs. State of Tamil Nadu

rules.case_name: Ram Singh vs. Col. Ram Singh

rules.case_name: Panna Damodar Rathi vs. State of Maharashtra
