rules.relevance: Holds that if a grading falling below the benchmark has not been communicated to the concerned employee, it must be ignored while considering promotion. The court distinguished this case on the basis that communication had already occurred in the present matter.

rules.case_name: Baikunth Nath Das v. Chief District Medical Officer
rules.reference: Baikunth Nath Das v. Chief District Medical Officer
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case for the principle that adverse remarks prior to an earlier promotion lose their sting and that more importance should be attached to recent records.

rules.case_name: Daulat Ram and others vs. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Daulat Ram and others vs. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Establishes that cancellation of bail requires cogent and overwhelming reasons and differs from the initial grant of bail; highlights that bail should not be cancelled mechanically but considers supervening circumstances.

rules.reference: Parity with co-accused
rules.relevance: Parity cannot be granted if the allegations against the accused are materially different or if the accused's conduct (such as absconding) distinguishes them from co-accused.

rules.case_name: X vs. State of Telangana and Another
rules.reference: X vs. State of Telangana and Another
rules.relevance: Reiterates principles regarding bail cancellation and the necessity of considering whether circumstances render bail unconducive to a fair trial.

rules.case_name: Kanwar Singh Meena v. State of Rajasthan & Anr.
rules.reference: Kanwar Singh Meena v. State of Rajasthan & Anr.
rules.relevance: Holds that bail can be cancelled if the order suffers from serious infirmities, ignores relevant material, or takes into account irrelevant material.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code
rules.relevance: Defines the gravity of the offences (dowry death and murder) for which bail was sought, influencing the discretion of the court.

rules.reference: Effect of contributory negligence on damages
rules.relevance: Where the injured party is partly responsible for the accident, the claim is not defeated, but the recoverable damages are reduced in proportion to the claimant's contributory negligence.

rules.reference: Distinction between composite and contributory negligence
rules.relevance: The court clarified that 'composite negligence' applies when a third party claims damages against multiple wrongdoers, making them jointly and severally liable. In contrast, 'contributory negligence' applies when the claimant is one of the drivers involved, requiring an assessment of the claimant's own share of responsibility.

rules.case_name: Sarla Verma and Ors. v. Delhi Transport Corporation and Ors.
rules.reference: Sarla Verma and Ors. v. Delhi Transport Corporation and Ors.
rules.relevance: Provided the multiplier table; the court applied a multiplier of 17 for a 29-year-old claimant.

rules.case_name: National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi & Others
rules.reference: National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi & Others
rules.relevance: Mandates a 40% addition for future prospects in the calculation of compensation.

rules.reference: No automatic apportionment of liability
rules.relevance: There is no legal basis for an automatic 50:50 split of liability in head-on collisions; the extent of contributory negligence must be determined based on the specific facts and circumstances of the case.

rules.reference: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
rules.relevance: Defines the offence of penetrative sexual assault and prescribes the punishment, including a minimum sentence of five years, which the court considered in evaluating the adequacy of the trial court's sentence.

rules.reference: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
rules.relevance: Provides that where an act constitutes an offence under both the IPC and POCSO Act, the offender is liable to punishment only under the law providing for the greater punishment.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: Defines the punishment for rape of a woman under twelve years as rigorous imprisonment for not less than 20 years extending to life imprisonment (remainder of natural life) or death, along with a mandatory fine for medical expenses and rehabilitation.

rules.reference: Protection of Children From Sexual Offences Act, 2012
rules.relevance: Prescribes punishment for aggravated penetrative sexual assault; at the time of the offence, the range was ten years to life imprisonment.

rules.case_name: Mulla v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Mulla v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Establishes that it is open to the sentencing court to prescribe the length of incarceration when a death sentence is replaced by life imprisonment.

rules.case_name: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited v. EMCO Limited and another
rules.reference: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited v. EMCO Limited and another
rules.relevance: Held that the Commission cannot extend the control period to allow a project to benefit from an earlier tariff order if commissioned later, as the PPA stipulates the lower of the two tariffs.

rules.case_name: Vinod Seth v. Devinder Bajaj and Another
rules.reference: Vinod Seth v. Devinder Bajaj and Another
rules.relevance: Established that inherent powers under Section 151 CPC are procedural and cannot be used to create substantive rights or alter contractual terms.

rules.reference: Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2004
rules.relevance: Allows extension of time for acts prescribed by regulations or orders, but not for substantive control periods of tariff orders.

rules.reference: Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2004
rules.relevance: Saves inherent powers of the Commission for procedural matters and ends of justice, but does not confer substantive power to alter contracts.

rules.reference: Electricity Act, 2003
rules.relevance: Specifies the powers of the Commission, limiting them to those of a civil court in specific procedural matters.

rules.case_name: Delhi Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works Pvt. Ltd. v. Himgiri Realtors Pvt. Ltd.
rules.reference: Delhi Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works Pvt. Ltd. v. Himgiri Realtors Pvt. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Cited to note that the precedent relied upon by the Single Judge (Bhandari Engineers) had been overruled.

rules.reference: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
rules.relevance: The court considered the enforceability of the Emergency Arbitrator's order as an order of the court under these provisions.

rules.reference: Seat of Arbitration Jurisdiction
rules.relevance: The court at the seat of arbitration has exclusive supervisory jurisdiction over challenges to the award, including bias; objections not raised there should not be entertained at the enforcement stage.

rules.case_name: Canara Bank v. Debasis Das
rules.reference: Canara Bank v. Debasis Das
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that when an order is struck down for violation of natural justice, the proceedings are not terminated but remitted back for fresh consideration.

rules.reference: Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
rules.relevance: Provides that in any proceedings for contempt, it may be shown that the alleged contemnor had not intended to insult the dignity of the court or interfere with the due course of justice; the court considered whether the breach substantially interfered with justice.

rules.reference: Standard of proof in corruption cases
rules.relevance: The court held that demand and acceptance must be proved by cogent evidence and beyond reasonable doubt, not merely by preponderance of probabilities.

rules.reference: Appellate interference with order of acquittal
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that an appellate court should not interfere with an acquittal if the trial court's view is reasonable and plausible, even if another view is possible.

rules.case_name: Meena (Smt) w/o Balwant Hemke vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Meena (Smt) w/o Balwant Hemke vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to hold that mere recovery of currency notes and a positive phenolphthalein test are insufficient to establish guilt without proof of demand and acceptance.

rules.case_name: Mukut Bihari and Anr. v. State of Rajasthan
rules.reference: Mukut Bihari and Anr. v. State of Rajasthan
rules.relevance: Cited to confirm that demand is sine qua non and mere receipt of amount is not sufficient to fasten guilt without evidence of demand and acceptance.

rules.reference: Definition of 'Accept'
rules.relevance: The court held that 'accept' means to take with a consenting mind. Consent can be inferred from circumstances surrounding the transaction, so a prior demand is not strictly necessary for conviction under Section 161 IPC.

rules.reference: Presumption against foreign court's wrongful jurisdiction
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that a foreign court cannot be presumed to be exercising its jurisdiction wrongly merely because the parties are governed by Indian matrimonial law.

rules.case_name: Modi Entertainment Network and Another vs. WSG Cricket PTE Ltd.
rules.reference: Modi Entertainment Network and Another vs. WSG Cricket PTE Ltd.
rules.relevance: The court applied the principles from this case for granting anti-suit injunctions: the defendant must be amenable to personal jurisdiction, the ends of justice must be defeated without the injunction, and the principle of comity must be respected.

rules.reference: Equitable nature of anti-suit injunctions
rules.relevance: The court noted that anti-suit injunctions are equitable remedies that impinge on foreign jurisdiction and must be granted sparingly and with caution.

rules.reference: Specific Relief Act, 1963
rules.relevance: The court considered the statutory restrictions on granting injunctions, particularly clauses (a) and (b), which limit injunctions against proceedings in non-subordinate courts unless necessary to prevent multiplicity of proceedings.

rules.reference: Limitation Act, 1963
rules.relevance: Prescribes a twelve-year limitation period for a person excluded from joint family property to enforce a right to share therein. The appellant relied on this to argue the claim was not time-barred.

rules.case_name: Hemal Ashwin Jain v. Union of India
rules.citation: R/Special Civil Application No. 6369 of 2020 (Gujarat High Court)
rules.reference: Hemal Ashwin Jain v. Union of India
rules.relevance: The Court agreed with this decision that Section 15A(3) of the SC/ST Act is mandatory and non-compliance renders the order null and void.

rules.reference: Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
rules.relevance: The Court held that these provisions are mandatory, requiring notice to and hearing of the victim/dependent before granting bail. Non-compliance renders the bail order null and void.

rules.reference: Mandatory nature of statutory procedural safeguards
rules.relevance: The Court held that the defect of not issuing notice to the victim cannot be cured by providing a hearing in a subsequent cancellation of bail proceeding.

rules.case_name: Ramesh Bhavan Rathod v. Vishanbhai Hirabhai Makwana
rules.reference: Ramesh Bhavan Rathod v. Vishanbhai Hirabhai Makwana
rules.relevance: The Court relied on this precedent to establish that recording reasons for bail orders is a significant safeguard and not a formality.

rules.case_name: Kalyan Chandra Sarkar v. Rajesh Ranjan @ Pappu Yadav and another
rules.reference: Kalyan Chandra Sarkar v. Rajesh Ranjan @ Pappu Yadav and another
rules.relevance: Establishes parameters for granting bail, including nature of accusation, severity of punishment, and apprehension of witness tampering.

rules.reference: Expanded Option in Sentencing
rules.relevance: The court can impose a fixed-term sentence exceeding 14 years but less than death in cases that do not warrant death penalty but where 14 years is inadequate.

rules.case_name: Jagat Bahadur v. State of Madhya Pradesh
rules.reference: Jagat Bahadur v. State of Madhya Pradesh
rules.relevance: Distinguished on the basis that the trial court in the present case had the competence to impose the death penalty, unlike the case in Jagat Bahadur.

rules.case_name: Swamy Shraddananda (2) v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Swamy Shraddananda (2) v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Established the principle of 'expanded option' for sentencing when death penalty is not warranted but 14 years is inadequate.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. V. Sriharan @ Murugan & Ors.
rules.reference: Union of India v. V. Sriharan @ Murugan & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that courts can impose a special category of life sentence (e.g., 30 years without remission) as an alternative to the death penalty in cases that do not fall under the 'rarest of rare' category but where standard life imprisonment is inadequate.

rules.case_name: Muthuramalingam and others v. State represented by Inspector of Police
rules.reference: Muthuramalingam and others v. State represented by Inspector of Police
rules.relevance: Clarified that consecutive life sentences cannot be awarded as humans have only one life; such sentences must run concurrently.

rules.case_name: S. Satyapal Reddy v. Govt. of A.P.
rules.reference: S. Satyapal Reddy v. Govt. of A.P.
rules.relevance: Confirms that the State is entitled to prescribe qualifications for recruitment that are higher than the minimum prescribed by the Central Government.

rules.case_name: Devender Bhaskar v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Devender Bhaskar v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Holds that equivalence of educational qualifications is a technical academic matter for the expert body, not the court, and cannot be implied without a specific order.

rules.case_name: Employees’ State Insurance Corporation v. Union of India
rules.reference: Employees’ State Insurance Corporation v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Establishes that administrative instructions cannot amend or supersede statutory rules.

rules.reference: NCTE (Determination of Minimum Qualifications...) Regulations 2014
rules.relevance: Confirms the 2-year Diploma as the prescribed minimum qualification for Level 3 teachers.

rules.reference: Uttarakhand Government Elementary Education (Teacher) Service Rules 2012
rules.relevance: Prescribes the 2-year D.El.Ed. as the mandatory minimum qualification for recruitment, which cannot be overridden by executive instructions.

rules.case_name: N.P. Thirugnanam (dead) by Lrs. vs Dr. R. Jagan Mohan Rao & Ors
rules.reference: N.P. Thirugnanam (dead) by Lrs. vs Dr. R. Jagan Mohan Rao & Ors
rules.relevance: Supported the finding that the plaintiff must prove readiness and willingness from the date of the agreement till the decree, considering conduct and circumstances.

rules.case_name: Sidheshwar Mukherjee v. Bhubneshwar Prasad Narain Singh and Ors.
rules.reference: Sidheshwar Mukherjee v. Bhubneshwar Prasad
rules.relevance: Holds that a purchaser of an undivided interest does not acquire title to a defined share and is not entitled to joint possession or specific demarcation without a suit for partition.

rules.case_name: P.R. Deb & Associates Vs. Sunanda Roy
rules.reference: P.R. Deb & Associates Vs. Sunanda Roy
rules.relevance: Held that a plaintiff in a suit for specific performance must be ready and willing to carry out his part of the agreement at all material times.

rules.case_name: Smt. Chand Rani (dead) by LRs. Vs. Smt. Kamal Rani(dead) by LRs
rules.reference: Smt. Chand Rani (dead) by LRs. Vs. Smt. Kamal Rani(dead) by LRs
rules.relevance: Held that while time is generally not the essence of a contract for immovable property, parties can agree to make it so, and such intention must be expressed in unequivocal language.

rules.reference: Specific Relief Act, 1963
rules.relevance: Grants the court discretionary power to refuse specific performance if it would cause hardship or if the plaintiff is in breach of contract.

rules.reference: Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
rules.relevance: Defines the violation of human rights by state functionaries, which was the basis of the complaint and the Commission's findings.

rules.reference: Norms of Custody
rules.relevance: Physical torture of a person in police custody violates established norms, regardless of the accused's antecedents or criminal history.

rules.case_name: T. Subramanian v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.reference: T. Subramanian v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.relevance: Cited to support the proposition regarding the burden of proof under Section 20 of the Act.

rules.reference: Definition of FIR
rules.relevance: The first information given to the police that sets the machinery in motion constitutes the FIR, even if it lacks specific details like names of accused.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure
rules.relevance: The court interpreted this section to hold that it does not mandate that information can only be given to an officer in charge of a police station.

rules.reference: Punjab Recruitment of Ex-servicemen Rules, 1982
rules.relevance: The court considered this saving clause but held it did not extend benefits to the appellant as no right to seniority weightage had accrued prior to joining service.

rules.reference: Demobilized Indian Armed Forces Personnel (Reservation of Vacancies in the Punjab Civil Service) (Executive Branch) Rules, 1972
rules.relevance: The court examined this rule to identify the specific benefit of counting military service for seniority that the appellants claimed, noting it was repealed by the 1982 Rules.

rules.case_name: Ishwar Singh and others versus State of Punjab
rules.citation: Writ Petition No.3236 of 1995 (High Court of Punjab and Haryana)
rules.reference: Ishwar Singh and others versus State of Punjab
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this judgment, holding that while it determined the percentage of reservation based on when vacancies arose, it did not govern the determination of seniority for appointments made under the 1982 Rules.

rules.reference: Punjab Recruitment of Ex-servicemen Rules, 1982
rules.relevance: The court noted that this rule superseded the 1972 Rules and did not contain the provision for counting military service towards seniority.

rules.reference: Punjab Recruitment of Ex-servicemen Rules, 1982
rules.relevance: The court relied on this repeal clause to establish that the 1972 Rules were explicitly repealed by the 1982 Rules.

rules.reference: Guardians and Wards Act, 1890
rules.relevance: These sections provide the statutory framework for the court to appoint a guardian and make orders for the custody of a minor, prioritizing the minor's welfare.

rules.reference: Guardians and Wards Act, 1890
rules.relevance: This provision mandates that the court shall regard the wishes of the minor as a relevant factor, though not necessarily decisive, when determining custody.

rules.case_name: Kumar V Jahgirdar v. Chethana Ramatheertha
rules.reference: Kumar V Jahgirdar v. Chethana Ramatheertha
rules.relevance: Cited by the appellant regarding the need for a mother's care during puberty; the court distinguished this case noting the respondent had arranged for female care via his sister.

rules.reference: Parental Alienation Syndrome (PAS)
rules.relevance: Treated as a question of fact requiring identification of specific alienating behaviors rather than a medical diagnosis; the court found no evidence of such behavior in this case.

rules.case_name: Vivek Singh v. Romani Singh
rules.reference: Vivek Singh v. Romani Singh
rules.relevance: Discussed to clarify that Parental Alienation Syndrome (PAS) cannot be invoked as a straitjacket formula without identifying specific instances of alienating behavior.

rules.case_name: Shyam Lal Verma v. Central Bureau of Investigation
rules.reference: Shyam Lal Verma v. Central Bureau of Investigation
rules.relevance: Establishes that where a specific provision prescribes a mandatory minimum sentence without discretion, the PO Act cannot be invoked.

rules.reference: Definition of Mandatory Minimum Sentence
rules.relevance: A mandatory minimum sentence leaves no discretion to the court; if a statute allows reduction of sentence for special reasons, it does not constitute a mandatory minimum that bars probation.

rules.case_name: Superintendent, Central Excise, Bangalore v. Ballubali
rules.reference: Superintendent, Central Excise, Bangalore v. Ballubali
rules.relevance: Held that provisions prescribing minimum sentences are inconsistent with the PO Act and must yield to the specific statute if it bars discretion.

rules.case_name: Dhbir Singh v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Dhbir Singh v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Interprets 'expedient' in Section 4 of the PO Act to require the court to consider the nature of the offence and circumstances before granting probation.

rules.case_name: Om Prakash & Ors. v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Om Prakash & Ors. v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: The appellant relied on this case for probation; the court distinguished it because the present case involved intentional harm (mens rea), unlike the accidental nature of Om Prakash.

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: Establishes the maintainability of the appeal against the trial court's order.

rules.reference: Bonnard standard
rules.relevance: A common law principle requiring exceptional caution in granting interim injunctions in defamation cases to protect free speech; injunctions should not restrain publication unless the libel is clearly untrue or malicious.

rules.case_name: R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.reference: R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.relevance: Cited in the context of balancing fundamental rights regarding free speech and privacy in defamation suits.

rules.case_name: Fraser v. Evans
rules.reference: Fraser v. Evans
rules.relevance: Supports the principle that courts will not restrain publication if the defendant intends to justify it or make fair comment on a matter of public interest.

rules.case_name: Morgan Stanley Mutual Fund v. Kartick Das
rules.reference: Morgan Stanley Mutual Fund v. Kartick Das
rules.relevance: Elucidates factors for granting ex-parte injunctions, including exceptional circumstances, irreparable mischief, good faith, and limited duration.

rules.case_name: Madras Petrochem Ltd. v. Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction
rules.reference: Madras Petrochem Ltd. v. Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to interpret Section 37 of the SARFAESI Act as limited to securities laws, thereby excluding the Transfer of Property Act from its saving clause.

rules.case_name: Valji Khimji and Company v. Official Liquidator of Hindustan Nitro Product (Gujarat) Ltd.
rules.reference: Valji Khimji and Company v. Official Liquidator of Hindustan Nitro Product (Gujarat) Ltd.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case for the principle that confirmed auctions have sanctity and can only be interfered with on limited grounds like fraud.

rules.case_name: Pal Alloys and Metal India Private Limited v. Allahabad Bank
rules.reference: Pal Alloys and Metal India Private Limited v. Allahabad Bank
rules.relevance: The court held that this decision of the Punjab and Haryana High Court did not lay down the correct position of law.

rules.case_name: Sri. Sai Annadhatha Polymers v. Canara Bank
rules.reference: Sri. Sai Annadhatha Polymers v. Canara Bank
rules.relevance: The court agreed with this decision of the Andhra Pradesh High Court that the right of redemption is extinguished upon publication of the auction notice under the amended Section 13(8).

rules.case_name: United Bank of India v. Satyawati Tondon
rules.reference: Satyawati Tondon v. United Bank of India
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case for the principle that High Courts should not entertain writ petitions under Article 226 when effective statutory remedies are available under the SARFAESI Act.

rules.case_name: State of Andhra Pradesh, through Inspector General, National Investigation Agency v. Mohd. Hussain @ Salim
rules.reference: State of Andhra Pradesh v. Mohd. Hussain @ Salim
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to confirm that bail applications in NIA cases must be heard by a Division Bench of the High Court.

rules.case_name: K.A. Najeeb v. Union of India
rules.reference: K.A. Najeeb v. Union of India
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to hold that constitutional courts can grant bail under Article 21 despite statutory restrictions if detention is prolonged.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Basti Ram
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Basti Ram
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case, holding that the principle of remanding for first-instance appreciation of evidence is not mandatory for pre-trial bail pleas.

rules.case_name: Vernon v. The State of Maharashtra & Anr.
rules.reference: Vernon v. The State of Maharashtra & Anr.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment for the interpretation of 'terrorist act' and the requirement of surface analysis of probative value for bail.

rules.reference: National Investigation Agency Act, 2008
rules.relevance: The court relied on this provision to establish the jurisdiction of the High Court Division Bench to hear the bail appeal and examine subsequent facts.

rules.case_name: Ude Singh & Ors. Vs. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Ude Singh & Ors. Vs. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Clarifies that mere allegations of harassment are insufficient unless actions compelled the suicide; considers the psyche of the deceased and whether the accused created a situation with no other option.

rules.case_name: S.S. Cheena Vs. Vijay Kumar Mahajan and Anr.
rules.reference: S.S. Cheena Vs. Vijay Kumar Mahajan and Anr.
rules.relevance: Holds that abetment requires a positive act and clear mens rea; mere harassment without intent to push the deceased to suicide is insufficient.

rules.case_name: Chitresh Kumar Chopra v. State (Government of NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: Chitresh Kumar Chopra v. State (Government of NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: Established that 'instigation' involves goading, urging forward, or provoking, and that a continued course of conduct creating circumstances where the deceased has no option but to commit suicide can amount to instigation.

rules.case_name: Swamy Prahaladdas v. State of MP. & Anr
rules.reference: Swamy Prahaladdas v. State of MP. & Anr
rules.relevance: Distinguished on facts; held that casual remarks in the heat of the moment do not constitute instigation, unlike the persistent harassment in the present case.

rules.case_name: Madan Mohan Singh v. State of Gujarat & Anr.
rules.reference: Madan Mohan Singh v. State of Gujarat & Anr.
rules.relevance: Distinguished on facts; held that a one-time occurrence of harsh rebuke by a superior does not constitute abetment, unlike the prolonged harassment in the present case.

rules.case_name: State of M.P. vs. Bhooraji and Others
rules.reference: State of M.P. vs. Bhooraji and Others
rules.relevance: Interprets 'failure of justice' in the context of Section 465 CrPC, supporting the view that proceedings should not be axed down merely for error unless justice fails.

rules.case_name: Nanjappa Vs. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: Nanjappa Vs. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: Clarifies that Section 19(3) bars appellate/revisional interference but does not prevent the Special Judge from discharging an accused if sanction is invalid; emphasizes that objections should be raised at the earliest stage.

rules.case_name: Mrs. Rupan Deol Bajaj v. Kanwar Pal Singh Gill
rules.reference: Mrs. Rupan Deol Bajaj v. Kanwar Pal Singh Gill
rules.relevance: The court cited this case to support the principle that quashing powers should be exercised sparingly and not to enquire into the reliability of allegations at the preliminary stage.

rules.case_name: Veeraswami v. Union of India
rules.reference: Veeraswami v. Union of India
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to establish that the burden to satisfactorily account for assets lies on the accused during trial, and no pre-FIR hearing is mandated.

rules.case_name: State of Bihar v. P.P. Shanna
rules.reference: State of Bihar v. P.P. Shanna
rules.relevance: The court used this precedent to hold that sanction is an administrative act requiring application of mind, not a quasi-judicial one requiring a hearing, and that mala fides of the informant are of secondary importance.

rules.reference: Possession is sine qua non for permanent injunction
rules.relevance: Confirms that proof of possession is essential for granting a permanent injunction.

rules.case_name: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai & Anr. v. Kamla Mills Ltd.
rules.reference: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai & Anr. v. Kamla Mills Ltd.
rules.relevance: Supports the principle that new grounds cannot be raised for the first time in appeal.

rules.reference: Appellate court cannot interfere with findings of fact unless perverse
rules.relevance: Guides the Supreme Court's review of the High Court's factual findings regarding possession and survey boundaries.

rules.reference: Tamil Nadu City Tenants Protection Act, 1921
rules.relevance: Provides statutory protection to tenants against eviction, subject to valid termination of tenancy.

rules.reference: Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921
rules.relevance: Mandates notice before eviction suit; the court held this does not apply when the tenant denies the title of the person claiming to be the landlord.

rules.reference: Tariff Policy (Revised 2016)

rules.case_name: Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co.
rules.reference: Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co.
rules.relevance: Established that impossibility under Section 56 includes impracticability if the foundation of the agreement is upset, but not mere commercial hardship.

rules.reference: Power Purchase Agreements

rules.reference: Power Purchase Agreements
rules.relevance: Defined 'Law' as laws in force in India, restricting 'change in law' claims to Indian law.

rules.reference: Electricity Act, 2003
rules.relevance: The court interpreted 'composite scheme' to mean generation and sale in more than one State, establishing CERC jurisdiction.

rules.case_name: Samar Bahadur Singh v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Samar Bahadur Singh v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Held that acquittal in a criminal case has no bearing on departmental proceedings due to different standards of proof.

rules.case_name: Inspector General of Police v. S. Samuthiram
rules.reference: Inspector General of Police v. S. Samuthiram
rules.relevance: Clarified that unless an accused is 'honourably acquitted', the acquittal does not automatically lead to reinstatement in service.

rules.case_name: Ajit Kumar Nag vs. General Manager (PJ), Indian Oil Corporation Ltd.
rules.reference: Ajit Kumar Nag vs. General Manager (PJ), Indian Oil Corporation Ltd.
rules.relevance: Established that acquittal does not preclude disciplinary action, but such action cannot be mala fide and must comply with natural justice; bias renders proceedings a nullity.

rules.case_name: State of Rajasthan v. B.K. Meena
rules.reference: State of Rajasthan v. B.K. Meena
rules.relevance: Clarified that while simultaneous proceedings are generally permissible, it is advisable to stay departmental proceedings if the criminal charge is grave and involves identical facts to prevent prejudice.

rules.reference: Standard of judicial review in departmental enquiries

rules.reference: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
rules.relevance: Defines the offence of penetrative sexual assault and prescribes the punishment, including a minimum sentence of five years, which the court considered in evaluating the adequacy of the trial court's sentence.

rules.case_name: Surjit Singh and others vs. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Surjit Singh and others vs. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Established that a High Court cannot enhance a sentence without issuing notice to the appellants to show cause, adhering to rules of natural justice.

rules.relevance: Disputes between rival tenderers are essentially commercial; judicial interference is warranted only if the process is vitiated by mala fides, unreasonableness, or arbitrariness, or if substantial public interest is involved.

rules.case_name: Raunaq International Ltd. Vs. I. V.R. Construction Ltd. & Ors.
rules.reference: Raunaq International Ltd. Vs. I. V.R. Construction Ltd. & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that contract awards are commercial transactions and courts should not intervene under Article 226 unless there is a substantial element of public interest or mala fides.

rules.reference: Circular No. STA/19/4/3 dated 06.12.1993 issued by Assistant Director General (Training), Department of Post
rules.relevance: Mandates that preference must be given to candidates with 'adequate means of livelihood derived from landed property or immovable assets' if otherwise eligible, and specifies that no weightage is given for higher qualifications.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions And Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971
rules.relevance: The Industrial Tribunal declared the strike illegal under this provision, establishing the context for the employer's retaliatory actions.

rules.case_name: Air India Ltd. Vs. Cochin International Airport Ltd. & Ors.
rules.reference: Air India Ltd. Vs. Cochin International Airport Ltd. & Ors.
rules.relevance: Reiterated that while the State must adhere to norms, judicial intervention should be exercised with great caution and only in furtherance of public interest, not merely on legal points.

rules.reference: Notification No. 21/2002-Cus dated 01.03.2002
rules.relevance: This notification provided the concessional duty rate for non-edible crude palm oil used for manufacturing soaps, industrial fatty acids, or fatty alcohol.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Bhatinda District Co-op Milk P. Union Ltd.
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Bhatinda District Co-op Milk P. Union Ltd.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent for the principle that where no limitation period is prescribed, the statutory authority must exercise jurisdiction within a reasonable period.

rules.reference: Notification No. 66/2004-Cus dated 09.07.2004
rules.relevance: This notification amended Notification No. 21/2002-Cus to insert the condition that the goods must be used for the manufacture of soap or industrial fatty acid.

rules.reference: Role of HSN Explanatory Notes
rules.relevance: The court held that HSN Explanatory Notes serve only as a guide for interpreting exemption notifications and do not override the specific conditions of the notification.

rules.reference: Customs (Import of goods at concessional rate of duty for manufacture of excisable goods) Rules, 1996
rules.relevance: Rule 8 governs the recovery of duty when goods are not used for the intended purpose but does not prescribe a specific limitation period.

rules.case_name: Rosy Jacob vs. Jacob A Chakramakkal
rules.reference: Rosy Jacob vs. Jacob A Chakramakkal
rules.relevance: Established that custody orders are temporary and interlocutory, and can be modified if the welfare of the child so demands, even if based on consent.

rules.case_name: Mausami Moitra Ganguli vs. Jayant Ganguli
rules.reference: Mausami Moitra Ganguli vs. Jayant Ganguli
rules.relevance: Held that the welfare of the child may have primacy even over statutory provisions.

rules.reference: No advantage from wrongdoing
rules.relevance: A parent should not gain an advantage by wrongfully removing a child from the jurisdiction of the court that has the most intimate contact with the child.

rules.reference: Comity of nations
rules.relevance: Courts should give due weight to foreign custody orders, especially those passed by consent, to respect the jurisdiction of the child's native country.

rules.case_name: Mrs. Elizabeth Dinshaw v. Arvand M. Dinshaw
rules.reference: Mrs. Elizabeth Dinshaw v. Arvand M. Dinshaw
rules.relevance: Approved the principle that courts must ensure a parent does not gain advantage by wrongdoing and that comity requires giving weight to foreign custody orders.

rules.case_name: Thulia Kali v. The State of Tamil Nadu
rules.reference: Thulia Kali v. The State of Tamil Nadu
rules.relevance: Held that delay in lodging FIR often results in embellishment and requires a satisfactory explanation to avoid doubt about the prosecution case.

rules.case_name: Kattukulangara Madhavan (dead) through LRs. v. Majeed and Ors.
rules.reference: Kattukulangara Madhavan (dead) through LRs. v. Majeed and Ors.
rules.relevance: Laid down tests to determine if an accused shared the common object of an unlawful assembly based on their conduct and knowledge.

rules.case_name: Arjun Marik & Ors. v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Arjun Marik & Ors. v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Clarified that Section 157 Cr.P.C. requires sending the report forthwith to avoid improvement in the prosecution story and to enable the Magistrate to watch the investigation.

rules.case_name: Kunju Muhammed Alias Khumani & Anr. v. State of Kerala
rules.reference: Kunju Muhammed Alias Khumani & Anr. v. State of Kerala
rules.relevance: Reiterated that delay in sending the FIR to the Magistrate without a satisfactory explanation creates serious doubt about the prosecution case.

rules.case_name: Masalti v. State of UP
rules.reference: Masalti v. State of UP
rules.relevance: Established the rule that in cases of mob violence, it is safe to examine that at least two persons depose about the presence of an accused.

rules.case_name: Centre for Environmental Law, World Wide Fund-India v. Union of India
rules.reference: Centre for Environmental Law, World Wide Fund-India v. Union of India
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to affirm that the National Wildlife Action Plan has statutory status and must be implemented with an ecocentric approach.

rules.case_name: S. Jagannath v. Union of India
rules.reference: S. Jagannath v. Union of India
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to interpret the Polluter Pays Principle, extending liability to include the cost of restoring environmental degradation.

rules.case_name: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India
rules.reference: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to establish that environmental justice requires an ecocentric approach rather than an anthropocentric one.

rules.reference: Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980
rules.relevance: The court considered the requirement of forest clearance for non-forestry activities, noting the irregularities in obtaining clearance for the Tiger Safari construction.

rules.reference: Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: The court relied on this provision to determine that construction of zoos and safari parks inside sanctuaries requires prior approval of the National Board, and to distinguish between core and buffer areas.

rules.case_name: Reliance Industries Ltd. v. Collector of Central Excise
rules.reference: Reliance Industries Ltd. v. Collector of Central Excise
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case, noting the order in question was part of adjudication proceedings, whereas the internal order in the present case was not.

rules.case_name: Union of India and another vs. Guwahati Carbon Limited
rules.reference: Union of India and another vs. Guwahati Carbon Limited
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision for the principle that excise law is a complete code and writ courts should not entertain petitions against mere show cause notices.

rules.case_name: GKN Driveshafts (India) Ltd. v. Income Tax Officers and others
rules.reference: GKN Driveshafts (India) Ltd. v. Income Tax Officers and others
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case, noting it pertained to Section 148 of the Income Tax Act which explicitly requires recording reasons before issuing notice, unlike the Central Excise Act.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Central Excise, New Delhi v. Harichand Shri Gopal
rules.reference: Commissioner of Central Excise, New Delhi v. Harichand Shri Gopal
rules.relevance: Constitution Bench held that exemption provisions must be construed strictly and conditions must be complied with; pleas of substantial compliance or intended use are rejected if procedural safeguards are ignored.

rules.case_name: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. Vs. District Magistrate
rules.reference: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. Vs. District Magistrate
rules.relevance: Relied upon to support the view that the legislature intended to confiscate only 'goods' and not immovable property like land and buildings after the omission of Rule 173Q(2).

rules.case_name: Harshad Govardhan Sondagar v. International Assets Reconstruction Company Limited and Ors.
rules.reference: Harshad Govardhan Sondagar v. International Assets Reconstruction Company Limited and Ors.
rules.relevance: Held inapplicable; the court clarified that while notice and hearing are required for certain lessees, the DM/CMM does not adjudicate rights between parties.

rules.case_name: Harshad Govardhan Sondagar v. International Assets Reconstruction Co. Ltd.
rules.reference: Harshad Govardhan Sondagar v. International Assets Reconstruction Co. Ltd.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to hold that the SARFAESI Act does not override the rights of a lessee under a valid lease created prior to the mortgage or in accordance with Section 65A of the TP Act, and clarified that registration is not a mandatory condition for protection.

rules.case_name: Vishal N. Kalsaria v. Bank of India and Ors.
rules.reference: Vishal N. Kalsaria v. Bank of India and Ors.
rules.relevance: Held inapplicable as it dealt with a conflict between the Maharashtra Rent Control Act and SARFAESI Act, not the scope of Section 14 powers.

rules.case_name: NKGSB Cooperative Bank Limited v. Subir Chakravarty & Ors.
rules.reference: NKGSB Cooperative Bank Limited v. Subir Chakravarty & Ors.
rules.relevance: Relied upon to affirm that the act of taking possession under Section 14 is a ministerial step and does not involve quasi-judicial functions.

rules.case_name: M/s R.D. Jain and Co. v. Capital First Ltd. & Ors.
rules.reference: M/s R.D. Jain and Co. v. Capital First Ltd. & Ors.
rules.relevance: Referred to support the view that the District Magistrate's role under Section 14 is ministerial and time-bound, without adjudicatory powers.

rules.case_name: Kari Choudhary v. Most. Sita Devi and Ors.
rules.reference: Kari Choudhary v. Most. Sita Devi and Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment for the principle that rival versions of the same incident can result in two different FIRs investigated by the same agency, and that quashing proceedings merely because a final report was laid in the first FIR is too technical.

rules.reference: Academic Nature of 'First FIR' Controversy
rules.relevance: The court held that when a single common agency (CBI) is directed to investigate all FIRs, the question of which FIR was the 'first' becomes academic and does not bar the investigation.

rules.reference: Independence of Criminal Proceedings
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that the outcome of one criminal investigation (Crime No. 2/2014) does not automatically determine the status of property seized in a different, independent criminal proceeding (CBI cases).

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: These sections govern the disposal of property seized during investigation or trial. The court analyzed whether the order for disposal was validly passed in the specific proceedings where the seizure occurred.

rules.reference: Procedure for Release of Seized Property
rules.relevance: The court established that a claimant must approach the jurisdictional criminal court handling the specific seizure to establish existence and ownership rights for release, rather than relying on writ jurisdiction based on unrelated proceedings.

rules.case_name: Usmanbhai Dawoodbhai Memon v. State of Gujarat
rules.reference: Usmanbhai Dawoodbhai Memon v. State of Gujarat
rules.relevance: Held that High Courts lack jurisdiction to entertain bail applications under Section 439 Cr.P.C. when special statutes like TADA apply, a principle extended to the NIA Act.

rules.case_name: Harikisan v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Harikisan v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Constitution Bench decision holding that communication of grounds of detention under Article 22(5) must be in writing to be effective.

rules.reference: National Investigation Agency Act, 2008
rules.relevance: The court interpreted Section 21 in its entirety to determine that Section 21(4) creates an exception to the exclusion of interlocutory orders in Section 21(1), thereby subjecting bail appeals to the Division Bench requirement of Section 21(2).

rules.reference: Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967
rules.relevance: Mandates that an officer arresting a person shall inform him of the grounds for such arrest. The court held this is pari materia with Section 19(1) of the PMLA.

rules.reference: National Investigation Agency Act, 2008
rules.relevance: Empowered Special Courts with all powers of a Court of Session, including the power to grant bail.

rules.case_name: Dena Bank (Now Bank of Baroda) vs. C. Sivakumar Reddy and Another
rules.reference: Dena Bank (Now Bank of Baroda) vs. C. Sivakumar Reddy and Another
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to hold that additional documents acknowledging debt (like balance sheets and OTS proposals) can be introduced at the appellate stage and constitute valid acknowledgments under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.

rules.case_name: Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited vs. Bishal Jaiswal and Another
rules.reference: Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited vs. Bishal Jaiswal and Another
rules.relevance: The court cited this case to support the proposition that a balance sheet acknowledging debt is a relevant document for calculating limitation under Section 18.

rules.reference: Distinction between Acknowledgment and Promise
rules.relevance: Section 18 of the Limitation Act requires acknowledgment within the limitation period, whereas Section 25(3) of the Contract Act allows a promise to pay a time-barred debt to create a fresh cause of action.

rules.case_name: Dena Bank vs. C. Shivakumar Reddy and Another
rules.reference: Dena Bank vs. C. Shivakumar Reddy and Another
rules.relevance: Clarified that Babulal was fact-specific and reaffirmed that limitation for Section 7 petitions can be calculated from the date of a recovery certificate or acknowledgment.

rules.case_name: Babulal Vardharji Gurjar vs. Veer Gurjar Aluminium Industries Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
rules.reference: Babulal Vardharji Gurjar vs. Veer Gurjar Aluminium Industries Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
rules.relevance: The NCLAT relied on this to bar the petition, but the Supreme Court distinguished it as fact-specific, noting it did not preclude the application of Section 18 or other accrual points in different contexts.

rules.reference: West Bengal Primary School Teachers Recruitment Rules, 2016
rules.relevance: Rule 8 mandates a comprehensive selection procedure involving evaluation of academic qualifications, training, TET performance, extra-curricular activities, viva-voce, and aptitude tests. The court held that directing appointments based solely on TET ranks violates this statutory procedure.

rules.reference: West Bengal Primary School Teachers Recruitment Rules, 2016
rules.relevance: Rule 12 stipulates that the validity of a panel or Merit List is one year from the date of approval. The court relied on this to determine that the 2021 Merit List expired on 15.02.2022.

rules.case_name: Union of India and Others Vs. O. Chakradhar
rules.reference: Union of India and Others Vs. O. Chakradhar
rules.relevance: Holds that if irregularities are widespread and segregation of tainted candidates is impossible, the entire selection process may be cancelled without individual show-cause notices.

rules.case_name: State of Bihar v. Mohd. Kalimuddin
rules.reference: State of Bihar v. Mohd. Kalimuddin
rules.relevance: Held that successful candidates do not acquire an indefeasible right to appointment unless the relevant rules indicate otherwise, and the State's refusal to appoint from an expired panel is not arbitrary.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. B. Valluvan
rules.reference: Union of India v. B. Valluvan
rules.relevance: Confirmed that the life of a panel is ordinarily one year and courts do not extend it unless statutory rules permit; once exhausted or expired, it cannot be enforced.

rules.case_name: Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India
rules.reference: Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Held that criminal defamation is a private offence requiring a complaint by the aggrieved person; no FIR can be filed or investigation initiated by police.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Stipulates that prosecution for defamation requires a complaint by the aggrieved person; no FIR can be registered for this offence.

rules.case_name: P. Chidambaram v. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.reference: P. Chidambaram v. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.relevance: Held that courts should not monitor the investigation process or dictate the nature of questions asked by the investigating agency.

rules.reference: Consolidation of investigations
rules.relevance: The principle that where FIRs are based on similar allegations and common informants, consolidating the investigation under one agency (SIT) meets the ends of justice and avoids harassment.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: The Court emphasized that arrest is not routine and must be justified by specific conditions such as preventing further offences, tampering with evidence, or influencing witnesses.

rules.reference: Service on authorized representative
rules.relevance: Service of an arbitral award on a party who is the head of the family and has explicitly authorized representation for other family members constitutes valid service on those members.

rules.reference: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
rules.relevance: This section mandates that a signed copy of the arbitral award shall be delivered to each party. The court used this to define the substantive nature of delivery and receipt.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra and Ors. v. Ark Builders Pvt. Ltd.
rules.reference: State of Maharashtra and Ors. v. Ark Builders Pvt. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Confirmed that the limitation period commences from the date a signed copy of the award is delivered to the party.

rules.case_name: State of Arunachal Pradesh v. Damini Construction Co.
rules.reference: State of Arunachal Pradesh v. Damini Construction Co.
rules.relevance: Established that the phrase 'but not thereafter' in the proviso to Section 34 is mandatory, precluding condonation of delay beyond thirty days.

rules.case_name: Dr. Sheo Shankar Sahay v. Commissioner, Patna Division and Ors.
rules.reference: Dr. Sheo Shankar Sahay v. Commissioner, Patna Division and Ors.
rules.relevance: Supported the principle that limitation does not start until the order is received in the manner prescribed by law, rather than merely communicated or shown.

rules.case_name: Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Limited (UHBVNL) & Anr. v. Adani Power Limited & Ors.
rules.reference: Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Limited (UHBVNL) & Anr. v. Adani Power Limited & Ors.
rules.relevance: Held that carrying cost is payable from the date of the change in law event based on the principle of restitution.

rules.reference: Statutory Guidelines under Section 63 of the Electricity Act (2005)
rules.relevance: Establishes eligibility criteria for fuel arrangements in bidding, requiring firm arrangements for domestic or imported coal.

rules.case_name: Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and Ors.
rules.reference: Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that changes in domestic coal policy constitute a 'Change in Law' and that FSAs are for demonstrating readiness, not determinative of contract terms.

rules.reference: Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs)
rules.relevance: Article 11.3.4 specifies the Late Payment Surcharge (LPS) rate as 2% in excess of SBAR per annum, compounded monthly. Article 11.8.3 applies this LPS rate to delayed payments of supplementary bills, including those for Change in Law.

rules.reference: SHAKTI Policy, 2017
rules.relevance: Confirmed the domestic coal basis of the PPA, as eligibility was restricted to generators with domestic coal-based PPAs.

rules.reference: Effect of non-reply to statutory notice
rules.relevance: Failure to reply to a statutory notice under Section 138 allows the complainant to believe the allegations are accepted, strengthening the case for trial.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Governs the procedure for returning a complaint to a proper court if the Magistrate is not competent to take cognizance.

rules.reference: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
rules.relevance: Prescribes that a complaint must be made within one month of the cause of action, but empowers the Court to take cognizance after the prescribed period if the complainant satisfies the Court of sufficient cause for the delay.

rules.case_name: Ashutosh Ashok Parasrampuria v. Gharrkul Industries Pvt. Ltd.
rules.reference: Ashutosh Ashok Parasrampuria v. Gharrkul Industries Pvt. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Held that High Courts should not quash complaints unless unimpeachable evidence shows the director could not have been concerned with the issuance of cheques.

rules.case_name: Superintendent and Remembrancer of Legal Affairs, West Bengal v. Mohan Singh
rules.reference: Superintendent and Remembrancer of Legal Affairs, West Bengal v. Mohan Singh
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to support the proposition that a second application under inherent powers may be maintainable if there is a changed set of circumstances.

rules.case_name: Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Limited
rules.reference: Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Limited
rules.relevance: Established principles for quashing complaints under Section 482 Cr.P.C., including that proceedings can be quashed if allegations do not prima facie constitute an offence.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: The sections under which the FIR was registered; the court examined whether the facts disclosed a prima facie case for cheating, forgery, and criminal conspiracy.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code
rules.relevance: These sections were invoked for criminal breach of trust and cheating, which the court examined to determine if they were misapplied to a civil dispute.

rules.case_name: Anand Kumar Mohatta v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: Anand Kumar Mohatta v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: Held that a petition for quashing under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is not rendered infructuous merely because a charge-sheet has been filed.

rules.case_name: Pepsi Foods Ltd. & Anr. v. Special Judicial Magistrate & Ors.
rules.reference: Pepsi Foods Ltd. & Anr. v. Special Judicial Magistrate & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that the High Court can exercise jurisdiction under Section 482 to quash proceedings even if an application for discharge is pending before the Magistrate.

rules.reference: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
rules.relevance: Empowers the Central Government to prohibit or restrict the location of industries and processes in different areas, forming the basis for ESZ notifications.

rules.reference: Site-specific delineation of ESZs
rules.relevance: The Court adopted the principle that ESZ width and regulations must vary based on specific ecological and geographical circumstances of each Protected Area, rather than applying a uniform standard.

rules.reference: Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986
rules.relevance: Prescribes the detailed procedure for notifying ESZs, including public consultation, objection handling, and expert committee review, which the Court directed must be strictly followed.

rules.reference: Office Memorandum issued by MoEF & CC
rules.relevance: The Court directed that this memorandum be strictly followed while granting Environmental and Forest Clearances for project activities in ESZs.

rules.reference: Guidelines for declaration of Eco-Sensitive Zones around National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries
rules.relevance: The Court found these Guidelines reasonable and directed that they be strictly followed for determining prohibited, regulated, and permissible activities, emphasizing site-specific regulation over uniform prohibition.

rules.reference: Standard of Satisfaction under Section 319 CrPC
rules.relevance: The court must form a prima facie opinion based on evidence that is more than mere probability but does not require satisfaction that the evidence, if unrebutted, would lead to conviction.

rules.case_name: Brijendra Singh & Ors v. State of Rajasthan
rules.reference: Brijendra Singh & Ors v. State of Rajasthan
rules.relevance: Reiterated that the power under Section 319 CrPC is discretionary and extraordinary, to be exercised sparingly only when strong and cogent evidence occurs against a person.

rules.case_name: Labhuji Amratji Thakor & Ors. v. The State of Gujarat & Anr.
rules.reference: Labhuji Amratji Thakor & Ors. v. The State of Gujarat & Anr.
rules.relevance: The court referred to this order to support the view that summoning additional accused based merely on witness statements without substantive evidence is unsustainable.

rules.case_name: Rakesh & Anr. v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Rakesh & Anr. v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Held that 'evidence' in Section 319 is comprehensive and includes prima facie material from examination-in-chief, allowing the power to be exercised before cross-examination is complete.

rules.reference: Standard for exercising power under Section 319 Cr.P.C.
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that summoning an additional accused requires evidence that is more than prima facie but short of satisfaction that unrebutted evidence would lead to conviction, and cannot be based on mere suspicion.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. v. Ashok Kumar Srivastava
rules.reference: State of U.P. v. Ashok Kumar Srivastava
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that if circumstantial evidence is capable of two inferences, the one favoring the accused must be accepted, and great care must be taken in evaluation.

rules.case_name: Chandreshwar Sharma v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Chandreshwar Sharma v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Established that if a court does not grant the benefit of Section 360 Cr.P.C., it must record specific reasons for not doing so; failure to consider this provision is a procedural oversight.

rules.case_name: Ashabai & Anr. Vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Ashabai & Anr. Vs. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Holds that multiple dying declarations must be separately assessed and one cannot be rejected solely due to variations in another.

rules.case_name: Muthu Kutty and another v. State of T.N.
rules.reference: Muthu Kutty and another v. State of T.N.
rules.relevance: Establishes that a conviction can be based solely on a dying declaration if it is trustworthy, reliable, and free from infirmities.

rules.case_name: Dhbir Singh v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Dhbir Singh v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Interprets 'expedient' in Section 4 of the PO Act to require the court to consider the nature of the offence and circumstances before granting probation.

rules.reference: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
rules.relevance: Defines statutory grounds for divorce (cruelty and desertion) which the appellant failed to prove, necessitating the invocation of Article 142.

rules.case_name: Durga Prasanna Tripathy v. Arundhati Tripathy
rules.reference: Durga Prasanna Tripathy v. Arundhati Tripathy
rules.relevance: Cited as authority for affirming divorce and directing alimony under Article 142 due to irretrievable breakdown.

rules.case_name: K. Srinivas Rao v. D.A. Deepa
rules.reference: K. Srinivas Rao v. D.A. Deepa
rules.relevance: Establishes that making unfounded defamatory allegations and filing false complaints against a spouse amounts to mental cruelty.

rules.reference: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
rules.relevance: These provisions provide the statutory grounds for divorce based on cruelty and desertion for a continuous period of not less than two years.

rules.reference: Definition and nature of cruelty in matrimonial law
rules.relevance: The court articulated that cruelty is a question of fact, need not involve direct action or intention to hurt, and must be weighed based on the impact on the spouse's mind.

rules.case_name: Ram Govind Upadhyay v. Sudharshan Singh
rules.reference: Ram Govind Upadhyay v. Sudharshan Singh
rules.relevance: Establishes that bail decisions must consider the nature of accusations, severity of punishment, nature of evidence, and apprehension of witness tampering.

rules.reference: Bail conditions based on apprehension of witness tampering
rules.relevance: The court relied on the principle that bail conditions restricting movement are justified when there is a serious apprehension that the accused will influence witnesses due to their power and influence, especially when past apprehensions have been proven true.

rules.case_name: Kalyan Chandra Sarkar v. Rajesh Ranjan
rules.reference: Kalyan Chandra Sarkar v. Rajesh Ranjan
rules.relevance: Held that mere long incarceration does not entitle an accused to bail if the offense is severe and there are allegations of tampering with witnesses or subverting justice.

rules.reference: Expedition of trial in serious cases
rules.relevance: The court held that early conclusion of trial enhances faith in the justice delivery system and that attempts to delay trial must be dealt with strictly to prevent further opportunities for witness influence.

rules.case_name: Vipan Kumar Dhir v. State of Punjab and Anr.
rules.reference: Vipan Kumar Dhir v. State of Punjab and Anr.
rules.relevance: The court used this case to explain the impact of supervening circumstances, such as interference in the administration of justice, warranting bail cancellation.

rules.case_name: ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India
rules.reference: ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India
rules.relevance: Established that writ petitions are maintainable for asserting contractual rights against the State, even if an arbitration clause exists, provided the state's action is arbitrary or unfair.

rules.reference: Demerger Scheme
rules.relevance: The specific demerger scheme executed by APIIC and TSIIC apportioned liabilities based on the location of the project site.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. v. Hari Ram
rules.reference: State of U.P. v. Hari Ram
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to interpret 'deemed vesting' versus 'de facto possession' under the Repeal Act, holding that actual possession is required for the saving clause to apply.

rules.reference: Andhra Pradesh Reorganization Act, 2014
rules.relevance: Governed the apportionment of assets and liabilities of corporations like APIIC between the successor states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

rules.reference: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999
rules.relevance: The court considered whether pending proceedings abated under this section, distinguishing between land where possession was taken and where it was not.

rules.reference: Indian Police Service (Fixation of Cadre Strength) Regulations, 1955
rules.relevance: Determines the strength and composition of cadres, including deputation reserves. The court held these are subordinate to Cadre Rules and do not confer rights on service members.

rules.reference: Conditions for extending benefit of concluded decision to non-parties
rules.relevance: The court laid down four specific circumstances under which the benefit of a concluded decision extends to those who did not approach the court: (a) representative capacity, (b) declaratory relief for a category, (c) quashing of general rules without restriction, or (d) express direction by the court. None applied here.

rules.case_name: Smt. Santosh Kapoor and Others v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.reference: Order dated 07.07.1992 in O.A. No. 1455 of 1991
rules.relevance: The court interpreted this order to find that it directed benefits only for the specific applicants in that case and did not expressly extend benefits to non-parties like the respondents in the present appeal.

rules.case_name: A. P. Sharma v. Union of India
rules.reference: A. P. Sharma v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Upheld the validity of similar seniority rules in the IAS, supporting the validity of Rule 3(3)(b) of the IPS Seniority Rules.

rules.case_name: K. I. Shephard and others v. Union of India and others
rules.reference: K. I. Shephard and others v. Union of India and others
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this precedent, holding that its principle of extending benefits to non-parties applies only in specific circumstances (e.g., representative capacity or declaratory relief), which were not present here.

rules.case_name: Haryana Financial Corporation and Anr. Vs. Kaifash Chandra Ahuja
rules.reference: Haryana Financial Corporation and Anr. Vs. Kaifash Chandra Ahuja
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to establish that non-supply of an inquiry officer's report does not ipso facto nullify proceedings; the delinquent must plead and prove prejudice.

rules.case_name: State Bank of Patiala and Ors Vs. S.K. Sharma
rules.reference: State Bank of Patiala and Ors Vs. S.K. Sharma
rules.relevance: The court relied on the principle that violation of procedural provisions does not automatically vitiate an enquiry unless it falls under 'no notice', 'no opportunity', or 'no hearing' categories, or causes specific prejudice.

rules.case_name: State Bank of India and Ors Vs. S. N. Goyal
rules.reference: State Bank of India and Ors Vs. S. N. Goyal
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment which distinguished the D.C. Aggarwal case, supporting the view that non-supply of CVC reports does not vitiate proceedings if not relied upon.

rules.reference: Principle of Natural Justice and Proof of Prejudice
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that a breach of procedural rules or natural justice does not automatically vitiate disciplinary proceedings unless the employee proves that the breach caused actual prejudice to their defense.

rules.case_name: State Bank of India and Ors. Vs. D. C. Aggarwal and Anr.
rules.reference: State Bank of India and Ors. Vs. D. C. Aggarwal and Anr.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Rules, 1961
rules.relevance: The court held that the borrower failed to apply to set aside the sale within 30 days on grounds of material irregularity or fraud, and that no sale can be set aside unless substantial injury is shown.

rules.case_name: Sundaram Finance Limited v. Abdul Samad
rules.reference: Sundaram Finance Limited v. Abdul Samad
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to hold that Sections 38 and 39 of the CPC do not apply to deemed decrees from arbitration-like proceedings, allowing execution in any court with jurisdiction.

rules.reference: Deemed decree execution jurisdiction
rules.relevance: The court established that for orders deemed decrees under special statutes (like the Gujarat Co-operative Societies Act), the strict transfer requirements of CPC Sections 38 and 39 do not apply, and execution can be sought in any court having jurisdiction over the judgment debtor or property.

rules.case_name: Janatha Textiles v. Tax Recovery Officer
rules.reference: Janatha Textiles v. Tax Recovery Officer
rules.relevance: Distinguished because the auction purchaser in the present case was not bona fide due to the illegality of the sale and prior repayment of the debt.

rules.case_name: V.N. Shrikhande v. Anita Sena Fernandes
rules.reference: V.N. Shrikhande v. Anita Sena Fernandes
rules.relevance: Distinguished as it pertained to the Consumer Protection Act with a specific negative legislative mandate against delayed complaints, unlike the KCS Act.

rules.case_name: Noor Aga vs. State of Punjab and Anr.
rules.reference: Noor Aga vs. State of Punjab and Anr.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to establish that Section 35 imposes a heavy reverse burden and applies only after the prosecution discharges the initial burden to prove foundational facts.

rules.case_name: Kamal Singh Vs. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Kamal Singh Vs. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: The State relied on this precedent to argue that non-compliance with Section 42 does not vitiate the case if no prejudice is caused to the accused. The court distinguished the facts regarding sample collection from this principle.

rules.case_name: Mukesh Singh v. State (Narcotic Branch)
rules.reference: Mukesh Singh v. State (Narcotic Branch)
rules.relevance: Overruled Mohan Lal v. State of Punjab, clarifying that the identity of the complainant and investigator is not fatal if distinct or under the current legal position.

rules.case_name: Madan Lal v. State of H.P.
rules.reference: Madan Lal v. State of H.P.
rules.relevance: Defined 'possession' as a polymorphous term that can be constructive, involving power and control.

rules.case_name: State of H.P. v. Pawan Kumar
rules.reference: State of H.P. v. Pawan Kumar
rules.relevance: Clarified that 'person' in Section 50 means a human being, excluding bags or vehicles carried by them.

rules.reference: Central Excise Tariff Act
rules.relevance: Establishes that packing or repacking products of sub-heading 3402.90 into smaller packs or adopting treatment to render the product marketable amounts to 'manufacture'.

rules.reference: Central Excise Act, 1944
rules.relevance: Allows for a larger period of limitation for demand if there is fraud, concealment, misstatement, or suppression of facts to evade duty.

rules.reference: Distinction between Manufacture and Valuation
rules.relevance: The court clarified that excisability (whether an activity constitutes manufacture) and valuation are distinct concepts; value addition affects assessable value regardless of whether the process is manufacture.

rules.reference: Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985
rules.relevance: Defines metal waste and scrap. The court ruled this note extends coverage to tariff entries but does not deem the process of generating scrap as 'manufacture' unless expressly stated.

rules.reference: Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985
rules.relevance: Clarifies that Heading 39.25 applies to reservoirs, tanks, vats, and similar containers.

rules.case_name: Bimla Tiwari vs. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Bimla Tiwari vs. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Reiterated that criminal law processes cannot be utilized for arm-twisting or money recovery, especially in private disputes.

rules.case_name: Munish Bhasin vs. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: Munish Bhasin vs. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: Established that conditions for anticipatory bail must not be freakish, harsh, onerous, or excessive.

rules.reference: Criminal proceedings are not for recovery of civil dues
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that bail conditions should not facilitate the recovery of money alleged to be cheated in private disputes, distinguishing this from cases involving public money.

rules.case_name: Mahesh Candra vs. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Mahesh Candra vs. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Held that courts cannot decide civil disputes or impose maintenance payments as conditions for anticipatory bail.

rules.case_name: Dilip Singh vs. State of Madhya Pradesh

rules.relevance: Held that criminal proceedings are not for the realization of disputed dues and courts should not act as recovery agents.

rules.reference: Gujarat Control of Terrorism and Organized Crime Act, 2015
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this Act from the Gangsters Act, noting that the former contains specific provisions requiring multiple offences, which are absent in the Gangsters Act.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Control of Organized Crime Act, 1999
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this Act from the Gangsters Act, noting that the former contains specific provisions requiring multiple offences, which are absent in the Gangsters Act.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Gangsters and Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986
rules.relevance: Defines 'gang' to determine if the FIR allegations of violence and intimidation fit the statutory definition.

rules.reference: Jurisdiction of High Court under Article 226 regarding FIRs

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Gangsters and Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986
rules.relevance: Defines 'gangster' to assess the applicability of the Act to the appellant.

rules.reference: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881

rules.reference: Negotiable Instruments (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2002

rules.case_name: Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed & Anr.
rules.reference: Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed & Anr.
rules.relevance: Clarifies the requirements for service of notice, emphasizing that actual communication is imperative and that deemed service rules apply primarily to postal service.

rules.reference: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
rules.relevance: Mandates that a complaint be made within one month of the cause of action arising, but allows the court to take cognizance after the prescribed period if the complainant satisfies the court that he had sufficient cause for not making the complaint within such period.

rules.case_name: Maria Cristina De Souza v. Amria Zurana Pereira Pinto
rules.reference: Maria Cristina De Souza v. Amria Zurana Pereira Pinto
rules.relevance: Distinguished between the substantive right of appeal and the procedural nature of the forum where the appeal is lodged.

rules.reference: Retrospectivity of Procedural Law

rules.case_name: New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Smt. Shanti Mishra
rules.reference: New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Smt. Shanti Mishra
rules.relevance: Established that a change of forum is a matter of procedure and generally operates retrospectively unless a contrary intention is shown.

rules.reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019
rules.relevance: Referenced as pari materia provisions to confirm that appeals to the Supreme Court are restricted to orders passed in the NCDRC's original jurisdiction.

rules.reference: Consumer Protection Act, 1986

rules.reference: Court's focus on child welfare rather than parental disputes

rules.case_name: Nithya Anand Raghavan v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: Nithya Anand Raghavan v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: Reiterates that the best interest of the child is paramount and foreign orders must yield if repatriation causes harm, but distinguishes cases where no harm is shown.

rules.case_name: V. Ravi Chandran v. Union of India
rules.reference: V. Ravi Chandran v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Supports summary jurisdiction to return a child to their native country if removal was contrary to foreign court orders.

rules.reference: Juvenile Justice (Care & Protection) Act, 2015
rules.relevance: Defines 'best interest of the child' as the basis for decisions regarding the child's welfare.

rules.reference: Preference of a mature minor
